n: Offer, voluntarily, without any command. Some sacrifices were of precept, Exodus xxii. 29. (Menochius) --- These first chapters are addressed to the people; the 6th [chapter] from ver. 9, to the priests. Oxen, goats, and sheep, pigeons, and turtles, were to be offered in sacrifice, and small birds also, in the purification of lepers, (chap. xiv. 4,) as they might easily be procured. (Calmet) --- By sacrifice, we testify the dominion of God over all. They were offered by the patriarchs, and by all nations. God requireth that the victim should be without blemish, and slain with certain ceremonies wisely ordained, Psalm ciii. 24. (Worthington) --- A sacrifice. Hebrew korban, a present of any sort, Mark vii. --- Sheep and goats, ver. 10. The same term, tson, signifies both. (Menochius)

A holocaust. That is, a whole burnt-offering; (olocauston) so called, because the whole victim was consumed with fire; and given in such manner to God as wholly to evaporate, as it were, for his honour and glory; without having any part of it reserved for the use of man. The other sacrifices of the Old Testament were either offerings for sin, or peace-offerings: and these latter again were either offered in thanksgiving for blessings received, or by way of prayer for new favours or graces. So that sacrifices were then offered to God for four different ends or intentions, answerable to the different obligations which man has to God: 1. By way of adoration, homage, praise, and glory, due to his divine Majesty. 2. By way of thanksgiving for all benefits received from him. 3. By way of confessing and craving pardon for sins. 4. By way of prayer and petition for grace and relief in all necessities. In the New Law we have but one sacrifice, viz. that of the body and blood of Christ: but this one sacrifice of the New Testament perfectly answers all these four ends; and both priests and people, as often as it is celebrated, ought to join in offering it up for these four ends. (Challoner) (St. Augustine, City of God viii. 17.; St. Chrysostom in Psalm xcv.) --- We have an altar, (Hebrews xiii. 10,) on which the unbloody sacrifice is offered, (Matthew xxvi. 25,) as the blood of Christ was on the cross, Hebrews ix. 25. (Worthington)

Victim. To transfer all the curses due to him upon it, (Eusebius, Demon. i. 10,) and to testify that he gives it up entirely for the honour of God. (Lyranus) --- The Egyptians cut off the head of the victim, and vented upon it imprecations, begging that the gods would discharge upon it all the evils which they had deserved. Then they sold it to some foreigner, or threw it into the Nile. (Herodotus ii. 39.) All nations seem to have acknowledged, that life should be given for life. Hanc animam vobis pro meliore damus: (Ovid, Fast. i.) and they had holocausts, in imitation of the Hebrews. (Bochart) --- Expiation. Hebrew, "it shall be accepted for him to make atonement for him," provided he be in proper dispositions. (Menochius) --- The primary intention of the holocaust was to honour God: but this insured his favour also, and pardon. (Du Hamel)

He, by the hands of the priests, (chap. x. 1,) as the Septuagint express it, "they shall immolate;" (Menochius) though we might infer from this text, that the person who offered the victim, had to slay it; (Calmet) while the priests alone could pour the blood upon and around the altar. Without the effusion of blood remission is not made, Hebrews ix. 22. (Haydock)
They. Regularly the Levites performed this office. The skin belonged to the priest, chap. vii. 8. (Calmet)

Fire. Hebrew and Septuagint place the fire first, then the wood. It was the sacred fire which was never extinguished, but removed from the altar in marches, (chap. iv. 13,) perhaps in a censer or pan. (Haydock)
All things, &c. Hebrew pador, may signify the fat, or the trunk of the animal. (Calmet)

Sweet. Not that the Deity can take delight in sweet odours: but he is pleased with the devotion of men. For their advancement in piety, he required these sacrifices; 1. to keep the people from idolatry; 2. to teach them to consecrate their body and effects to him, as well as their souls, to serve justice unto sanctification; (Romans vi. 19; John iv. 24) as without the help of exterior observances, the mind will hardly rise to the contemplation of truth; 3. to prefigure the greater mysteries of the Christian religion, of which the law was only a shadow, incapable of conferring justifying grace. (John i. 17; Galatians iii. 11.) (Worthington) --- The law was our pedagogue, in Christ, that we might be justified by faith, Galatians iii. 24.

Male. Lyranus seems to have read "a year old," in the Vulgate. But it is not found in the Hebrew or in any version. It may have been taken from Exodus xii. 5, where the paschal lamb must be a male of one year. --- Blemish. The Septuagint add, "and he shall put his hand upon its head." (Haydock)

Pigeons. Hebrew and Septuagint say nothing about the age; though the Rabbins assure us, that old turtles and young pigeons were to be immolated, as being more excellent. God requires only what each person may easily procure. This third species of holocaust was chiefly intended for the poor, chap. xii. 8. But if they could not afford even this, they might offer flour, chap. ii.
The neck. Some say, without pulling the head off (Grotius); which the Rabbins deny. (Calmet)
Throat. Hebrew mierath, is rendered "the crop and its contents," by the Chaldean, Syriac, and Samaritan.

Pinions, as if it were to be roasted. Eusebius remarks, that the pagans plunged their birds into the sea, then poured the blood round the altar, and afterwards burnt them. Abram did not divide the birds, Genesis xv. 10. (Calmet) --- Oblation. Hebrew, "made by fire;" or which must be all consumed, except the crop and feathers. (Haydock)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 1

Just as "in the last days" the Word of God, clothed with flesh from Mary, came forth into this world, and one thing indeed was that which was seen in him, another that which was understood — for the appearance of the flesh in him lay open to all, but the recognition of his divinity was granted to few and to the elect —, so also, when through the prophets or the lawgiver the Word of God is brought forth to men, it is not brought forth without fitting garments. For as there it is covered by the veil of the flesh, so here by the veil of the letter, so that the letter indeed is looked upon as flesh, but the spiritual sense lying hidden within is perceived as divinity. Such, then, is what we now also find as we unroll the book of Leviticus, in which the rites of sacrifices and the diversity of victims and the ministries of the priests are described. But these things according to the letter, which is as it were the flesh of the Word of God and the garment of his divinity, perhaps both the worthy may look upon or hear and the unworthy also. But "blessed are those eyes" which see the divine Spirit concealed within under the veil of the letter; and blessed are those who bring pure ears of the inner man to hear these things. Otherwise, in these discourses they will plainly perceive "the letter that kills." For if, following the simple understanding of even certain of our own people, and without any — as they are wont to laugh at us — trick of word or cloud of allegory, I take up the voice of the lawgiver, then I, a churchman living under the faith of Christ and placed in the midst of the Church, am compelled by the authority of the divine precept to sacrifice bull-calves and lambs and to offer fine flour with frankincense and oil. For this is what they do who force us to be slaves to the history and to keep the letter of the law. But it is time for us to use against the wicked elders the words of holy Susanna, which they indeed, repudiating the history of Susanna, cut out of the catalogue of the divine volumes, but which we both receive and, opportunely, bring forth against them, saying: "Straits are upon me on every side." For if I consent to you, to follow the letter of the law, "it will be death to me"; but if I do not consent, "I shall not escape your hands. But it is better for me, without any deed, to fall into your hands than to sin in the sight of the Lord." Let us therefore, we too, if it is thus necessary, fall into your detractions, provided only that the Church, now turned to Christ the Lord, may know the truth of the Word of God covered under the covering of the letter; for so the Apostle also said, that: "if anyone shall be turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away; for where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." Therefore the Lord himself, the Holy Spirit himself, must be entreated by us, that he may deign to take away every mist and every darkness which, thickened by the filth of sins, obscures the sight of our heart, so that we may be able to contemplate the spiritual and wonderful understanding of his law, according to him who said: "Uncover my eyes, and I will consider the wonders of your law." Therefore, as briefly as we can, let us touch upon a few things out of many, not so much striving after the explanation of individual words — for to do this belongs to one who writes at leisure — but bringing forth the things that pertain to the edification of the Church; that we may rather give the hearers occasions of understanding than pursue a breadth of expositions, according to that which is written: "Give occasion to the wise man, and he will be the wiser."
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

And first I should like to see what this distinction is: that of one it says that "a man" offers, of another that "a soul" offers, of another "the high priest", of another "the synagogue", of another "one soul from the people of the land". And I think indeed that "a man" is to be understood as one who, made "to the image and likeness" of God, lives rationally. This man, then, offers to God an offering — a "bull-calf", when he has overcome the pride of the flesh; a "sheep", when he has corrected the irrational and foolish motions; a "kid", when he has conquered wantonness. He offers too "a pair of turtledoves", when he has not been alone, but has joined his mind to the Word of God as to a true spouse, just as this kind of bird is said to keep a single and chaste marriage. He offers too "two young pigeons", when he too has understood the mystery in which "the eyes of the bride" are said to be "like doves" "by the fulnesses of the waters" "and her neck like a turtledove's". These, then, are the offerings of the man, according to what we have expounded above.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 1

The beginning, then, of Leviticus says that "the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony," that he might promulgate to the sons of Israel the laws of sacrifices and of offerings, and it says: "If a man offer an offering to God, let him offer from the oxen or the flock," that is, lambs or kids; "but if from the birds, turtledoves or young of doves." "But if" not a man, but "a soul offer an offering to God, from fine flour," it says, "let him offer unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or indeed fine flour from the pan sprinkled with oil, or from the griddle likewise kneaded in oil." Then next we are taught that nothing "leavened" ought at all to be offered at the altar of God, nor should "honey" anywhere be mixed with the sacrifices, but every sacrifice or offering should be salted with "salt." In the second place he gave precept concerning the "sacrifices of the first-fruits," which he commands to be offered to the Lord "fresh, roasted," well purged. After these things, under the same content of the law, there is joined the matter of the "peace offerings," first "from the oxen," second "from the sheep," in which nevertheless it is permitted, whether in "lambs" or in "kids," to offer either "females" or "males," and he decrees that nothing besides these animals is to be offered in the peace offerings. But let us go back a little and see, first of all, what it is that he says: "a man from among you, if he offer an offering," as though indeed some other than a man could offer. And surely it would have sufficed to say: if any one of you offer an offering; but now he says: "a man from among you, if he offer an offering"; while in what follows he says: "but if a soul offer an offering." Further, in the later passages, when the Lord speaks a second time to Moses and gives command concerning the sacrifices to be offered for sin, he says thus: "If the high priest shall have sinned, let him offer this and that." Or "if the whole synagogue shall have sinned," or "if the ruler shall have sinned," or if "one soul shall have sinned," it is commanded to each several one what they are to offer. What then? Do we think this distinction of persons to be empty, that one thing is commanded to be offered under the designation of "man," another under that of "soul," another under that of "high priest," another under that of "synagogue," and yet another under the name of "ruler" or of "one soul"? I, meanwhile, according to the smallness of my understanding, judge that in this place "the man" — whom he named and set first of all for offering an offering to God — is to be understood as the whole human race, and that he is called man who offers as a "whole burnt offering" a "bull-calf from the oxen without blemish." But this "bull-calf without blemish" — see whether it is not that "fatted calf" which the father slaughtered for that son who had perished and was restored to him, and who "had squandered all his substance," and made a great banquet and had joy, so that "the angels rejoiced in heaven over one sinner doing penance." This man, then, who "had perished and was found," since he had nothing of his own substance to offer — for he "had squandered all, living luxuriously" — found this calf, sent indeed from heaven, but coming from the order of the patriarchs and the linked successions of the generations from Abraham; and therefore he did not say a calf and remain silent, so that any commanded calf might seem meant, but a calf from the oxen, that is, coming from the generation of the patriarchs. And it is "a male without blemish." He is truly "a male" who knows not sin, which is of feminine frailty. He alone, therefore, is "male," he alone is "without blemish," who "did no sin, nor was guile found in his mouth," and who, "accepted before the Lord," is offered "at the door of the tabernacle." "At the door of the tabernacle" is not within the door, but outside the door. For Jesus was outside the door, because "he came unto his own, and his own received him not." He did not, therefore, enter that tabernacle to which he had come, but "at the door" of it he was offered as a "whole burnt offering," because he suffered "outside the camp." For those wicked "husbandmen also cast the son of the householder, when he came, forth outside the vineyard and killed him." This, then, is what is offered "at the door of the tabernacle, accepted before the Lord"; and what is so "accepted" as the victim of Christ, "who offered himself to God"?
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 1

But if you wish to incline these things also to the moral level, you too have a "calf" which you ought to offer. Your flesh is a "calf," and indeed a very proud one; and if you wish to offer it as an offering to the Lord, so as to keep it chaste and modest, lead it "to the door of the tabernacle," that is, where it may be able to receive the hearing of the divine books. Let your offering be "male," let it not know woman, let it spurn concupiscence, let it flee frailty, let it seek nothing dissolute or soft. "Lay" also "your hand upon" your "victim," that it may be acceptable to the Lord, and slaughter it "before the Lord," that is, place upon it the bridle of continence, and do not take away from it the hand of discipline, just as that man laid his hand upon his own flesh who said: "I macerate my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself should be made a reprobate." And slaughter it "before the Lord," mortifying without doubt your "members which are upon the earth." But let "the sons of Aaron the priest" also offer its blood. The priest in you is the mind which is in you, and his sons are your senses, which are rightly called the priest or "the sons of the priest"; for they alone are the ones that understand God and are capable of the knowledge of God. The divine word wishes, therefore, that with a rational sense you offer your flesh to God in chastity, according to what the Apostle says: "a living victim, holy, pleasing to God, your reasonable service." And this is to offer blood to the altar through the priest or the sons of the priest, when one is made chaste both in body and in spirit. For there are also others who indeed offer their flesh as a whole burnt offering, but not through the ministry of the priest. For they do not offer knowingly, nor according to the law which is in the mouth of the priest, but they are indeed chaste in body, while in mind they are found unchaste. For either they are stained by the concupiscence of human glory, or they are polluted by the greed of avarice, or they grow foul with the unhappiness of envy and spite, or they are vexed by the monstrousness of raging hatred and anger. Whoever, then, are such, though they be chaste in body, yet they do not offer their whole burnt offerings through the hands and ministry of the priest. For there is not in them the counsel and prudence which discharges the priesthood before God, but they are among those "five foolish virgins" who were indeed virgins and kept the chastity of the body, but knew not how to store up the "oil" of charity and peace and the remaining virtues "in their vessels," and were therefore shut out from the bridal chamber of the bridegroom, since the continence of the flesh alone cannot reach the Lord's altar, if it is deserted by the remaining virtues and the priestly ministries. And therefore we who read or hear these things, let us give our effort on both sides to be chaste in body, upright in mind, clean in heart, amended in morals, to advance in works, to be watchful in knowledge, to be perfect in faith and in acts, in deeds and in understandings, so that we may deserve to be conformed to the likeness of the victim of Christ, through our Lord Jesus Christ himself, through whom to God the Father almighty, with the Holy Spirit, is "glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 1

And yet: "he shall lay his hand," it says, "upon the head of the victim, and they shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer the blood, and they shall pour out the blood at the altar round about, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony." It can indeed seem to have been said for this reason, that Annas and Caiaphas and the rest were of the sons of Aaron, "all who, taking counsel against Jesus, pronounced him guilty of death" and poured out his blood "around the base of the altar of the tabernacle of testimony." For there the blood is poured out where the altar and its base were, as the Lord himself also said: "because it does not befall a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem." He "placed," then, also "his hand upon the head of the calf," that is, he laid the sins of the human race upon his own body; for he himself is the head of the body of his Church. But this too perhaps happens not without cause, that, when he had said above: "he shall bring it to the door of the tabernacle of testimony," in the later passages he repeats and again says: "to the altar, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," as though it had not sufficed to have designated the same place once under the same narration. Unless perhaps he wished this to be understood, that the blood of Jesus was poured out not only in Jerusalem, where the altar and its base and the tabernacle of testimony were, but that this same blood also sprinkled the heavenly altar, which is in the heavens, where also is "the Church of the firstborn," as the Apostle too says, that: "he made peace through the blood of his cross both for the things that are on earth and for the things that are in the heavens." Rightly, therefore, he names a second time "the altar which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," because Jesus was offered as a victim not only for earthly things but also for heavenly ones; and here indeed for men he poured out the very corporeal matter of his blood, but in the heavenly places, with priests ministering — if there be any there — he immolated the vital power of his body as a kind of spiritual sacrifice. But do you wish to know that there was a twofold victim in him, suited to earthly things and fitted to heavenly ones? The Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: "through the veil, that is, his flesh." And again he interprets the inner veil as "heaven," which Jesus "penetrated," and "now stands before the face of God for us," "always," he says, "living to make intercession for these." If, therefore, two veils are understood, which Jesus entered as a high priest, consequently a twofold sacrifice too must be understood, through which he saved both earthly things and heavenly ones. In short, the things that follow also seem to be fitted more to the heavenly sacrifice than to the earthly.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 1

"And flaying," it says, "the whole burnt offering, they shall divide it limb by limb, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall put fire upon the altar, and shall pile up wood on the fire; and the sons of Aaron the priest shall lay on the divided limbs and the head and the fat and the wood which are upon the altar. But the entrails and the feet they shall wash with water, and the priest shall lay all upon the altar; it is a victim and a sacrifice, an odor of sweetness to the Lord." How the flesh of the Word of God, which here is named a "calf," is flayed, and how it is divided "limb by limb" by the priests, is worth observing. I think that that priest strips off the hide of the "calf" offered as a "whole burnt offering" and draws off the skin by which its limbs are covered, who strips from the Word of God the veil of the letter and lays bare its inner parts, which are the limbs of spiritual understanding; and these limbs of the inner Word he places not in some lowly place, but sets them on high and holy, that is, "upon the altar," when he opens the divine mysteries not to unworthy men who lead a lowly and earthly life, but to those who are the altar of God, in whom the divine fire ever burns and the flesh is ever consumed. Upon such as these, then, this "calf of the whole burnt offering," divided limb by limb, is placed. For he divides the "calf limb by limb" who can explain in order and discourse with fitting distinction what was the progress of one who "touched the fringe" of Christ, but of another who "washed his feet with tears and wiped them with the hairs of the head," and how much more excellent than these it is to have "anointed his head with myrrh"; and also what eminence he has who "reclined upon his breast." To discourse, then, on the causes of each of these, and to fit some things to beginners, other things to those who are already advancing in the faith of Christ, and yet other things to those who are already perfect in his knowledge and love — this is "to have divided the calf limb by limb." But also one who knows how to show what were the beginnings of the law, what progress too was made in the prophets, and what fullness of perfection is held in the Gospels; or who can teach with what "milk" of the word the "little ones" in Christ are to be fed, and with what "herb" of the word "those who are weak in the faith" are to be refreshed, and what also is that "solid and strong food" by which the athletes of Christ are to be fattened; whoever knows how to divide these single things by spiritual reasoning, such a teacher can be seen as that priest who "places upon the altar the whole burnt offering divided into limbs." He also adds "wood" to the altar, that the fire may be quickened and burn, who mingles his discourse not only concerning the corporeal virtues of Christ, but also concerning his divinity. For the divinity of Christ is from above, whither this fire hastens. Fittingly, therefore, the heavenly fire consumed all these things that were done in the body by the Savior, and restored them all to the nature of his divinity. Yet with wood applied this fire is kindled; for up to the wood was the passion of Christ in the flesh. But when he was hung upon the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was ended; for rising from the dead he ascended to heaven, whither the nature of fire shows its course. Whence the Apostle also said, that: "even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him." For the whole burnt offering of his flesh, offered through the wood of the cross, joined earthly things to heavenly and human things to divine. "The entrails" indeed "together with the feet" the word of the precept commands "to be washed with water," announcing the sacrament of baptism under a figurative proclamation. For he washes the "entrails" who purges the conscience; he washes the feet who receives the consummation of the sacrament and knows that "he who is clean has no need except to wash his feet," and that "no one can have a part with Jesus unless he wash his feet."
Homilies on the Gospels 1.18

In very many ceremonies of the law one who needed to be cleansed was ordered to be cleansed by [offering] these [birds]. A pigeon indicates simplicity and a turtledove indicates chastity, for a pigeon is a lover of simplicity and a turtledove is a lover of chastity—so that if by chance one loses its mate it will not subsequently seek another.

h.p: < Previous Chapter ----- Next Chapter > Leviticus ii. Notes & Commenatary:
n: One, (anima). The soul is put to denote the whole person. --- Of sacrifice. Hebrew mincha, which is applied to inanimate things, particularly to flour, "a present of wheat." (Vatable) --- As the other sacrifices have peculiar names, this is barely called sacrifice by the Vulgate. It was instituted, 1. for the poor; 2. to support the ministers of religion; 3. to shew that God was to be honoured with the fruits of the earth; 4. sacrifice being intended as a sort of feast, bread, salt, wine, and oil accompany it; and also incense, which was almost solely reserved for God. (Menochius) --- The person who offered the sacrifice, had to furnish all things belonging to it. The Samaritan and Septuagint add at the end of this verse, "Behold what is the offering of the Lord." Similar words occur, (ver. 6. and 16,) in Hebrew. Sacrifices of flour were the most ancient of all. Ovid (Fast. ii.) says, Farra tamen veteres jaciebant, farra metebant, &c. "Numa taught the people to worship the gods with fruits and flour, and to make supplication with a salted cake." (Pliny, xviii. 2.) Fruge deos colere, & molâ salsâ supplicare. (Calmet)
Memorial. "To worship and celebrate the name of God." (Louis de Dieu.)

Holy of holies. That is, most holy; as being dedicated to God, and set aside by his ordinance for the use of his priests. (Challoner) --- All was to be eaten or consumed in the tabernacle. The high priest offered a gomor full of flour and oil, rather baked, every day, chap. vi. 20. (Calmet)
Out of. The handful, which shall be burnt, shall cause God to remember and grant the request of the offerer, equally as if the whole were consumed. (Menochius)

Without leaven or honey. No leaven or honey was to be used in the sacrifice offered to God: to signify that we are to exclude from the pure worship of the gospel, all double-dealing and affection to carnal pleasures. (Challoner) --- The prohibition of leaven regarded these sacrifices. It was offered with the first-fruits, (chap. xxiii. 17,) and perhaps also in peace-offerings, chap. vii. 13. Honey is here rejected, as incompatible with the other ingredients, to admonish us to lead a penitential life, and to keep at a greater distance from the customs of the pagans, who generally accompanied their oblations with honey, Ezechiel xvi. 18. Herodotus (B. ii.) says, the Egyptians used honey in sacrifice. (Calmet) --- By unleavened bread, the Hebrews were reminded of their flight out of Egypt; and by refraining from honey, they were taught to act like men. (Menochius)

First-fruits, &c., to be voluntarily given to the priests, in honour of God. The honey arising from the dates might also be offered. --- It was little inferior to that of bees. (Josephus, Jewish Wars v. 3.) See Numbers xv. 19.

Salt. In every sacrifice salt was to be used, which is an emblem of wisdom and discretion, without which none of our performances are agreeable to God. (Challoner) --- Salt is not prescribed in the sacrifices of animals. But it was to be used in them, as we learn from the Jews, and from St. Mark ix. 48, Every victim shall be salted. The ancient poets never specify salt in their descriptions of sacrifices. But Pliny assures us, that in his time it was of the greatest authority, and always used in sacrifices, with cakes. Maxime in sacris intelligebatur salis auctoritas, quando nulla conficiuntur sine molâ salsâ. (B. xxxi. 7.) --- Covenant. It is so called, because it was a symbol of the durable condition of the alliance with God, which was renewed in every sacrifice; (Calmet) or it may signify "the salt prescribed" by God: for the law and covenant are often used synonymously. (Menochius) --- Let your speech be always in grace, seasoned with salt, Colossians iv. 6. See Numbers xviii. 19.
And break, &c. Hebrew has simply, "corn beaten out (or ready to be beaten out) of full ears." (Haydock) --- These were to be offered at the Passover. (Du Hamel)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But the offerings of the soul it describes as far inferior. This soul has neither a "bull-calf" nor a "sheep" nor a "kid" to offer to God; but it does not even find "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". It has only "fine flour"; from it, it "offers unleavened loaves from the oven", from it a work made "in the pan" or "mixed with oil on the griddle". Whence it seems to me that the one here called "a soul" is to be understood as that man whom Paul names "the animal (natural) man"; who, even if he is not pressed by sins nor headlong toward vices, nevertheless does not have anything spiritual in him, anything that might figuratively be reckoned the flesh of the Word of God. For thus Paul the Apostle himself says of him that: "the animal (natural) man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is spiritually discerned. But the spiritual man examines all things". This one, then, who is named "a soul", cannot offer all things, because he cannot examine all things; but he offers only "fine flour and unleavened loaves", that is, this common life — placed, for example, in agriculture or in seafaring or in some of the uses of common life; yet even he too offers an offering to God, although he is said "to offer" only "fine flour" merely "sprinkled with oil". For every soul needs the oil of the divine mercy, nor can anyone escape the present life unless the oil of the heavenly compassion be present to him.
LETTER 128.2

They quote the passage which says that "the lips of a strange woman drop as honeycomb," which is sweet indeed in the eater's mouth but is afterward found more bitter than gall. This, they argue, is the reason that neither honey nor wax is offered in the sacrifices of the Lord, and that oil, the product of the bitter olive, is burned in his temple.
HOMILIES ON NUMBERS 27.12

For just as flesh, if it be not sprinkled with salt, however great and choice it be, is corrupted, so also the soul, unless it be in some way salted with continual temptations, immediately is dissolved and grows slack. Whence it is clear that on this account it was said that "every sacrifice shall be salted with salt."
LETTER 125.1

Salt is good, and every offering must be sprinkled with it. Therefore also the apostle has given the commandment: "Let your speech be always with grace, seasoned with salt." But "if the salt have lost his savor," it is cast out.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

In the second place, the oblation "of the first fruits", that is, of the beginnings of the produce, is commanded. And this, if you remember well, the law commands to be done on the day of Pentecost. In which a "shadow" plainly was given to them, but for us the truth was reserved. For on the day of Pentecost, when the sacrifice of prayers had been offered, the Church received the first fruits of the coming "Holy Spirit" of the Apostles. And truly these were fresh, because it was new; whence they were even said to be "filled with new wine". "Roasted with fire". For fiery tongues settled upon each one. "And broken in the middle". For they were broken in the middle, when the letter was separated from the spirit. "And well cleansed". For the presence of the Holy Spirit cleanses all filth, granting remission of sins. The oil of mercy too is poured into this sacrifice, and the frankincense of sweetness, through which we are made "the good odor of Christ".
On Cain and Abel 2.6.19

There are indeed four types of sacrifices that were commended. Whether they were new of new things, or roasted, or divided, or continuous. The new of new things were in the first time of the year, which were valued for their appearance in the firstfruits: but now it has been revealed that they signify those who are renewed through the sacraments of baptism. For this is truly the primitive sacrifice, when each person offers themselves as a victim, and begins with themselves, so that they may later be able to offer their own gift.

n: Peace-offerings. Peace, in the Scripture language, signifies happiness, welfare, or prosperity; in a word, all kind of blessings. Such sacrifices, therefore, as were offered either on occasion of blessings received, or to obtain new favours, were called pacific or peace-offerings. In these some part of the victim was consumed with fire on the altar of God: other parts were eaten by the priests, and the persons for whom the sacrifice was offered. (Challoner) --- Female beasts might here be sacrificed, but not birds. The victims were either offered to praise God for past favours, or to comply with some vow, or were perfectly free, chap. vii. 12. Three sorts of victims, the ox, the sheep, and the goat, denoted all those who served God in innocence, or in the state of penance. (Du Hamel) --- Of these sacrifices "of the perfect," none of the unclean could taste, chap. vii. 20. When only flour or bread was given, the donor received no part again.
Which shall. Hebrew, "which he gives, he shall slay it....the priests shall pour," &c. Yet some assert, that laymen were not allowed to approach the altar.
Fat. All the fat was carefully presented to the Lord. The Persians offered this alone. Omentum in flammâ a pingue liquefaciens. (Catullus, Epig. de Magis.)

Flanks. St. Jerome sometimes translates the Hebrew loins, as the Septuagint and Symmachus do; (Psalm xxxvii. 7) and this Bochart believes is the most proper signification. (Calmet) --- Two is not specified in the Latin, nor little in the Hebrew.

For a. Some translate, "upon the," others "after the burnt-sacrifice;" as if that were always to be offered first, every day. (Calmet) --- But is seems that the peace-offering was an imitation of the holocaust, with respect to the fat, caul, and kidneys, which were to be entirely consumed. (Haydock)
It. Hebrew and Septuagint, "he shall slay," ver. 2, 13. (Calmet)

Whole rump. Septuagint, "the loin without blemish." The tail of the Arabian sheep is extremely large and fat, weighing eight or ten pounds; so that it is necessary to support it on a vehicle. (Busbecque, ep. 3.) The tail was not sacrificed in any other species. (Menochius)

With, &c. Hebrew, "and the two kidneys with their fat by the flanks, and the great lobe of the liver, above the kidneys, shall they take." (Haydock) --- All our affections must be consecrated to God, and our passions kept under. (Du Hamel)
Food, destined for the honour of God, and to be consumed by fire. In other places, God calls these sacrifices his food, and the altar his table. (Chap. xxi. 21.; Malachias i. 7, 12.)

Fat. It is meant of the fat, which by the prescription of the law was to be offered on God's altar: not of the fat of meat, such as we commonly eat. (Challoner) --- This distinction is sufficiently insinuated; (chap. vii. 25,) whence it also appears that the fat, here forbidden, is only that, which, in all sacrifices, appertains to the Lord, ver. 9, 10. The fat which was intermingled with the flesh might be eaten, and even the rest if the animal was not sacrificed. God repeatedly forbids the use of blood, chap. xvii. 13. Yet the Jews abstain from the fat also of all oxen, sheep, and goats; (Josephus, [Antiquities?] iii. 10,) and some, adhering to the words of this text, forbid the use of fat indiscriminately. (Calmet) --- Cornelius a Lapide condemns it, if the animal might be offered in sacrifice, though it were slain at home.

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

After this it speaks of the peace (salutary) offerings, which are offered from animals, that is, from "oxen" or "goats and sheep"; and nothing beyond these is admitted for immolation — not even the birds, which above had been admitted among the offerings to be offered. For this one, who offers the peace offerings, is without doubt already conscious of his own salvation; and therefore he who has arrived at salvation must of necessity offer things that are great and perfect. For thus the Apostle too says: "solid food, however, is for the perfect".
40 Homilies on the Gospels (Homily 25)

And by the precept of the law, the tail of the victim is commanded to be offered in sacrifice. In the tail, of course, is the end of the body; and he sacrifices well who brings the sacrifice of a good work to the end of the required action.

n: Ignorance. To be ignorant of what we are bound to know is sinful: and for such culpable ignorance, these sacrifices, prescribed in this and the following chapter, were appointed. (Challoner) --- Not to be done. Hence the Rabbins admit sins of ignorance, only against the negative precepts. But when God forbids one thing, he commands the contrary; and we may sin by ignorance against any of his ordinances. If the ignorance be voluntary, it enhances the crime; and Aristotle well observes that drunkards, who do an injury, are to be doubly punished, because their fault is voluntary in its cause, (ad Nicom. iii. 7). But if the ignorance were perfectly involuntary, and inculpable, no sacrifice was required; so that God here speaks only of that sort of ignorance which involved some degree of negligence. This fault could not be forgiven without interior good dispositions. The sacrifice only reached to the cleansing of the flesh, (Hebrews ix. 13,) or to screen the culprit from the severity of the law and of the magistrates; (Calmet) though they might help the inward dispositions of the heart, and thus contribute to obtain God's pardon. (Origen; St. Augustine, q. 20) The difference between peccatum and delictum, is not perfectly ascertained. Some think the former word denotes sins of malice, and the latter those of ignorance. Tirinus maintains the contrary, as a more costly sacrifice, he says, is required for the latter. (Haydock)

Anointed. That is, "the high priest," Septuagint. Inferior priests were not anointed, except the sons of Aaron, at the beginning. (Calmet) --- Ignorance in such a one is greatly to be avoided, as it tends to scandalize the people. (Haydock) --- The same ceremonies are prescribed, as on the day of expiation; only the priest did not enter the most holy place. --- Offend, in some smaller matter. If he engaged his brethren in the crime of idolatry, he should die, Deuteronomy xiii. 15. (Calmet) --- Before the solemn unction, he might be expiated, like one of the princes. (Menochius)
Calf. Hebrew par, does not specify the age. (Calmet)
The blood. As the figure of the blood of Christ shed for the remission of our sins; and carried by him into the sanctuary of heaven.

Seven. A number consecrated in Scripture, (Calmet) and not superstitious. (Worthington) --- Apuleius (Met. xi.) mentions it. Septies submerso fluctibus capite. (Calmet) --- Sanctuary, or most holy place. (Menochius)

Ashes of the victims. They were first laid beside the altar of holocausts. By this ceremony, the priest begged that his sins might be removed from the sight of God, (Menochius) by virtue of Christ's sacrifice, who suffered out of the gate of Jerusalem, Hebrews xiii. 13. The high priest was obliged to offer this sacrifice himself, to expiate his own sin, as well as that of the people, Hebrews ix. 7.

Multitude assembled. Septuagint add, "be involuntarily ignorant, and no one of the congregation perceive the truth, (or word,) and shall transgress, by commission or omission, one of all the precepts of the Lord." Such was the offence of Saul and the people, 1 Kings xiv. 33. On these occasions, the elders were to put their hands on the victim, to acknowledge the general offence, if it were not of too heinous a nature to be expiated by sacrifice. See Deuteronomy xiii. 12.
A prince. King, magistrate, general, chief of a tribe, or great family; in a word, one elevated above the rest (Nasi), as appears, Numbers i. 4. and vii. 2.
He. Samaritan and Septuagint read, "they shall have," referring it to the priests.

Him. Moses does not here specify what was to be done with the flesh. But (chap. vi. 26,) he commands it to be given to the priests. (Calmet) --- In the sacrifices for the sins of the multitude, or of the priest, all was consumed; to express a greater detestation of such offences, (Tirinus) and that the priests might derive no benefit from them. (Theodoret, q. 3.; St. Thomas Aquinas i. 2, q. 102, a. 3.) (Worthington) --- Those who offered these victims received no part of them again, nor were oil or incense used; as all delicacies must be rejected by penitents. (Tirinus)
The land. A rustic or plebeian. (Menochius) --- The offences of such might be expiated by the sacrifice of a goat, ewe, lamb, ram, two pigeons, or flour, chap. v. 7. and xi. 15. (Calmet)

Of, &c. One Hebrew manuscript, the Septuagint, and Syriac read, "in the place in which he shall slay the holocaust." The Samaritan has they slay, both here and ver. 24. and 33, which seems the truer reading. (Kennicott)
For a. Hebrew may be "according to, like (Haydock) upon, besides, after the holocausts." (Calmet) See chap. iii. 5.

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

Thereupon the order of the sacrifices is directed to the offering of victims for sins, in which it is said a second time: "the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: whatever soul shall sin before the Lord unwillingly". Rightly does it say "soul" of the one whom it describes as sinning; for it would not have called it spirit, of which it would say that it would sin; but neither would it call this one a man, in whom, with sin intervening, the "image of God" in no way stands firm. It is not, then, the spirit that sins; for "the fruit of the spirit" — as the Apostle describes — "is love, joy, peace, patience", and the rest like these, which are also called "the fruits of life". Finally, elsewhere too he says: "he who sows in the flesh shall from the flesh reap corruption; and he who sows in the spirit shall from the spirit reap eternal life". Since, then, there is one who sows and another in whom it is sown, and it is sown either "in the flesh", when one sins, so that "corruption" be reaped, or "in the spirit", when one lives according to God, so that "eternal life" be reaped — it is established that it is the soul which sows either "in the flesh" or "in the spirit", and that it is the soul which can either rush into sin or be turned back from sin. For the body is its follower to whatever it may choose; and the spirit is its guide to virtue, if it be willing to follow it.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

For "on account of sins not voluntary" it is in general the "soul" that is commanded to offer, but after this the text proceeds through diverse and various persons; and it is commanded that, "if indeed it be the high priest who has transgressed and offers a sacrifice for sin, he should offer a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering, but not by that same rite by which he offered the one for an offering. For of this one he shall place upon the altar of the whole burnt offerings "the fat and the two kidneys with their fat, and the fat that covers the inner parts", only these. "Of its blood" too, "dipping his finger, he sprinkles seven times before the Lord, and anoints from it the horns of the altar of incense. But the rest of the flesh, with the hide and the entrails and the dung, he commands to be burned with fire outside the camp, in a clean place". It must indeed be observed that in the sin of the high priest the lawgiver did not add that he had sinned through ignorance or unwillingly. For ignorance could not befall one who has been advanced in order that he might teach the rest.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But these things have been said in general; now, however, they are divided by kinds. "If the high priest", it says, "who has been anointed, should sin, so as to make the people sin, he shall offer for his own sin a bull-calf from the oxen, without blemish, to the Lord". Both terror and mercy are displayed together in the divine laws. Is nothing, then, after all, safe — not even the high priest? And what high priest? The very one who has been anointed, the very one who kindles the divine altars with the sacred fires, who immolates offerings and peace offerings to God; who intervenes as a certain mediating re-propitiator between God and men — not even he, I say, remains immune from the contagion of sin. But see the mercy of God, and know it more fully from Paul's teaching. For he himself, writing to the Hebrews, says: "for every high priest taken from among men is appointed for men to offer victims to God", and a little later he says: "the law appoints as priests men having weakness", so that they may be able to offer, as for their own weakness, so also for the weakness of the people. You see, then, the dispensation of the divine wisdom. It appointed as priests, not those who could in no way sin — otherwise they would not be men — but those who ought indeed to imitate him "who did no sin", yet "to offer victims first for their own, and then also for the people's transgressions". But what especially is to be admired in a priest of this kind? Not that he should not sin — which cannot be — but that he should acknowledge and understand his own sin. For he never amends who does not think that he has sinned. And at the same time, because he too can more easily pardon those who sin who is himself stung by the consciousness of some weakness of his own. But what is the oblation of the priest "for sin"? "A bull-calf", it says, "for a whole burnt offering". We find in the second place that a "bull-calf" is offered by the high priest "for a whole burnt offering", once for an offering, once "for sin". But the one that is offered for an offering is consumed "upon the altar" of the whole burnt offering. But the one that is offered "for sin" is commanded to be burned "outside the camp, with the hide and the entrails and the dung, in a clean place", only the fat and the kidneys being offered on the altar. Although to divide and distinguish these several matters is both beyond our powers and beyond your hearing, nevertheless we shall attempt to seek out for you some occasions for understanding and to bring them into the open. See, then, whether perhaps Jesus, whom Paul says "made peace" through his blood "not only for the things that are on earth, but also for the things that are in the heavens", is himself this bull-calf, who "in the heavens" indeed was offered not "for sin" but for an offering, but "on the earth", where sin "reigned from Adam until Moses", was offered "for sin". And this is to have suffered "outside the camp" — outside those, I think, the camps which Jacob had seen, the heavenly camps of the angels of God, of which it is written in Genesis: "and Jacob, looking up, saw the camps of God in array, and the angels of God met him, and Jacob said, when he saw them: these are the camps of God". Outside those heavenly camps, then, is this whole earthly place in which we dwell, in which Christ suffered in the flesh. But as for its saying that it is burned "with the dung and the entrails", see whether perhaps, by comparison with the heavenly bodies, this body of human nature is figuratively called dung. For it is earth and taken from earth. But that basket of dung too, which is put at the roots of the fig tree to be cut down, what else does it show but the mystery of the dispensation assumed in a body? Nor yet are the entrails said to be lacking to him. For although he bore the lowly "form of a servant", nevertheless "the fulness of the divinity dwelt in him". Although these things have been discussed boldly, nevertheless the hearing of the faithful ought always to be nourished toward greater things. The same things too are to be understood of the bull-calf of the synagogue.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But in the moral sense this high priest can be seen as that faculty of piety and religion which within us performs, as it were, a certain priesthood, through the prayers and supplications that we pour out to God. If this transgress in anything, it forthwith "makes sin" the whole people of good acts that is within us. For we do nothing of a right work when the guiding sense of good works has declined into what is depraved; and therefore for the amending of this, not any victim whatever, but the sacrifice of "the fatted calf" itself is required. Likewise too the fault of the synagogue — that is, the amending of all the virtues that are within us — is repaired not otherwise than by the mortification of Christ.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

The discourse concerns the sacrifices which are offered by those who have sinned through ignorance or not by will. Hence also in what went before, when we were speaking of the high priest's sacrifice, we observed that it was not written of him that he had been in ignorance. But if anyone remembers well the things that were said, he can say to us that the sacrifice which we said the high priest offered "for sin" we set down as holding the figure of Christ. And it will not seem fitting that Christ, "who knew no sin", should be said to have offered a sacrifice "for sin", even though the matter is transacted through a mystery and the same one is set down both as high priest and as victim. See, therefore, whether we can meet this too in this way: that Christ indeed "did no sin", yet was made "sin for us"; while he who was in the form of God deigns to be in the form of a servant; while he who is immortal dies, and the impassible suffers, and the invisible is seen; and, because for us all either death or all the rest of frailty was brought upon the flesh from the condition of sin, he too, who "was made in the likeness of men and found in fashion as a man", without doubt "for sin", which he had taken up from us, because "he bore our sins", offered "the spotless bull-calf", that is, the uncontaminated flesh, "as a victim to God". But what do we make of what is joined in the sequel? For where it says: "if indeed the high priest who is anointed sins", there is added: "so that he makes the people to sin, he shall offer for his own sin". How then will it fit that through the flesh which Jesus took up from us, he himself, made sin, "made the people to sin"? Listen concerning this too, whether perchance we can answer with some consistency. The passion of Christ confers life on those who believe, but death on those who do not believe. For although through his cross there is salvation for the Gentiles and justification, yet for the Jews there is destruction and condemnation. For so it is written also in the Gospels: "behold, this one is born for the ruin and the resurrection of many". And in this way, through his own sin, that is, through the flesh driven to the cross, in which he had taken up our sins, he indeed freed us who believe from sin, but "the people who did not believe" he made to sin, for whom to the evil of unbelief there was added also the impiety of sacrilege. And in this way that high priest through his own sin "made the people to sin", while, being set in the flesh, he could both be seized and slain. For let us suppose, for example, that if "the Lord of majesty" had not come in the flesh, he would not have reproved the Jews, he would not have been grievous to them even to look upon, he could by no means have been seized nor delivered to death; without doubt "his blood" would never have come "upon them and their children". But because he came in the flesh and was made "sin for us" and could suffer these things, therefore he himself is said to have "made the people to sin", who made it possible for them to sin against him.
Catechetical Lecture 10.11

He is called by two names, Jesus Christ; Jesus because he is a savior, Christ because he is a priest. With this in mind the divinely inspired prophet Moses gave these two titles to two men eminent above all, changing the name of his own successor in the sovereignty, Auses, to Jesus, and giving his own brother, Aaron, the surname Christ, that through these two chosen men he might represent at once the high priesthood and the kingship of the one Jesus Christ who was to come.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

It will now be a great task to pursue the diversities of victims and the rites and varieties of sacrifices, and one belonging to a work far other than that discourse which the common crowd receives in the general assembly. But that we may seem to touch upon some things in passing: almost every victim, indeed, which is offered has something of the form and image of Christ. For every victim is recapitulated in him, so much so that, after "he himself was offered", all the victims ceased which had preceded him in type and "shadow"; concerning which, as far as we could, we showed in what went before how the bull-calf offered by the high priest, whether as an offering or "for sin", held his form. But the "fat", which is offered in the offering, "covering the inward parts" and clinging to the kidneys, can be understood as that holy soul of his which veiled the "inward parts", that is, the secrets of his divinity, but clung to the "kidneys", that is, to the corporeal matter which had been chastely taken up from us; and, set in the middle between the flesh and God, to be sanctified upon the sacred altars and to be made bright by the divine fires, it imposes the nature of the flesh, to be preserved with itself unto the heavens. But that the little kidneys are delivered to the fires — who would doubt that they indicate that there were no motions of the generative parts in Christ? But that "of the blood of the victim the priest" is recorded "to sprinkle seven times before the Lord", evidently the power of the Holy Spirit, of sevenfold grace, is designated under a mystery. The four "horns of the altar", which are anointed "with blood", indicate that the passion of Christ is reported by the four Gospels. As for the caul of the liver which is offered — in the liver anger is slaughtered, in the caul the swift and impetuous force of fury is shown. But the rest of the blood, which "is poured out at the base of the altar", I think designates the form of that grace by which "in the last days", after "the fullness of the Gentiles has entered in", "all Israel" that is left, placed at the last as it were "at the base of the altar", will itself also receive the outpouring of the blood of Christ. But concerning the lambs and the kids, the turtledoves and the doves, and also the "fine flour sprinkled with oil" or baked "in unleavened loaves", as far as the matter could bear, it has been said above.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But if there be a sin "of the whole synagogue", the synagogue is none the less commanded to offer "a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering. But in the sin of the synagogue it is said: "if it should be ignorant, and the matter be hidden from the eyes of the synagogue, and it should do one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"; from which it is clear that "the whole synagogue" too can transgress through ignorance. And this the Lord also confirms in the gospels, when he says: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

"But if a ruler", it says, "should sin, he shall offer a goat from the she-goats". This ruler can be seen as the power of reason which is within us. And if this should sin in us, and we should do something foolish, that sentence of the Savior is to be greatly feared by us, which says: "you are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, it is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men". This one too, then, has his own victim.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But "one soul", it says, "if it should sin, shall likewise offer a female goat", according to that substitution of victims which we mentioned above. But perhaps the hearers of the church may say: it was dealt with almost better among the ancients than with us, when, sacrifices being offered by diverse rites, pardon was granted to those who sinned. Among us there is only one pardon of sins, which is given at the beginning through the grace of the laver; after this no mercy is granted to the one who sins, nor any pardon. It befits indeed a Christian, "for whom Christ died", to be of stricter discipline. For them sheep, goats, oxen were slaughtered, and birds, and fine flour was sprinkled; for you the Son of God was slaughtered, and does it delight you to sin again? And yet, lest these things lift up your spirit not so much toward virtue as cast it down toward despair, you have heard how many are the sacrifices for sins in the law; hear now how many are the remissions of sins in the gospels. There is that first one, by which we are baptized "unto the remission of sins". The second remission is in the suffering of martyrdom. The third is that which is given through almsgiving; for the Savior says: "but nevertheless give the things that you have, and behold, all things are clean to you". The fourth remission of sins comes to us through this, that we too remit sins to our brothers; for thus the Lord and Savior himself says that: "if you remit to your brothers from the heart their sins, your Father too will remit to you your sins. But if you do not remit to your brothers from the heart, neither will your Father remit to you", and just as he taught us to say in the prayer: "remit to us our debts, as we too remit to our debtors". The fifth remission of sins is when "someone turns a sinner from the error of his way". For thus the divine Scripture says that "he who causes a sinner to be turned from the error of his way saves a soul from death, and covers a multitude of sins". A sixth remission too comes about through the abundance of love, as the Lord himself also says: "Amen, I say to you, her many sins are remitted to her, because she loved much", and the Apostle says: "because love covers a multitude of sins". There is still a seventh also, though hard and laborious — the remission of sins through penance, when the sinner washes "his bed with tears" and his "tears" become to him "bread day and night", when he is not ashamed to make known his sin to the priest of the Lord and to seek the remedy, according to him who says: "I said: I will declare against myself my injustice to the Lord, and you remitted the impiety of my heart". In which is fulfilled also that which the Apostle James says: "but if anyone is sick, let him call the elders of the church, and let them lay hands on him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the sick man, and if he be in sins, they will be remitted to him". And you therefore, when you come to the grace of baptism, have offered "a bull-calf", because you are baptized "into the death of Christ". But when you are led to martyrdom, you have offered "a goat", because you have slaughtered the devil, the author of sin. And when you have given alms and, with careful piety, have paid out toward the needy the affection of mercy, you have laden the sacred altar with fat kids. For if you "remit from the heart the sin to your brother" and, laying aside the swelling of anger, have gathered again within you a mild and simple mind, be confident that you have immolated a ram or offered a lamb in sacrifice. Furthermore, if, instructed by the divine readings, "meditating like a dove" and keeping vigil "in the law" of the Lord "day and night", you turn a sinner from his error and, his wickedness cast off, recall him to the simplicity of the dove, and by making him cleave to the saints cause him to imitate the fellowship of the turtledove, you have offered to the Lord "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". But if that "love" which is "greater" than hope and faith should abound in your heart, so that you "love your neighbor" not only "as yourself", but as he showed who said: "no one has greater love than this, that he lay down his soul for his friends", know that you have offered loaves of fine flour "kneaded in the oil" of love, without any "leaven of malice and wickedness, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth". But if you are in the bitterness of your weeping, worn out with grief, tears, and lamentation, if you have mortified your flesh and made it dry with fasts and much abstinence, and have said that "my bones are burned up like a frying-pan", then you have offered "the sacrifice of fine flour from the pan or from the griddle"; and in this way you will be found to offer more truly and more perfectly, according to the gospel, the sacrifices which Israel can no longer offer according to the law.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 2

But let us see what is also to be thought concerning the things that have just now been read: "but if", it says, "one soul should sin unwillingly from the people of the land, by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and should transgress, and the sin which it sinned should become known to it, it shall bring its gift: it shall bring a female goat from the kids, without blemish, for the sin which it sinned". And after this it recounted the whole rite of the sacrifice, according to what we expounded above. Concerning the soul which, made under sin, it says offers, how it is to be thought, we have explained in the foregoing as far as we could; but what it added in this place, saying "a soul, if it should sin from the people of the land", does not seem to me idle. For who would doubt that the things which the law says are said to souls or to a people that are on the earth? What need, then, was there that to what it said, "one soul, if it should sin", it should add: "from the people of the land"? But it must be seen whether perhaps, for distinction from another people, which "is not of the land", this soul which "should sin" is said to be "of the people of the land". For this saying cannot suit him who said: "but our citizenship is in the heavens, whence too we await the Savior, the Lord Jesus". How, then, could I rightly call "of the people of the land" that soul which has nothing in common with the land, but is wholly in the heavens and dwells there, "where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God", whither too it "desires" to return "and to be with Christ: for it is much better; but to remain in the flesh he judges necessary for our sake"? This soul, then, which sins, is "of the people of the land", "doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done". For a long time a certain astonishment held me stunned in this saying; for I do not see it said consistently that "a soul has sinned and done one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done". For if it is a commandment of the Lord, how ought it not to be done, since surely the commandments of the Lord are given precisely for this, that they be done? And how is the soul here said to have sinned which "did one of the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"? And perhaps to some it will seem an error of expression made by the translators; but to me, inquiring more curiously, it has been found that all the translators rendered it alike, and therefore not an error of expression, but a sense of deeper understanding, is to be sought. As far, then, as it can occur to us, this seems to me the resolution. Certain commandments of the Lord were given that they should be done, certain that they should not be done. But as for those which ought to be done, human necessity demanded that there should be brought forth, inserted among them, those which ought not to be done. For example — to bring forth an illustration from these very sacrifices which we now have in hand — a lamb is commanded to be immolated at the Passover, not because God truly required the victim of a lamb year by year, but because it signified that "that Lamb which takes away the sin of the world" ought to be immolated. This, then, he willed to be done, that he did not will. For thus he says through Isaiah: "what to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full; the whole burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and of goats I do not will". You have heard how he does not will "the victim of rams nor the fat of lambs"? Yet he gave the commandment as to how the victim either of bulls or of lambs ought to be offered. But he who understands the law spiritually seeks to offer these things spiritually. But if anyone offers according to the appearance of the carnal commandment, this is "one soul from the people of the land, which sinned unwillingly by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and transgressed", and therefore it adds in what follows: "and when the sin which it sinned shall have become known to it, it shall bring its offering before the Lord". For the soul ought to offer an offering when "it has become known to it" that God does not seek a carnal sacrifice, because "a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit". "Its sin becomes known" to it, then, when it has learned from the Lord who says: "I prefer mercy to sacrifice", and when it has come to know how to immolate "the sacrifice of praise" in the church and to render "to the Most High its vows", through Christ our Lord, "to whom be praise and glory unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

n: Swearing. We are accountable for the sins of others, to which we are accessory, as appears from this and part of the following chapter. No distinction of persons is here noticed. If any one, therefore, be witness to another's promise, confirmed by oath, and, being cited to the bar, refuse to speak, he shall be guilty of sin, and offer the sacrifice proscribed (ver. 6,) for all the preceding cases. Restitution must also be made to the injured person. (Menochius) --- But others suppose that no sacrifice was allowed for such an obstinate wretch as when not answered when the judge swore or adjured him. He was liable to be put to death. The associate of the thief fell under the like punishment as the thief himself, when he would not reveal the theft to the judge, Proverbs xxix. 24. Others again understand this swearing to mean blaspheming God. If the hearer do not reprehend him, he shall suffer as his accomplice. (Origen; Philo) --- Junius thinks that the neglect of fraternal correction, was to be expiated by the sacrifice prescribed for the sins of ignorance, concerning which Moses is treating. But it seems that the person here mentioned was to die, as the words he shall bear his iniquity, commonly denote, chap. xix. 8.; &c. (Calmet) --- When perjury prejudiceth another's cause, we are bound to reveal what we know to the judge, if it can be done so as to avoid scandal. (Worthington) --- Not. Hebrew editions read loa, instead of la, both here and in 34 other places; an irregularity unknown in some manuscripts, and to the Samaritan copy. Perhaps it may have been occasioned by lu, "to him," being of the same sound with la. (Kennicott)

Beast. All wild beasts were deemed unclean; but domestic clean cattle, though slain, did not defile; (Calmet) while some of the unclean did, even alive, chap. xi. 26, 31. (Haydock) --- Fishes are comprised under the name of reptiles; yet some were not unclean, chap. xi. 9. The Septuagint neglect reptiles, and put "the carcasses of impure abominations;" by which they probably mean dogs, and such things as the Egyptians adored. This verse does not regard those who had only touched something unclean, as such were to be purified at night, by washing their garments; but it refers to those who, having neglected that ordinance, had still ventured to touch something sacred, and were therefore required to offer the sacrifice, assom, (Calmet) as for an irreligious behaviour towards God. (Tirinus)

Of man, who may be in a state of legal uncleanness. If he neglect or forget to purify himself, he must offer a sacrifice, either such as he may choose, (St. Augustine, q. 2.) or such as the priest may require. (Lyranus) (Calmet)

Lips. This is necessary before he can be punished by men; but every secret promise binds before God. (Tostat) --- Evil or good: any thing whatsoever, whether favour or punishment, whether the completion of it be difficult or easy. (Calmet) --- Thus parents sometimes foolishly swear that they will chastise their children unmercifully; libertines that they will live in luxuries as long as they have any money; ill-natured people that they will never speak to such a one, that they will murder, &c. To execute such promises, even confirmed by an oath, would be a double crime. Let them ask pardon of God for their rash oath. (Philo) --- Herod made his oath a pretext for killing John the Baptist, deluding himself, perhaps, with a false interpretation of this law. (Haydock) --- As such hasty oaths are easily forgotten, when the guilty person recollected himself, he was bound to confess his fault to the priest in the following manner, according to the Rabbins: Placing his hands between the horns of his victim, he shall say, "I beseech you, Lord, I have sinned; I have committed iniquity and prevarication; I have committed such a fault. I repent, I am filled with sorrow and confusion for having done so; I will relapse no more." These doctors teach, that without confession and sorrow no sacrifice will remit sin. (Calmet) --- To preserve the secret of confession, the priests were ordered to eat the victims alone. (Philo, &c.) (Tirinus)

Let, &c. Hebrew, "and surely when he is guilty in one of these things, he shall confess that he hath sinned therein; (ver. 6.) and he shall bring his sin-offering unto the Lord, for his transgression," &c. Confession to the priest was requisite, before all the other sacrifices for sin. See Josephus, [Antiquities?] iii. 10. (Haydock)
Sin. The flesh belonged to the priest, chap. vi. 26.

Ephi, or a gomor, which is the tenth part of three pecks and three pints, English. (Arbuthnot.) --- For sin, and therefore to shew how odious sin is to God, he will not allow any frankincense to be offered. (Menochius)
Memorial. See chap. ii. 2. At the end, the Hebrew and Septuagint add, "It is a sin-offering;" peccatum. (Calmet) --- Hence the priests are said to eat the sins of the people, Osee iv. 8.

The ceremonies: omitted in Hebrew and Septuagint --- Sanctified[Sacrificed?], neglecting to pay the first-fruits; or, by mistake, eating any of the victims reserved for God, or for the priests. --- Two sicles. St. Jerome seems to have read in the dual number, whereas the Hebrew pointed copies have sicles indefinitely; and the Rabbins understand two, when the word is plural and undetermined. Theodoret reads fifty, which some maintain is the ancient translation of the Septuagint, though it is not found in any of our copies. Hebrew may be rendered "a ram (or) according to thy estimation, sicles of silver." The particle or is sometimes understood. It is probable that when the fault was considerable, a ram was to be sacrificed, and restitution made of what was due with the fifth part besides; but if the fault was small, the priest determined how many sicles were to be presented for sacred purposes. --- Sanctuary. See Exodus xxx. 13.

Through ignorance. These words are not found in the Hebrew or Septuagint; but the context shews, that they must be understood. Some pretend that the ignorance here spoken of, is that by which a person doubts whether the thing which he touched was unclean or not. But we may explain these last verses as a recapitulation of what had been already ordered. (Calmet)
Sin. If it were grievous, the priest required a more valuable victim, ver. 15.

Lord. Hebrew, "It is a victim for the sin which he has committed against the Lord." From this chapter, as well as from Numbers v. 7, it is obvious that a special confession was necessary, not only for those who had fallen into the disorder of leprosy, which was a figure of sin, and often inflicted by God in punishment of it; but also, when they had given way to the smallest transgression against the commands and ceremonies of the Lord. (Haydock) --- This custom is still observed by the Jews. (Galatinus x. 3.)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

But let us now see what that soul also does which "hears the voice of one swearing an oath and is a witness", "or" which "sees" something "and is privy to it and does not disclose it", from which it too "has borne his sin" — without doubt his who either did something wickedly or swore. This also, according to the history, builds us up and teaches us never to pollute our consciences in another's sins, nor to lend consent to those who act wickedly. And I call it consent not only to act along with them, but also to keep silent about the things that have been done unlawfully. Do you wish to know that these things agree also with the Gospel precepts? The Lord himself says: "if you see your brother sin, reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you two others or three. But if he does not hear even them, tell the church. But if he does not hear even the church, let him be to you as a heathen and a publican". But the Gospel precept was given more perfectly in this, that it established the manner and discipline of disclosing the sin. For it does not wish you, if perchance you have seen your brother's sin, at once to fly out into public and everywhere to proclaim and divulge another's sins — which would surely be the mark not of one correcting, but rather of one defaming. "Alone", it says, "between yourself and him, rebuke him". For when he who sins sees the mystery kept for him, he too will keep the modesty of amendment; but if he sees himself defamed, he will at once turn to the shamelessness of denial; and you will not only not have amended the sin, but will even have doubled it. Learn, therefore, the order from the Gospels. First, it says, "alone, between yourself and him". Second, "take with you two others or three". Why "two or three"? "For in the mouth", it says, "of two or three witnesses shall every word stand". Since indeed in the third place it commanded the correction to be brought to the church, in the second it wishes "two or three" witnesses to be brought in. In their presence, if the one rebuked will not amend himself, then, when his sin has been brought to the church, he may be confuted by the witnesses previously brought in; for it frequently happens that one wishing to fulfill the Gospel command may seem a slanderer, if he brings a charge to the church and lacks witnesses. Lest, therefore, this happen, for that reason he commanded "two or three" witnesses to be brought in at the second meeting. Since, therefore, such is the command of the Gospel, and the law prescribes that, if one keeps silent, "he shall bear his sin", it is to be known that, if anyone either does not disclose the things which he sees in his neighbor's fault according to the rule given above, or, when called to testimony, does not speak the things that are true, he himself will take upon himself the sin which the one he conceals has committed, and the penalty of the deed will roll back upon the one privy to it. Sufficiently, therefore, in this chapter has the very text of the history built us up. Yet I think that that soul too, which reads what is written in the law of God: "the Lord has sworn and will not repent; you are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek", "hears the voice of one swearing an oath", as do the scribes and Pharisees, always meditating on these things, but they are silent and are unwilling to announce them to the people, lest they testify to the coming of Christ. Therefore for this reason they will bear the sin, in which, not announcing to the people the things that are true, they make Israel to sin.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

After these things another law is promulgated. "Whatever soul", it says, "touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of unclean beasts, and it is hidden from him, and he is defiled; or if he touches of the uncleanness of a man, of any uncleanness by which he may be defiled", and so forth. These things indeed are observed among the Jews quite unbecomingly and uselessly. For to what end is he held unclean who has touched, for example, a dead animal or the body of a deceased man? What if it be the body of a prophet? What if the body of a patriarch, or even of Abraham himself? What if he has touched even the bones, will he be unclean? What if he touches the bones of Elisha, which raise up the dead? Will he who touches be unclean, and do the bones of the prophet make unclean even that very one whom they raise from the dead? See how unfitting the Jewish understanding is. But let us first see what it is to touch, and what is the touch that makes unclean, and what indeed is the touch that makes clean. The Apostle says: "it is good for a man not to touch a woman". This touch is unclean; for this is that which the Lord said in the Gospel: "if anyone looks upon a woman to lust after her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart". For the vice of concupiscence touched his heart, and his soul was made unclean. If, therefore, anyone touches something in this way, that is, either through lust for a woman, or through desire for money, or by any other craving of sin whatever, he has touched something unclean and is defiled. It behooves you, therefore, if you have touched anything of this kind, to know how you may offer a sacrifice, according to the things we recalled in what went before, so that you may be made clean. Do you wish me to show you "what" is "the soul which touched the unclean thing" and was made unclean, and again touched the clean thing and was made clean? She "who suffered an issue of blood and spent all her substance on physicians and could gain nothing" was brought down to this through the uncleanness of sin. For she had touched sin, and for that reason had received the "scourge" of the flesh. But after, full of faith, "she touched the fringe of Jesus, the flow of her blood stood still", and suddenly she was made clean who before had lived unclean for so long a time.
