And just as, when she had touched the Lord and Savior, he himself said: "who touched me? For I felt power go out from me" — that power, without doubt, which had healed the woman and made her clean — so it is to be understood that, if anyone touches sin, there goes out from that very sin a certain malignant power, which makes him who has touched it unclean; and this is truly to have touched the unclean thing. By a like reasoning it is to be said also concerning the "carcass" of a man, or the "carcass" of a clean or unclean beast. For he touches the "carcass" of a man who either follows or imitates someone dead in his sins. But if the differences of each are to be examined, let us review them one by one. The carcass of a man, as we said above, we can say to be that which the Apostle says to the Corinthians: "I wrote", he says, "to you in the epistle that you should not mingle with fornicators; not indeed with the fornicators of this world, or the covetous, or the rapacious, or those serving idols; otherwise you would have had to go out of this world. But now I have written to you that you should not mingle, if anyone named a brother is a fornicator, or covetous, or serving idols, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious — with such a one not even to take food". This, therefore, is to touch the "carcass" of a man: for one to offer himself as a companion, even in food, to one who, having been made a man in Christ, has again died in his sins. For that widow too, of whom the Apostle says, "who, living in delights, is dead while she lives", can be called the "carcass" of a man. But it must also be examined what the carcasses of animals are in the church. If any of the simpler sort, in that they have done nothing of prudence, also wallow in the filth of sins, if anyone follows or touches these with that touch which we expounded above, he has touched the "carcass" of animals. But that the church has animals also, hear how it says in the Psalms: "men and beasts you will save, O Lord". These, therefore, who bear zeal for the word of God and for a rational discipline, are called men; but those who live without such zeal and do not seek out the exercises of knowledge, yet are faithful, are called animals indeed, but clean. For just as there are certain men of God, so there are also certain sheep of God. For it is written that Moses was not a sheep of God, but "a man of God". And Elijah was not a sheep of God, but "a man of God"; for so he himself says: "if I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty". But do you wish to hear of the sheep of God? It is said through the prophet: "my sheep, my sheep are holy, says the Lord". And again the Savior says in the Gospel: "my sheep hear my voice". And I do not think he would have said of men that "men hear my voice". But let him who has "ears to hear" hear these things, how the sheep hear the voice, but the men hear his word. These, therefore, are animals clean indeed on account of Christ, but "carcasses" on account of sin. If anyone "touches" these, that is, if anyone follows another in sin, he will be unclean. And if anyone "touches the carcass" of a man of this kind, that is, of one who, living at first according to reason and exercising himself in the word of God, afterward fell into sin — if anyone follows or imitates him, he touches the "carcass" of a man and will be unclean. But if you touch also "what is caught by a wild beast", you will be unclean. What is the wild beast? Is it a lion or a wolf, which snatches away men or beasts? That, I believe, is the wild beast of which the Apostle Peter says: "your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour. Resist him, strong in faith". And again, of whom does the Apostle Paul say: "for after my departure there will enter in ravening wolves, not sparing the flock". If, therefore, you see one "caught" by these "wild beasts", do not follow him, do not touch him, lest you too be made unclean. There are, besides, also other unclean animals, whose carcass it forbids to be touched. The unclean animals are men who are outside Christ, in whom there is neither reason nor any religion. If, therefore, you see the "carcasses" of all these, that is, their sins, the lawgiver tells you not to touch them, not to defile yourself with them, not to handle them. And these are the uncleannesses which are rightly to be fled. But to shun the touch of a man, or of a dead body, to which rather a religious burial is to be given, these are Jewish and useless fables, "having indeed a form of piety, but denying the power thereof". The first law, therefore, was given concerning uncleannesses, if anyone "was a witness" of some "oath" or fault "and did not disclose it", and through this was himself in a manner made unclean by the fellowship of sin. The second law is that by which it is forbidden to touch "anything unclean and a carcass".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

Now a third law of this kind is promulgated: "and the soul", it says, "which swears, pronouncing with its lips to do evil or to do good, according to all things whatsoever he shall utter to a man with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and afterward he knows it, and has sinned in some one of these — let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned, and he shall bring for the things in which he has offended, to the Lord, for the sin by which he has sinned, a female of the sheep" and so forth. How indeed, "if I pronounce with my lips or swear to do good" and do not do it, I am guilty of sin, there is no difficulty in showing; but how, "if I swear or pronounce to do evil" and do not do it, I have sinned, it is difficult to assign in word. For it seems absurd, for example, that if in anger I say I am going to kill a man and do not do it, I should, lest I seem to perjure myself or to deceive, be compelled to fulfill the deed which I rashly and unlawfully promised. Let us seek, therefore, what the matter is in which, if we promise to do evil and do not do it, we sin; but if we do it, we are excused from sin, so that the truth of the precept may reasonably stand. As far as it seems to be understood in this place, to do evil is to oppose someone and not to indulge him, that he may do what he wishes. And so we too, when we come to God and vow to serve him in chastity, "pronounce with our lips" and "swear" that we "will chastise our flesh", or do evil to it, "and reduce it into servitude", that we may be able to save the spirit. For so also did he say that he had sworn, who says: "I have sworn, and have determined to keep all your precepts". Since, therefore, it is the voice of the flesh which says: "for I do not do what I will, but what I hate, that I do", without doubt it has been afflicted by the spirit and constrained; "for it resists and fights against the spirit", and, unless evil is done to it, that it may be afflicted and weakened, the spirit cannot say: "when I am weak, then am I strong". If anyone, therefore, "has sworn and pronounced to do evil" to this "flesh which resists and fights against the spirit", and to afflict and mortify it, and has not done it, he is guilty of sin, in that he swore to torment his flesh and to subject it to servitude, and did not do it. But by the same oath he also determines to do good to the spirit. For in that he does evil to the flesh, he does good to the spirit. If anyone, therefore, has sworn this and has not done it, he is made guilty of sin. But do you wish to know that good cannot be done to one of these, unless you do evil to the other? Hear also the Lord himself saying: "I will kill and I will make to live". What does God kill? The flesh, surely. And what does he make to live? The spirit, without doubt. And again in the sequel he says: "I will strike, and I will heal". What does he strike? The flesh. What does he heal? The spirit. To what do these things avail? That he may make you "mortified in the flesh, made alive in the spirit"; lest perchance you too "serve the law of God with the mind, but with the flesh", if it be not mortified, "the law of sin". If, therefore, you have promised this order and have not been able to keep it, hear what the order of the law prescribes: "if he has sinned", it says, "in some one of these, let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned". There is in this something a marvelous secret, that it orders one to "pronounce the sin". For indeed all the things we do are to be pronounced in every manner and brought forth into public. If "we do anything in secret", if we have committed anything in speech alone or even within the secrets of our thoughts, all must needs be published, all brought forth; and brought forth by him who is both the accuser and the instigator of sin. For he himself now instigates us to sin, he himself also, when we have sinned, accuses. If, therefore, in this life we forestall him and are our own accusers, we escape the malice of the devil, our enemy and accuser. For so also elsewhere the prophet says: "do you", he says, "tell your iniquities first, that you may be justified". Does he not evidently show the mystery of which we treat, when he says: "do you tell them first?" — that he may show you that you ought to forestall him who is ready to accuse. "Do you", therefore, he says, "tell them first", lest he forestall you; for if you tell them "first" and offer the sacrifice of repentance according to the things which we said above are to be offered, and hand over your flesh to destruction, "that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord", it will be said to you also that "you have received your evils in your life, but now rest here". But David too speaks in the same spirit in the Psalms and says: "I made known my iniquity, and I did not cover my sin. I said: I will pronounce against myself my injustice, and you forgave the impiety of my heart". You see, therefore, that "to pronounce the sin" merits the remission of sin. For the devil, forestalled in the accusation, will not be able to accuse us further, and, if we are our own accusers, it profits us unto salvation; but if we wait to be accused by the devil, that accusation turns to our punishment; for he will have companions in gehenna, whom he has convicted as companions of his crimes.
The Instructor Book 1

Through Moses God orders that two young birds, a pair of pigeons or of turtledoves, be offered for any sin. This means that the sinlessness of such gentle birds and their guilelessness and forgetfulness of injury is very acceptable to God. So he is instructing us to offer a sacrifice bearing the character of that against which we have offended. The plight of the poor doves, moreover, will instill into us a beginning of abhorrence for sin.
HOMILIES ON THE SONG OF SONGS, HOMILY 2

Not without cause is a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons, taken in the sacrifices: for they are of equal worth, and it is never said separately, a pair only of pigeons, but a pair of turtledoves, and two young pigeons. The dove is the Holy Spirit. But the Holy Spirit, when he speaks of great and more hidden mysteries, which many cannot receive, is signified by the name of the turtledove — that is, of that bird which dwells always on the ridges of the mountains and on the tops of the trees; but in the valleys, and in the things which reach even to men, the dove is taken.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

Let us now see what law is set forth in offering victims "for sin". "And the Lord spoke", it says, "to Moses, saying: if any soul is hidden and sins unwillingly against the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer for his offense to the Lord a spotless ram of the sheep, at the price of a silver shekel of the sanctuary, for that in which he offended. And what he has sinned against the holy things, he shall restore, and shall add a fifth to it, and shall give it to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him with the ram of the offense, and it shall be forgiven him". In the foregoing laws, which were reported concerning the sacrifices for uncleanness, wherever it said something was to be offered — for example, a sheep or a kid — it added: "but if his hand does not suffice for a kid or a lamb, let him offer a pair of turtledoves or two young doves", and again: "but if it does not suffice even for this, let him offer fine flour". But in this law, where it discourses of the sin which is committed against "the holy things", it substituted no substitution of a lesser victim, a second or a third, but appointed only a "ram" to be offered; nor did it show that the sin which is committed against "the holy things" can be loosed otherwise than if one slaughters a "ram"; and not simply a ram, but a "ram" bought "at a price" and at a fixed "price": "at a shekel", it says, "of the sanctuary". What then? If someone is poor and does not have "a shekel of the sanctuary" wherewith he might purchase a "ram", will his sin not be loosed? Riches, therefore, must be sought by each one, that his sin may be able to be absolved. But if the Lord deigns either to open our eyes to see or the ears of your heart to hear, let us seek out what the meaning of the lawgiver, veiled in mysteries, intends. And first indeed let us see of what sort this very thing is that has been recited, according to the letter. It seems to speak of those in whose hands "holy things" have been committed, that is, the things which have been offered among the Lord's gifts — for example, vows and offerings which are offered in the churches of God for the use of the saints and the ministry of the priests, or which, for the need of the poor, are offered by devout and religious minds. If anyone withdraws any of these by any presumption whatever, the law decrees that, if he is reminded that he has sinned and of his own accord receives compunction of heart — for concerning him who is not compunct of his own accord, but is convicted by another's reproving, the remedy is more difficult — this one, therefore, who has of his own accord remembered his sin, "shall restore", it says, that very thing which he had withdrawn, "and shall add to it a fifth, and shall offer a ram for sin" bought "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary". As for what it says: "he shall add to it a fifth", the simpler sort suppose it was said thus: that, for example, if five coins were withdrawn, one is added, so that for five he is seen to restore six. But those who have skill in the discipline of numbers reckon the number of this word far otherwise. For in the Greek it does not have that which simply makes "a fifth", but has that which we can indeed say "above a fifth", unless it were said that this is the term for a certain special number among them, by which it is indicated that for five, five others are to be given and one over; so that, for example, it is understood that one who has stolen five coins both restores those very five and five others, with one added over. Yet these things are not straightway to be understood of thefts or frauds, but that also, if anyone has taken money from the holy things for his own necessary uses and has brought delays in restoring it, he is bound by a law of this kind. And this law ought to build up the hearers even according to the letter. For the observance is very useful and necessary, especially to those who preside over ecclesiastical dispensations, that they may know that they must observe more cautiously and diligently with regard to the things offered for the use of the saints.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

But what shall we say concerning the sacrifice of the "ram" bought "at a price" and "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary", which is commanded to be offered for the expiation of sin? He is going to be rich who can purge his offenses "at the price of a ram". What these riches are, let us seek. The most wise Solomon teaches us, saying: "the redemption of a man's soul is his own proper riches". Do you hear the words of wisdom, how with necessary properties it declares the force of each word? He speaks of riches suited to "the redemption of the soul", and riches not another's nor common, but "proper riches". By which he shows that there are certain "proper riches" and certain riches not proper. But this the Lord more evidently declared in the Gospels, when he says: "but if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own?", showing that the riches of the present age are not our own proper, but another's. For they pass away and "pass by like a shadow". But those are the "proper riches" of which the prophet says: "and to you I will gather the riches of the nations". From these riches perhaps also "Abraham was made very rich in gold and silver and cattle" and all furnishings. Do you wish me to show you from what treasuries these riches come down? Hear the Apostle Paul saying of the Lord Jesus Christ: "in whom", he says, "are all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden". But in the Gospels too the Lord says that: "the rich scribe brings forth from his treasures new things and old". Of these the Apostle Paul too says that: "in all things you have been made rich in him, in all speech and in all knowledge". From these riches, therefore, which are brought forth from "the treasures of wisdom and knowledge", this "ram" is to be bought by us, which ought to be offered for sins — those, namely, which are committed against the holy things — and it is to be bought at the reckoning of a "shekel of the sanctuary". We already said above that every victim bears a type and image of Christ, much more the ram, which was once substituted by God to be sacrificed in place of Isaac. "At a shekel of the sanctuary", therefore, Christ is to be procured by us, who may dissolve our sins. "The shekel of the sanctuary" holds the form of our faith. For if you offer faith as a price, from Christ, as from a spotless ram given as a victim, you will receive the remission of sins. I feel that in explaining, the greatness of the mysteries surpasses our strength. But although we are not able to discourse of all things, yet we feel that all things are filled with mysteries. And therefore let it suffice to have set down indications for the studious, by which, stirred up, they may arrive at things higher and deeper than these, and understand from which flocks the "bull-calf" is to be sought for a victim, from which sheep the "ram" is to be provided. "For I have", says Jesus, "also other sheep, which are not of this fold; and those too I must bring, that there may be one flock and one shepherd". Let them know also where the turtledoves, where the doves are to be sought. "Your eyes", it says, "are like doves upon the fullness of the waters" (to the "fullness of the waters", therefore, we must hasten, for in these the beauty of the bride is described), "and your neck", it says, "like a turtledove's". In the doves the eyes are praised. For as to what it said: "doves upon the fullness of the waters" — they report that this kind of bird, when it comes to the waters, because there it is wont to suffer the ambushes of the hawk, catches sight of the enemy coming from above, the shadow of the flying one seen in the waters, and by the sharpness of its eyes evades the treachery of the imminent danger. If you too can thus foresee the ambushes of the devil and beware of them, you have offered "doves" as a sacrifice to God. But let those to whom such things are a care seek out also this: from which fields "fine flour" ought to be offered. I judge that it is from the crops of that land which "makes one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold fruit". Let them seek out also — unless it seem more curious than it ought — by which grinders this fine flour is prepared for the sacrifices. And let it not escape them that there are "two who grind", of whom "one shall be taken and the other left". From that mill, therefore, which is to be taken, it will behoove one to offer "fine flour". But the "shekel of the sanctuary" too, which is said to be necessary for the price of the ram — see whence and how it is to be sought out. "Shekel" is the name of the Lord's money, and in many places of the Scriptures the Lord's money is mentioned by various names of appellation. But a certain kind is called "approved", and a certain kind "reprobate". Approved was that money which the householder, "about to go abroad, having called his servants, gave to each according to his own ability". Approved too was that money which is called a "denarius", which was agreed upon with the laborers and given "from the last even to the first". You ought, therefore, to know that there is also other money, reprobate. Hear the prophet saying: "your silver is reprobate". Since, therefore, there is a certain "approved" kind, and a certain "reprobate", therefore the Apostle says, as to "approved money-changers": "proving", he says, "all things, holding fast that which is good". For our Lord Jesus Christ alone is he who can teach you an art of this kind, through which you may know how to discern which money it is that holds the image of the true king, and which is counterfeit and, as is commonly said, struck outside the mint, which has indeed the name of the king, but does not hold the truth of the royal figure. For there are many who have the name of Christ, but do not have the truth of Christ. And on account of this the Apostle says: "for there must be heresies also, that the approved may be made manifest among you". Therefore for that reason also in the present reading the lawgiver, looking wholly to the mystical and spiritual sense, added that this "ram", which is procured for this, that it may be able to absolve sin, is to be procured not with any shekel whatever, that is, not with any money whatever, but with a "shekel of the sanctuary". But if he was not looking to a mystery, what reason did there seem to be that a bought ram should be offered as a victim, and at a fixed price? And it does not suffice to have named the money by "shekel", but he added also "of the holy shekel"? What if someone had in his flocks the best rams and worthy of divine sacrifices? Or what if someone were so poor that he could not have "a shekel of the sanctuary"? Is this the moderation of the lawgiver, that, unless one has a fixed sum of money, his sin cannot be absolved? Which openly, according to the letter indeed, seems absurd, but according to the spiritual understanding it is certain that no one receives the remission of sins unless he has brought whole, approved, and holy faith, through which he may be able to buy the "ram"; whose nature is such that it wipes away the sins of the believer. And this is the "shekel of the sanctuary", an approved, as we said, and sincere faith, that is, where no deceit of perfidy, no perversity of heretical cunning is mixed in, so that we, offering sincere faith, may be washed "by the precious blood of Christ, as of a spotless victim"; through whom is to God the Father almighty, with the Holy Spirit, "glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 3

But let us too, to whom these things perhaps do not happen, see in what part the discourse of the law may build us up. And I today, though I am a sinner, yet because the dispensation of the Lord's word has been entrusted to me, seem to have the holy things of God committed to me. Nor now for the first time, but often already and long since, do we use this dispensation toward you. If, therefore, anyone of you has received from me the Lord's money and, as is wont to happen, having gone out of the church and been snatched away by the various occupations of the world, has given to oblivion the things he had heard, and has fulfilled no work from the word which he received, this is he who has not restored the money received from the holy things. Wherefore, even at hearing these things, let him call to memory that he has neglected the things which had lately been committed to him in the word of God. Let him, therefore, restore both this which he received and add to it a fifth in that manner which we said before, that is, so that there be twice five and one added over. Let us see, therefore, how these five are restored. The number five is frequently — indeed almost always — taken for the five senses. We ought, therefore, to know that these five can be restored to the holy things in this way: that, if perchance we have presumed to abuse them in secular acts and have expended their use in the things which we have done not according to God, we now restore these very five to holy acts and religious ministries, and add to them five others, which are the senses of the inner man; through which we either, made "clean of heart", "see God", or "have ears to hear" the things which Jesus teaches, or take in that "odor" of which the Apostle says: "for we are the good odor of Christ", or take also that taste of which the prophet says: "taste and see, for the Lord is sweet", or that touch of which John says, that "we have beheld with our eyes and our hands have handled of the word of life". But to all these we add one over, that we may refer all these things to the one God. And let these things be said concerning the restoring of those things which had been taken away from the holy things by any fault whatever.

n: Despising: interpretatively; not formally, as Numbers xv. (Estius) --- The Lord, who knows the truth, and is an avenger of all injustice, even the most secret. (Haydock) --- The law inflicts indeed a smaller punishment, as these offences are supposed to be secret, and the offender is thus invited to repent, and to repair the injury done. When the crime is public, the law is more severe. (Calmet) --- Hebrew, "If a soul transgress and sin against the Lord." Septuagint, "If any one wilfully despise the commands," &c. (Haydock) --- Trust. Hebrew and Septuagint, "or a sum given for traffic for their common benefit." --- Oppression, by any means whatsoever detaining the wages of the labourer, &c.

Lost. We acquire no title to the thing by finding it. The Roman law, as well as divines, condemn those who appropriate the thing found to their own use, as guilty of theft, whether they knew to whom it belonged or not; and Plato greatly commends the law of Solon, "Take not what thou didst not put down," a rule which the Dyrbeans and the people of Biblos rigorously observed. We may, however, take up what is lost, (Calmet) and endeavour to find the owner, who must indemnify us for our trouble; and, if we never find him, we are directed to give the price to the poor, for the owner's welfare. (Haydock)

Convicted, by his own conscience, and by the judgment of the priest to whom he has confessed his sin. The Hebrew expresses the different sorts of sins specified above, which the Vulgate denotes by the word offence.

Wronged. Hebrew and Chaldean add, "in the day of his sin-offering;" and the Septuagint, "in which he is convicted." No unnecessary delay in making restitution can be allowed to the sincere penitent, who wishes to make his peace with God.
The. Hebrew, "thy estimation for a sin-offering." (Haydock) --- Wilful sins require a more noble victim than those of ignorance, which were expiated by the sacrifice of a goat. (Menochius)

Holocaust. The regulations respecting it, as they regard the priests, are here given, as chap. i., directions were given to those who presented the victims. --- Morning. All the parts of the victim were not laid on at the same time. The like was observed during the day also, when no other sacrifices were to be offered on this altar. --- Of the same, not strange, unhallowed fire, but such as was kept continually burning on the altar of holocausts, as the Hebrew intimates; "the fire of the altar shall be burning in it." During the marches in the desert, it is not written how this fire was preserved. The Persians believed that their eternal fire came down from heaven, and the vestal virgins kept their sacred fire at Rome, with superstitious care. Theophrastus (ap. Eusebius, præp. i. 9,) mentions the keeping of fire in the temples, as one of the most ancient rites of religion.

Others; such as were worn on common occasions, out of the tabernacle. --- And shall, &c. Hebrew has only, "unto a clean place," as the other versions and some Latin copies read. The meaning of the addition is, that all the bones, &c., must be perfectly reduced to dust, before they be carried out of the camp. (Calmet)
Fat, along with the whole burnt-offering. (Menochius)

The perpetual fire. This fire came from heaven, (chap. ix. 24,) and was always kept burning on the altar: as a figure of the heavenly fire of divine love, which ought to be always burning in the heart of a Christian. (Challoner) --- It must be fed by assiduous meditation on the Scripture and holy things. (Du Hamel)
Sacrifice of flour, moneé, chap. ii. 1. --- And libations. These words are added, to shew that oil and wine accompanied this sacrifice.
He. Only the priests, who were actually officiating, could partake of it. (Calmet)

Lord. As long as this law shall be in force. (Menochius) --- Sanctified. Theodoret (q. 5,) seems to assert, that all such were obliged to serve the altar in some function or other. If any unclean person touched the victims wilfully, he was slain; if, by mistake, the blood sprinkled a garment, it was to be washed, ver. 27.
Evening. And this shall continue as long as they are high priests, from the day of their consecration, (Josephus, [Antiquities?] iii. 20.; Cajetan,) a perpetual sacrifice. (Calmet)

Rightfully. According to the law, which decides that, if the first-born be deformed, the next shall succeed, chap. xxi. 18. Hebrew, "the priest, of his sons, who is anointed in his stead, shall offer it." No mention is made of its being hot, either here or in the Septuagint. (Haydock)
Sacrifice of flour, not of animals, Exodus xxix. 28.
Sin of individuals. The victims offered by the priest, or by the whole people, were to be burnt, chap. iv. 7.
Tabernacle. No part shall be given to those who are not of the sacerdotal race. (Calmet)
Place, in the court, that so it may be worn again. (Menochius)

Sodden, or boiled. Such vessels, of private people, as had been used to boil part of the victim, (1 Kings ii. 13,) were either to be abandoned to the service of the altar, or broken, &c. (Calmet) --- Earthen vessels might imbibe some part of the consecrated juice. (Menochius)
Fire. As they are the victims for the sins of the priest and of the people, chap. iv. 6, 18. (Menochius)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

If, according to the faith of the divine law, these things which are read to us were spoken by the Lord to Moses, I think that, as being the words of God, they ought to be understood not according to the incapacity of the hearers but according to the majesty of the one speaking. "The Lord," it says, "spoke." What is "the Lord"? Let the Apostle answer you, and learn from him that "the Lord is spirit." But if the word of the Apostle does not suffice for you, hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospels that "God is spirit." If therefore both the Lord and God is "spirit," the things which the spirit speaks we ought to hear spiritually. But I say yet something more: that the things the Lord speaks are to be believed not only spiritual, but even spirit. This I will prove not by my own opinion, but from the Gospels; hear our Lord and Savior saying to his disciples: "the words which I have spoken to you are spirit and life." If therefore we have learned from the voice of the Savior himself that the words which he spoke to the Apostles "are spirit and life," we ought in no way to doubt that the things also which he spoke through Moses are to be believed "spirit and life."

But let us see what these things are, concerning which we ought now, as far as we can, to say something. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: whatever soul shall sin, and passing over shall pass over the commandments of the Lord, and shall lie to his neighbor concerning a deposit or a partnership or a robbery, or has done some harm to his neighbor, or has found something lost and lies about it, and swears unjustly about any one of all the things which a man may do, so as to sin in these; and it shall be, when he has sinned and offended, that he shall restore the robbery which he robbed, or the injury which he inflicted, or the deposit which was entrusted to him, or the lost thing which he found, of every matter concerning which he swore unjustly, and he shall restore the principal itself, and shall add a fifth part over and above; and to whomever it belongs, to him he shall render it, on the day when he is convicted." Thus far, for the present, the kinds of sin are set forth, but afterward the purgation of it is commanded through offerings. If any are weak and incapable of the deeper mystery, let them be edified from the letter, and let them know that, if anyone "passing over shall pass over the commandments of the Lord and shall have lied to his neighbor concerning a deposit or a partnership or a robbery," he is declared guilty of an enormous sin. But far be it from the Church of God that I should believe there to be anyone in this assembly of the saints who conducts himself so wretchedly as to deny the "deposit" of his neighbor, or to defile a "partnership" by fraud, or himself to plunder what belongs to another, or to receive things robbed from others and, if they are demanded of him, to swear against his conscience concerning these. Far be it, I say, that I should suppose these things of any of the faithful. For confidently I say concerning you that "you have not so learned Christ," nor have you "been so taught." But neither does the law itself prescribe these things to the holy and faithful. Do you wish to know that these things are not spoken to the holy and just? Hear the Apostle distinguishing: "for the just," he says, "the law is not laid down, but for the unjust and the insubordinate, for the wicked and the defiled, for parricides, matricides," and the like of these. Since therefore the Apostle says the "law" is "imposed" upon men of this kind, let the Church of God — which far be it that it should be stained with crimes of this sort — leave the letter to others and be more holily edified by the spirit.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

Let us therefore now see what is the "deposit" which each of the faithful has received. I think that we have received both our own soul and our body as a deposit from God. And do you wish to see another, greater "deposit" which you have received from God? To your very soul God entrusted "his own image and likeness." This deposit, therefore, must be restored by you as whole as it is established to have been received by you. For if you are merciful, "as your Father in heaven is merciful," the image of God is in you and you preserve the "deposit" whole. If you are perfect, "as your Father also in heaven is perfect," the deposit of the image of God remains in you. And likewise all the rest: if you are devout, if you are just, if holy, if "pure in heart," and if all the things which are present in God by nature subsist in you by imitation, the "deposit" of the divine image is safe with you. But if on the contrary you act, and instead of merciful are cruel, instead of devout impious, instead of kind violent, instead of tranquil turbulent, instead of generous a plunderer, then, having cast away the image of God, you have taken up in yourself the image of the devil and have denied the good "deposit" entrusted to you from on high. Or was this not what the Apostle, under a mystery, was commanding to his chosen disciple Timothy, saying: "O Timothy, guard the good deposit"? I even add this, that we have received Christ the Lord as a "deposit" and have the Holy Spirit as a "deposit." We must therefore take heed that we do not use this holy deposit unholily and, when sins solicit us to consent to them, swear that we have not received a "deposit." For if indeed we have it within us, we cannot consent to sin. But also the rational sense itself, which is in me, has been entrusted to me, that I may use it for the understanding of divine things: talent, memory, judgment, reason, and all the movements which are within me seem to have been entrusted to me by God, that I may use them in those things which the divine law has prescribed. But if the talent, skillful and keen-sighted, be turned to evil arts, and we abuse the things of God in those things which God does not will, this is to forswear the "deposit" and to turn benefits into treachery.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

Let us now see what also is to be understood by "partnership." Do you suppose there is anyone who ought to be admonished according to the letter, lest perchance in a matter of money, or in any other kind of partnership, he deceive his partner by fraud? Of the utmost misery is that soul into which this kind of fraud can still fall. Yet nevertheless, because there is much fragility in man, let us admonish concerning these things also, since not even the Apostle was reluctant to command them. For he says: "let no one overreach his brother in business, since God is the avenger of all these things." But now let us inquire what also is the "partnership of the spirit." Hear the Apostle speaking concerning these very things: "if there is any comfort of love, if any partnership of the spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfill my joy." You see how the Apostle Paul understood the law of "partnership." Hear also John, how by one and the same spirit he speaks forth. "And we have partnership," he says, "with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ." And likewise Peter says: "you have been made partakers," he says, "of the divine nature" — which is to say, partners. And again the Apostle Paul says: "for what partnership has light with darkness?" But if there is no "partnership of light with darkness," then light can have "partnership" with light. Therefore, if "partnership with the Father and the Son" and with the Holy Spirit has been given to us, we must take heed that we do not by sinning deny this holy and divine "partnership"; for if we do "the works of darkness," it is certain that we have denied the "partnership" of light. But the Apostle also calls us partners "of the saints," and no wonder; for if it is said that we have "partnership with the Father and the Son," how not also with the "saints" — not only those who "are on earth," but also those who are "in heaven"? For Christ also "by" his "blood pacified things earthly and things heavenly," that he might make things earthly partners of things heavenly. This he clearly indicates where he says that there is joy in heaven "over one sinner doing penance," and again when he says that "those who rise from the dead will be as the angels of God in heaven," and when anew he promises "the kingdoms of the heavens" to men. This "partnership," therefore, whoever separates himself from the union of these by his evil deeds and evil thoughts breaks and denies. After these things it is spoken concerning "robbery"; there are robbers who are evil, and there are also good ones; and the good indeed are those of whom the Savior says that "they seize the kingdom of the heavens." But there are also evil robbers, of whom the prophet says: "and the robbery of the poor is in your houses." The Apostle, however, pronounces abruptly, saying: "do not err, for neither adulterers nor the effeminate nor those who lie with males nor thieves nor the rapacious shall possess the kingdom of God." Yet there is also, according to the spiritual understanding, a way of seizing culpably, just as those seize praiseworthily "the kingdoms of the heavens." To speak, for example: if a man not yet purged from vices, not yet separated from profane and sordid deeds, wishes stealthily to thrust himself into the assembly of the holy and perfect and to hear the discourse in which perfect and mystical things are treated: such a man has not rightly seized the knowledge of secret and perfect things. For it behooves us to remember the precept of the Savior, in which he says that "no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise both the wineskins will burst and the wine will perish," showing that to a soul not yet renewed, but persisting in the oldness of malice, the secrets of the new mysteries which the world came to know through Christ ought not to be committed.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

Then the lawgiver adds: "or if he has done any harm to his neighbor, or if he has found something lost." The law of the letter seems to command this, that, if anyone finds what another has lost and it is asked for, he restore it and let it "not perish for him." This too is a useful edification for the hearers. For many think it is without sin if they retain another's property which they have found, and they say: God gave it to me, to whom do I have to render it? Let them learn, therefore, that this sin is like robbery, if anyone does not return what he has found. Yet nevertheless, if the lawgiver had wished only this, which is thought according to the letter, to be understood, he could have said: if he finds what had perished, or what someone had lost. But now, when he says "he has found a perdition," he wished us to understand something more. Those who sin exceedingly are in the Scriptures called "perdition," as we read said in the prophet Ezekiel: "you have become perdition," he says, "and you shall not subsist unto eternal time." There is, therefore, one who by seeking too much "finds perdition," so that, for example, let us say: heretics, to construct and defend their dogmas, search and dispute much in the divine Scriptures, that they may "find perdition." For when they have sought many testimonies by which to buttress the things they perversely hold, they are to be said to have found perdition for themselves. But if perchance one of these, hearing in the church the word of God treated according to the catholic faith, comes to his senses and understands that what he had found is "perdition," "he shall restore," it says, "what he found."
AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS 3.10

For if Christ took away from us that very heavy yoke of many observances, so that we are not circumcised according to the flesh, we do not immolate victims of the cattle, we do not rest even from necessary works on the Sabbath, retaining the seventh in the revolution of the days, and other things of this kind; but keep them as spiritually understood, and, the symbolizing shadows being removed, are watchful in the light of those things which are signified by them; shall we therefore say, that when it is written that whoever finds another man's property of any kind that has been lost, should return it to him who has lost it, it does not pertain to us? and many other like things whereby people learn to live piously and uprightly? and especially the Decalogue itself, which is contained in those two tables of stone, apart from the carnal observance of the Sabbath, which signifies spiritual sanctification and rest? For who can say that Christians ought not to be observant to serve the one God with religious obedience, not to worship an idol, not to take the name of the Lord in vain, to honour one's parents, not to commit adulteries, murders, thefts, false witness, not to covet another man's wife, or anything at all that belongs to another man? Who is so impious as to say that he does not keep those precepts of the law because he is a Christian, and is established not under the law, but under grace?
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

Both this one, who "found perdition," and that one who found "robbery," and also he who "denied the deposit," and everyone whosoever in any part "has harmed the soul of his neighbor and has sworn unjustly": "he shall restore," it says, "the principal itself and shall add a fifth part over and above, and to him whose it is he shall render it," according, at least, to that exposition concerning the adding of the fifth parts which we have already given before. "And he shall offer," it says, "to the Lord a ram of the sheep without blemish, at a price, for that in which he offended; and the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be remitted him for the one of all the things which he did and offended in it." We have said above what it is to offer a "ram," and this one bought "at the price of the holy shekel." Now it remains for us to state that difference — that there he placed "the price of the holy shekel," while here he says only "the price" and has designated neither the amount of the price nor the name of the money. For above, where the law was given for a sin which had been committed in "holy things," we said the "holy shekel" was named, and that "shekel" is the name of a coin, as elsewhere it is called "obol," elsewhere "drachma," elsewhere "mina" or "talent" or "small copper coin" or "denarius." Here, therefore, none of these is named, but only "a ram to be offered at a price" is spoken of. For it makes a difference to sin in holy things and to sin outside holy things. Do you wish to see this same distinction elsewhere too? — Hear how in the books of the Kingdoms the priest Eli says to his sons: "for if a man sins against a man, then the priest shall entreat for him; but if he sins against God, who shall entreat for him?" Similarly also John the Apostle says: "there is a sin unto death; I do not say concerning that, that one should pray." Since therefore there is a diversity of sins, we ought to learn from the spiritual law in which sins only a "ram" is to be bought, and in which one is to be purchased "with the holy shekel"; and let us also inquire who these are that sell the rams. I judge them to be those who dispense the rams for sacrifice, who are also those who sell the oil for the lamps of the virgins, concerning whom the prudent ones said to the foolish virgins: "go to those who sell and buy for yourselves." They sell, therefore, either oil for the lights or rams for the sacrifices — who else but the holy prophets and the Apostles, who, when I have sinned, show me and give me counsel how I ought to correct my errors and amend my sins? Isaiah sells me a "ram" for sacrificing for sin, when he says to me as it were from the person of God: "the whole burnt offerings of rams and the fat of lambs and the blood of bulls and of goats I do not want." And a little after he adds: "take away your wickednesses from your souls, from before your eyes; learn to do good, rescue him who suffers injury, judge for the orphan and do justice for the widow; and come, let us dispute, says the Lord. And though your sins be as scarlet, I will whiten them as snow; but though they be as crimson, I will make them white as wool." Daniel too sells me a "ram," when he says that: "there is no place for sacrificing in your sight, that we might find mercy. But in a contrite soul and a spirit of humility may we be received, as if in a multitude of fat lambs; so let our sacrifice be in your sight today." David too sells us the "ram" of sacrifice, when he says: "a sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit, a broken and humbled heart God does not despise." Since therefore each of the prophets, or even of the Apostles, has given counsel to those who transgress, by which they may be able to correct or amend their sin, they will rightly be seen to have sold rams to these for sacrifice. But what price do they take from those who purchase? That, I suppose, the zeal of reading, the vigils of hearing the words of God, and above all I think the most worthy price is obedience, concerning which the Lord says: "I prefer obedience to sacrifice, and a hearing of the word rather than whole burnt offerings."
40 Homilies on the Gospels, Homily 40

Some think that the precepts of the Old Testament are stricter than those of the New; but these are certainly deceived by careless consideration. For in the Old Testament, not avarice but robbery is punished. There, property unjustly taken is punished by fourfold restitution. But here this rich man is not blamed for taking what belonged to others, but for not giving what was his own.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

After these things it follows: "and the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: command Aaron and his sons, saying: this is the law of the whole burnt offering. This whole burnt offering shall be in its burning upon the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it and shall not be extinguished. And the priest shall put on himself the linen tunic, and shall put on the linen undergarment about his body, and shall take away the victim which the fire has consumed, the whole burnt offering, from the altar, and shall place it beside the altar. And he shall strip himself of his robe and be clothed with another robe, and shall cast out the victim which has been burned outside the camp into a clean place. And the fire upon the altar shall burn and shall not be extinguished; and the priest shall burn wood upon it in the morning, and shall heap the whole burnt offering upon it, and shall place upon it the fat of the peace offering; and the fire shall burn always upon the altar and shall not be extinguished." Hear that there ought always to be "fire upon the altar" — you too, if you wish to be a priest of God, as it is written: "for all of you shall be priests of the Lord"; for to you also it is said: "a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a people for possession." If therefore you wish to exercise the priesthood of your soul, let the fire never depart from your altar. This is what the Lord also commanded in the Gospels, that "your loins be girded, and your lamps burning." Let therefore the "fire" of faith and the "lamp" of knowledge be always kindled for you. But also what the Lord said in the Gospel, "your loins girded," this is the very same thing which now too the lawgiver commanded, that the priest be girded with the linen undergarment and thus, the old ashes laid aside, renew the sacred fires. For it behooves us too to say: "behold, the old things have passed away, and all things have become new." For he is girded with the linen undergarment, or, as it is said elsewhere, uses breeches, who has restrained the luxury of flowing lust with the girdle of chastity. For before all things the priest who assists at the divine altars ought to be girded with chastity, nor otherwise will he be able to purge the old things and to restore the new, unless he is clothed in linen. Concerning linen it has often already been said, and then especially, when we were speaking of the priestly garments, that this species holds the form of chastity, because the origin of linen is so brought forth from the earth that it is conceived from no admixture. Yet it must be observed that the priest uses one set of garments while he is in the ministry of the sacrifices, and another when he goes forth to the people. This Paul too did, most learned of high priests and most skilled of priests. He who, when he was in the assembly of the perfect, as though placed within the "holy of holies" and clothed in the robe of perfection, said: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this world nor of the princes of this world, who are being destroyed; but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which none of the princes of this age knew. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty." But after these things, as though "going out to the people," he changes his robe and is clothed with another far inferior to that one. And what does he say? "I judged," he says, "that I knew nothing else among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified." You see, therefore, this most learned priest, how, when he is within among the perfect, as it were in the "holy of holies," he uses one robe of doctrine; but when he "goes out" to those who are incapable, he changes the robe of the word and teaches lower things, and gives some "milk" to drink as "little ones," nourishes others with "vegetables" as "weak," but for others prepares "strong food" — namely for those who "according to their capacity of receiving have their senses exercised for the discernment of good or evil." Thus Paul knew how to change robes and to use some for the people, others in the ministry of holy things. But he himself, the high priest of high priests and priest of priests, our Lord and Savior, of whom the Apostle says that "he is the high priest of the good things to come" — hear how he first did these things and thus left them to his disciples to be imitated. The Gospel relates concerning him and says that: "he spoke to the crowds in parables, and without a parable he did not speak to them, but privately he resolved these things for his disciples." You see how he himself taught that the high priest ought to use certain garments when he goes forth "to the crowds," and others when he ministers to the learned and "perfect" in holy things. Whence it is to be desired by us and to be striven for, that Jesus not find us such — so unprepared and so bound up with the cares of the world — that he speak to us as with the crowds "in parables," so that "seeing we do not see and hearing we do not hear"; but rather that we may merit to be found among those to whom he says: "to you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God."
On the Tabernacle 2.11

A holocaust is burned on the altar when a good work is performed with the burning fire of charity in the heart of any elect person who is devoted to God completely (that is, with both body and soul). This is done all night until the morning when one does not cease to persevere in good works throughout all the time of his life, until one is taken from the body and merits seeing the morning of the world to come. The fire will be on the same altar, because we ought to be burning with that charity alone which the Lord gives to his church through the Holy Spirit.
On the Tabernacle 2.11

The priest who offers the holocaust is the Lord who is himself accustomed to kindle in us the fire of his charity and through it to make the sacrifices of our good actions acceptable to himself. And he is clothed in linen garments when he does these things because, in order that he may excite us to works of virtue, he sets before us the examples of his own incarnation, passion and death, which can be signified by linen, as we have frequently said.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

After this: "this is," it says, "the law of the sacrifice which the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer before the altar in the presence of the Lord. He shall take from it a full hand of the fine flour of the sacrifice with its oil and with all its frankincense, which are for the sacrifice, and shall place upon the altar the victim, an odor of sweetness, its memorial to the Lord. But what remains of it, Aaron and his sons shall eat. Unleavened it shall be eaten in a holy place; in the court of the tabernacle of testimony they shall eat it. It shall not be cooked leavened; this portion I have given to them from the offerings of the Lord; they are a holy of holies, as is that for sin and for offense. All the males of the priests shall eat it; a perpetual statute throughout your generations, from the offerings of the Lord. Everyone who touches these things shall be sanctified." In these things which are set forth, indeed the manner of sacrificing is given to the priests, and the observances by which God might be seen to be worshiped, or the people purified, or even by which provision might be made for the priests and ministers in the necessities of sustenance. For a measure is fixed for the "fine flour" to be offered in the sacrifice, which is called "the tenth part of an ephah"; over this "oil" is poured and "frankincense" is placed. But when he comes to the altar, the priest, it says, "shall take from it a full hand," so as to enclose within the fullness of his hand both the "oil" which was poured on and the "frankincense" which was placed on top, that this may be a libation and a "sacrifice" to God for an "odor of sweetness." The rest, it says, let it remain to the priests for eating, but the law delivered these to be eaten "in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle, so that nothing of them be leavened." "This," it says, "I have given as a portion to the priests, and these are a holy of holies." But he willed this also to be observed, that only the "males eat of it," that no woman touch it. He adds this too, that "he who touches these things shall be sanctified." But if we should now wish to inquire from those who "are Jews in what is manifest" concerning the particulars — for what reason this was said in this way and that in another way — they will satisfy us with a ready answer, saying: so it seemed good to the giver of the law; no one disputes his own master. And therefore, yielding to them in the rest, let us inquire concerning this last statement, that they may say how "everyone who touches of the sacrifice of holy things shall be sanctified." If a murderer touches it, if a profane man, if an adulterer, if one incestuous, will he be sanctified? For he made no exception, but said: "everyone who touches these things shall be sanctified." For let us suppose that even now the state of that temple is intact, that victims are offered, that sacrifices are completed; someone has entered the temple, wicked, unjust, impure, has found the flesh set forth from the sacrifices, has touched it: will he immediately be pronounced sanctified? Indeed in no way does either the nature of the matter or the truth of religion admit this; and therefore we must return to the evangelical and apostolic expositions, that the law may be able to be understood. For unless the Gospel takes away the veil from the face of Moses, his countenance cannot be seen nor his meaning understood. See therefore how in the church the disciples of the Apostles stand by these things which Moses wrote and defend them, that they both can be fulfilled and were written reasonably; but the teachers of the Jews, following the letter, make these things both impossible and unreasonable.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

Therefore the sacrifice, for which all these sacrifices had gone before in type and figure, one and perfect — "Christ" has been "immolated." If anyone "touches" the flesh of this sacrifice, he is immediately "sanctified"; if he is unclean, he is healed, if he is under a "plague." Thus at last did she understand — she of whom I made mention a little before, "who was suffering an issue of blood" — that he himself was the flesh of the sacrifice and the flesh of the "holy of holies"; and because she truly understood what was the flesh of the "holy of holies," for this reason she drew near. And indeed she does not dare to touch the holy flesh itself — for she had not yet been cleansed, nor had she grasped the things that are perfect — but she "touched the fringe of the garment" with which the holy flesh was covered, and by her faithful touch she drew forth "power" from the flesh which both sanctified her from uncleanness and "healed" her "from the plague" which she was suffering. Do not the words of Moses seem to you to be able to stand better in this order, in which he says: "everyone who touches of the holy flesh shall be sanctified"? For this flesh, which we have expounded, all who believed "from the nations" have touched. This also that man touched who said: "for we too were once foolish, and unbelieving, going astray, serving desires and various pleasures, acting in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another. But when the kindness and humanity of our Savior God shone forth, he saved us through the laver of regeneration and of the renewal of the Holy Spirit." And elsewhere he says: "and these things," he says, "indeed you were, but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God." For if, as we have said, anyone touches the flesh of Jesus in the manner which we expounded above, with whole faith, with all obedience, and draws near to Jesus as to the Word made flesh, this one has touched the flesh of the sacrifice and has been sanctified. But he too touches the flesh of the Word of whom the Apostle says: "but solid food is of the perfect, of those who according to their capacity of receiving have their senses exercised for the discernment of good and evil." He too, therefore, touches the flesh of the Word of God who examines its inner parts and can explain its hidden mysteries. And we too, if we had such understanding that we could discern by spiritual interpretation each single thing that is written in the law, and bring forth into the light of a subtler knowledge the sacrament veiled in each word; if we could so teach the church that nothing of the things read should remain ambiguous, nothing be left obscure — perhaps it could be said of us too that we have touched the holy flesh of the Word of God and have been sanctified. In this way also I understand that which was said, that "all the males from the priests shall eat it." For no woman, nor a lax and dissolute soul, will be able to eat the holy flesh of the Word of God. A "male" is sought, who may eat them. "Males," finally, are those who are brought into the count; nowhere is a woman, nowhere are "little ones" counted; whence the Apostle too said: "but when I became a man, I put away the things that were of a little one." Such, therefore, is that "male" sought, and such a man, who can eat the holy flesh, and eat it not in any place whatever, but "in a holy place within the court of the tabernacle." Let those hear these things who split the churches and, introducing foreign and perverse doctrines, think that they can eat the sacred flesh outside the temple of God and outside the Lord's court. Profane are their sacrifices, which are performed against the law of the commandment. They are commanded to be eaten "in a holy place," "within the courts of the tabernacle of testimony." The "courts of the tabernacle of testimony" are those which the wall of faith surrounds, which the columns of hope hold up, which the breadth of charity widens. Where these things are not, the holy flesh can neither be had nor eaten.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

And well is it that the things which are offered from the sacrifice of fine flour are offered "with a full hand, with oil" and "frankincense, for an odor of sweetness to the Lord." This passage the Apostle Paul briefly explained to the Philippians, saying: "I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odor of sweetness, a victim accepted, pleasing to God." In which he shows that mercy toward the poor pours oil into the sacrifice of God, but the ministry which is rendered to the saints puts on the sweetness of frankincense. But this is commanded to be done "with a full hand." For thus the same Apostle says, that "he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessing." There is, however, something in the sacrifice itself which is called the "memorial," which is said to be offered to the Lord. If I could "meditate day and night in the law of the Lord" and retain all the Scriptures in memory, I would have offered the "memorial" of my sacrifice to the Lord. Surely, if we cannot do all things, let us at least commit to memory those things which are now taught in the church, which are recited, so that, going out from the church and doing works of mercy and fulfilling the divine precepts, we may offer a sacrifice "with frankincense and oil" for a "memorial to the Lord." From these things, therefore, be instructed, that the things you hear in the church you may, like clean animals, as it were ruminating them, call back to memory, and confer with your heart the things that have been said. But if any things exceed your memory and surpass your understanding, do what the authority of the present commandment prescribes, saying: "but what remains of them, Aaron and his sons shall eat." If anything surpasses and exceeds your understanding or your memory, keep it for Aaron, that is, reserve it for the priest, reserve it for the teacher, that he himself may eat these things, he examine them, he expound them; just as elsewhere the same Moses says: "ask your fathers and they will announce to you, your elders and they will tell you." For they themselves know how these unleavened things ought to be eaten and to be expounded "in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth."
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 4

It is added in what follows: "and the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: this is the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when you shall anoint him, the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour in sacrifice always, half of it in the morning, and half of it after noon. In a pan it shall be made with oil, sprinkled he shall offer it soft, a sacrifice of fragments, a sacrifice for an odor of sweetness to the Lord. The priest who shall be anointed in his stead from among his sons shall make them; an eternal law; all shall be consummated. And every sacrifice of a priest shall be a whole burnt offering, and shall not be eaten." In the other precepts indeed the high priest furnishes his office to the people in offering the sacrifices; but in this commandment he attends to what is proper to himself and carries out what pertains to himself. For he is commanded "from the day on which he shall be anointed, always and in perpetuity to offer fine flour sprinkled with oil, soft, from a pan." And this he names "a sacrifice of fragments, for an odor of sweetness," and he commands that this remain "by an eternal law" and be transmitted to posterity. He adds, indeed, that it be observed that no "sacrifice of a priest" — that is, what he offers for himself — "be eaten" by anyone, but that it become a "whole burnt offering," which is to be consumed by fire. The precept, indeed, according to the letter is clear, yet I should like to see what type is formed in this and what figure. He wills "half" of this sacrifice to be offered "in the morning" and "half in the evening," a fixed measure of "fine flour sprinkled with oil, soft, from a pan." See whether, as I suspect, this "sacrifice of the priest" is not this very law which is promulgated through Moses, of which "half" is commanded to be offered "in the morning" and "half" indeed "toward evening." Which law he commanded to be divided into two parts, namely into the letter and the spirit. And the "half part" indeed, which is the letter, he commands to be offered "in the morning" — that is, in the first time of the law, which brought forth a new light and a new day to those to whom it was then given according to the letter. But "half" of it he commanded to be offered "in the evening"; for in the evening the coming of the Savior was given to us, in which that "half part" — that is, the meaning or the spirit of the law, according to which "the law is spiritual" — is offered "sprinkled with oil, soft." "Oil" is referred to mercy, which ought to abound in priests. "Soft" pertains to a subtle and pure understanding. But as to what is said, "from a pan," I think that he wishes the priest to be strict and, by much continence, dry and parched, in whom nothing can be found relaxed toward luxury, nothing wavering toward lust. But as to the fact that he named the sacrifice itself "of fragments," "for an odor of sweetness," I think that he wishes the fragments of the priests to be understood, when through them the letter of the law is broken and the spiritual food hidden within is drawn from it; that the hearing "crowds" may be refreshed, just as the Lord too is related to have done in the Gospels, where he blessed the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples, breaking them, set them before the "crowds"; and when all had been satisfied, "there remained," it says, "twelve baskets of fragments." This, therefore, is the "sacrifice of fragments," when we examine in minute detail the holy things of the law, that from them we may take spiritual and pure food. And this, it says, is the "eternal law." John the Apostle indeed in the Apocalypse says there is an "eternal Gospel." We find here too that it is written "eternal law," but those who wish to follow the law according to the letter — I should like them now to tell me how the law of this sacrifice can be "eternal," when indeed, the temple destroyed, the altar overturned, and all the things which were called holy profaned, this rite of sacrifices could not endure. How, then, will they call eternal what is now established to have long ago ceased and been ended? It remains that this law be called "eternal" according to that part in which we say the "law" is "spiritual" and that through it spiritual sacrifices can be offered, which can neither ever be broken in upon nor cease. For they are not in a place which is overturned, or in a time which is changed, but in the faith of the believer and in the heart of the one who sacrifices. Certainly, as to what it says, "it shall not be eaten of the sacrifice of the priest, but it shall be a whole burnt offering," it is certain that this refers to the person of our Lord and Savior; for of his sacrifice "it shall not be eaten, but it shall be a whole burnt offering." In this place the sacrifice is to be taken as the word itself and the doctrine, of which none shall eat — that is, none disputes, none reconsiders, but it is a "whole burnt offering." For whatever he said, whatever he established, endures by an eternal consecration, nor is anyone found so insane or so profane as to be able to reconsider his words; which we ought to hold, as a "whole burnt offering, a sacrifice offered to God," in all worship and veneration; because "heaven and earth shall pass away, but his words shall not pass away," but always remain, just as he himself always remains. Through him to God the Father, with the Holy Spirit, "is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 5

"And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering; in the place where the whole burnt offerings are slaughtered, they shall also slay that which is for sin before the Lord; they are the holy of holies. The priest who offers it shall eat it; it shall be eaten in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle of testimony. Everyone who touches its flesh shall be sanctified; and whoever has been sprinkled with its blood upon a garment, whatever has been sprinkled, that too shall be washed in a holy place. And the earthen vessel in which it has been cooked shall be broken; but if it has been cooked in a bronze vessel, he shall scour it and rinse it with water. Every male of the priests shall eat of these; they are the holy of holies to the Lord. And all the things that are for sin, from whose blood some has been brought into the tabernacle of testimony to make supplication in the holy place, shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire." All these things, unless we take them in a sense other than the letter of the text shows — as we have already often said — when they are read in church, will present an obstacle and a subversion to the Christian religion rather than exhortation and edification. But if the matter is examined and it is found in what sense these things were said, and they are perceived in a manner worthy of God, who is written to have said them, then indeed one who hears these things will become a Jew — yet not that one "who is a Jew outwardly", but the one "who is a Jew inwardly"; according to that distinction of the Jew which the Apostle draws when he says: "For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor the circumcision which is manifestly in the flesh, but the one who is a Jew inwardly, by the circumcision of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; whose praise is not from men, but from God." The impious heretics, not understanding this distinction between the visible Jew and the invisible Jew, have fled not only from these Scriptures, but from God himself, who gave this law and the divine Scriptures to men, and have fashioned for themselves another God besides him "who founded heaven and earth" — whereas assuredly the truth of the faith holds one and the same God of the law and of the gospels, the creator "of things visible and invisible"; for even things visible preserve a great kinship with things invisible, so that the Apostle says: "the invisible things of God are seen from the creation of the world, being understood through the things that have been made". Just as, therefore, "things visible and invisible" bear a kinship to one another — earth and heaven, soul and flesh, body and spirit — and this world is composed of the conjunctions of these, so also it must be believed that Holy Scripture is composed of things visible and invisible: as of a kind of body, namely the letter which is seen, and of the soul of the sense which is apprehended within it, and of a spirit according to that by which it also holds within itself certain "heavenly" things, as the Apostle said: "they serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things". Since therefore these things are so, let us call upon God, who made the soul and body and spirit of Scripture — the body for those who were before us, the soul indeed for us, and the spirit for those who "in the age to come shall obtain the inheritance of eternal life", through which they may attain to the heavenly kingdoms — and let us now seek that soul of the law, of which we spoke, so far as it pertains to the present for the time being. But I do not know whether we can also ascend to its spirit in these things which have been read to us concerning the sacrifices. For we ought, just as we have shown that the one whom we called "the Jew inwardly" is circumcised not in the flesh but in the heart, so also to show that he sacrifices not in the flesh but in the heart, and that he eats of the sacrifices not in the flesh but in the spirit.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 5

But let us now see what those things are which are set forth in the law. "And the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons, saying: This is the law of the sin offering" and the rest which have been read in the present passage. And I remember that we have already said before that the law is not always given to the same persons, but one thing indeed is said to the sons of Israel, another to the sons of Aaron, and yet another, as we observed some time ago, to Moses and Aaron. There is also another law which is given to Moses alone, so that not even Aaron is made a partaker of that law. Who has been so illumined by God with the gift of knowledge as to be able to discourse fully and clearly on the distinctions and diversities of each of these? For we find in what follows a command of the Lord given to Moses alone, and it is ordered that "the little breast of the ram of consecration" be given to Moses, "as the Lord commanded Moses," it says. In which portion neither Aaron nor his sons are made partakers. And the law which pertains to "the ram of consecration" is found to be unable to reach even to Aaron nor to his sons — much less to the rest of the sons of Israel — but only to Moses, who was "the friend of God". But what need is there to anticipate the things that are to be read hereafter? For the present the law has now been read which is promulgated to Aaron and his sons, "the law of the sin offering", that is, of the victim which is offered "for sin": "in the place," it says, "in which the whole burnt offerings are slaughtered, there they shall also slay that which is for sin, in the sight of the Lord; they are the holy of holies". Many things indeed have already, with God's help, been said in the foregoing about the rite of the sacrifices according to the spiritual understanding; but even now, if the grace of the Lord deign to visit us and you strive with your prayers, we shall add whatever the Lord may grant. Certain of the victims belong to God alone, so that no man partakes of them. Certain belong to Aaron the priest and to his sons; certain to him and to his sons and daughters, so that even the wife of the priest is permitted to eat of them. Certain belong to the priests and their sons and daughters, but of which the sons of Israel too are permitted to eat. And in those victims of which the sons of Israel are permitted to eat, the priests and the sons of the priests without doubt also have a share; yet not of every victim which the priest shall eat will it be permitted that the sons of Israel too eat of it. Therefore, since these are the distinctions of the victims, that one which we said belongs to God alone, of which it is not lawful for either Moses or Aaron or his sons to partake, we find named sometimes indeed "whole burnt offerings" (holocaustomata), but sometimes not whole burnt offerings but "holocarpoma", as though we should say that it is wholly fruit — namely that which is offered to God. There is, then, a first legislation concerning the sacrifices, if indeed you have either observed or diligently retained what has been read and expounded, and if the things either that are said by us or that are read from the divine volumes do not run through your ears in vain. The first victim, then, is the "whole burnt offerings" (holocaustomata); for it was not fitting that any other victim be named first except that which was offered to almighty God. The second victim is that which is assigned to the priests for eating. The third is that which even the sons of Israel — namely those who offer — are permitted to touch or to eat. But not all the sons of Israel, only those who are "clean"; for only those who are "clean" are commanded to eat of the sacrifices. But all these victims, you who are "a Jew inwardly", I do not wish you to seek in visible animals, nor to suppose that what ought to be offered to God is to be found in dumb beasts. Seek these victims within your own self, and you will find them within your soul. Understand that you have within your very self herds of oxen, those which are blessed in Abraham. Understand that you have both flocks of sheep and flocks of goats, in which the patriarchs were blessed and multiplied. Understand that within you there are also birds of heaven. And do not marvel that we say these things are within you; understand that you are another world in miniature, and that within you are the sun, the moon, and also the stars. For if this were not so, the Lord would never have said to Abraham: "Look at the heaven and see the stars, if they can be numbered for their multitude; so shall your seed be". And do not marvel, I say, if it is said to Abraham that "so shall your seed be, as the stars of heaven are"; namely concerning those who, born of his faith, live rationally and keep the divine laws and precepts. Hear something further, the Savior saying to his disciples: "you are the light of the world". Do you doubt that there is within you a sun and a moon, you to whom it is said that you are "the light of the world"? Do you wish to hear still something further about yourself, lest perhaps, thinking small and lowly things of yourself, you neglect your life as something cheap? This world has its own governor, it has one who rules it and dwells in it, almighty God, as he himself says through the prophet: "do I not fill heaven and earth, says the Lord?". Hear, then, what almighty God himself says even about you, that is, about men. "I will dwell," he says, "in them and walk among them." He adds still something more with regard to your person.
