Ground. Hebrew and Septuagint, "the extremity of thy field." The Rabbins say, a sixtieth part of all the products of the earth, was to be left for the poor. (Selden, Jur. vi. 6.) Thus God teaches his people to exercise themselves in the acts of mercy. (Du Hamel)

Strangers. Septuagint and Syriac, "proselytes," who might dwell in the country. As the soil did not belong to them, great compassion was requisite: otherwise they must have perished, or become slaves. --- Lord; the sole proprietor. (Calmet)

Lie. "When no injury is done to another, it is a great question whether a lie can ever be justified. The case would perhaps be easily decided, if we considered the commandments alone, and not the examples," of those holy men who seem to have sometimes thought it lawful. (St. Augustine, q. 68) But is it not better to allow that these were under an inculpable mistake, than to defend one fault, because it is not attended with the guilt of another, by hurting others? Even lies of jest and of excuse, are contrary to the gravity and open-dealing of a Christian; and God never speaks of lying without marks of disapprobation. (Haydock) --- Hebrew, "you shall not deny, or extenuate yourselves," pretending that you cannot give alms. (Oleaster)
Profane. No greater indignity can be offered to God, than to solicit Him, as it were, to assist us in doing evil, by attesting falsehood. (Philo)
Morning. Pay what is due to the labourer, immediately, if he desire it. (Haydock) --- It was customary among the Jews to pay their workmen in the evening, Matthew xx. 8.

Deaf. The word Kophos, used by the Septuagint, means also the dumb, as these defects are generally found in the same person. Nothing can be more base, than to attack those who are unable to defend themselves. Solon forbids anyone "to speak ill of the dead," though he may receive an injury from his children. Those who undermine and ruin the reputation of the absent, are no less to be condemned.

Detracter, whisperer. Hebrew rakil, stands for both these terms. Some translate a parasite, a merchant, vilifying the goods of others to enhance the price of his own; or a spy, seeking to discover and laugh at others' faults. --- Neighbour; accusing him wrongfully, to the danger of his life; or lying in wait for him like an assassin. But strive rather to rescue those who are attacked. Those who neglect this duty, are responsible for the consequences, according to the Jews, (Selden, Jur. iv. 3,) and the laws of the Egyptians. (Diodorus 1.)

Openly, is not in the Hebrew or other versions. Instead of bearing malice at the heart, we are authorized to demand our right in a legal manner, or to correct in a fraternal matter, the person who may have injured us, lest we incur sin for our neglect, and the offender continue impenitent. Jesus Christ instructs us to do this with as little disturbance as possible, Matthew xviii. 15. Yet public sins must undergo a public correction, 1 Timothy v. 20. (St. Augustine, ser. 82.) Love should regulate our complaints. (St. Augustine, q. 70.)

Revenge, by private authority, or out of passion, which the pagans themselves acknowledged was more becoming a brute than a man, feræ est. (Musonias, Sen. de ira ii. 32.) --- Citizens. Hebrew, "observe or lie not in wait." Septuagint, "act not with fury against the son of thy people." (Calmet) --- Hebrew notor, means to upbraid when doing a kindness. --- Thy friend. Hebrew rehaka, may denote thy neighbour, or any one with whom we have any thing to do. Thus God orders us to love strangers as ourselves, (ver. 34,) and to help our enemy, Exodus xxiii. 4. The false insinuations of the Jews are fully exploded by Jesus Christ, Matthew xxii. 39. We must love the offender, but detest the offence. (St. Augustine, contra Faust. xix. 24.) If God required his people to exterminate the Chanaanites, he did not authorized them to entertain any personal animosity against their persons, but they were to act as ministers of his justice. "O Lord, (said Philo very justly) we do not rejoice at the misfortune of our enemy, (Flaccus) having learnt from thy holy laws to compassionate the distress of others. But we thank thee for....delivering us from our afflictions." (Calmet)

Kind. Mules were therefore either brought from other countries, (3 Kings x. 28,) or they were produced by some of the same species, as, good authors assert, is frequently the case in Syria, Cappadocia, &c. (Pliny, [Natural History?] viii. 44.; Pineda) (Tirinus) --- Spencer (Leg. ii. 20,) says, without any proof, that this law had a reference to the impure conjunctions of animals, in honour of Venus and of Priapus. --- Different seeds, &c. This law tends to recommend simplicity and plain-dealing in all things; and to teach the people not to join any false worship or heresy with the worship of the true God. (Challoner) --- Draw not the yoke with infidels, 2 Corinthians vi. (Theodoret, q. 27.) These different colours were not in themselves evil, since they were used in the priests' vestments. They insinuate, that we must avoid schisms. (Worthington) --- The sowing of different seeds tends to impoverish the soil. (Pliny, xviii. 10.) The Egyptians sowed various seeds on a board, covered with fine mould; and, observing which sort was destroyed by the heat of the sun in the dog-days, superstitiously refrained, that year, from sowing any of it, lest it should produce no crop. (Palladius) --- Sorts. The Rabbins say of linen and wool, as Deuteronomy xxii. 11. They allow other sorts. Josephus ([Aniquities?] iv. 8,) supposes, that garments of the former description were thus reserved for the priests alone. The Flamen, among the Romans, could not wear a woollen garment sowed with thread, without committing a sin; piaculum erat, says Servius. These precepts were to be literally observed, though they concealed a moral instruction of the greatest consequence, importing that all unnatural intercourse was to be avoided. Pythagoras conveyed his instructions under similar enigmatical expressions, saying, "we must not stir up the fire with a sword," &c., as Solomon does likewise. (Proverbs xxx. 15 and Ecclesiasticus xii. 3, 6.) (Calmet)

Marriageable. Hebrew, "promised, or given in marriage." Septuagint, "reserved for another....she shall," &c. Onkelos and the Arabic version suppose also, that the woman alone was to be scourged with leather thongs; a punishment to which the Samaritan copy condemns only the man. The Rabbins agree with the Septuagint. Others translate, "there shall be an enquiry made, or they shall be set free, and shall not die."
Pray. Hebrew and Septuagint, "shall atone for him with the ram of the sin-offering, before the Lord, for his sin."

The first-fruits. Præputia, literally their fore-skins: it alludes to circumcision, and signifies that for the first three years the trees were to be as uncircumcised, and their fruit unclean; till the fourth year their increase was sanctified and given to the Lord, that is, to the priests. (Challoner) --- In some countries, people take off the buds to strengthen the tree. (Calmet) --- The fruit, during the three first years, is not esteemed so good or wholesome; and therefore, it could not with propriety be presented to God. (Philo de Creatione.) --- Unclean. Hebrew, "three years shall it be as uncircumcised unto you; it shall not be eaten." (Haydock)

Lord. It was to be brought to the holy city, and offered with the other tithes, out of which a feast was made for the poor, &c. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] iv. 8.) Besides the first-fruits for the priests, and the tithes for the Levites, out of which they again paid tithes to the priests, there was an annual tithe prescribed, (Deuteronomy xii. 12,) to supply a feast for the indigent, &c., at Jerusalem, along with this fruit; and another, every third year, designed for the poor alone (Deuteronomy xiv. 28,) at the place of each one's abode. (Tirinus)

Blood. The flesh of any animal. The blood must belong to God. The members of the Sanhedrim eat nothing on the day that a criminal is executed, supposing that this is the meaning of the precept. The Septuagint read erim, "on the mountains;" and another version has, "on the roof," as if the worship of idols on high places were forbidden. (Haydock) --- Divine. Perhaps by means of "serpents," or "plates of brass," as the Hebrew néss, may insinuate. These methods were known to the ancients. (Horace, Ode iii. 37.; Pliny xxx. 2.) (Calmet) --- Dreams. Hebrew, times. See Galatians iv. 10. (Haydock)

Cut your hair, &c. This, and other such like things, of themselves indifferent, were forbidden by God, that they might not imitate the Egyptians or other infidels, who practised these things out of superstition, in honour of their false deities. (Challoner) --- The pagans consecrated locks of hair, and their beard, when it was first cut, to Apollo, the river gods, the hours, Esculapius, &c. Some, at Rome, hung the hair on a tree. (Tirinus) --- The Arabians and Macæ left only a tuft of hair at the top of their head, in imitation of Bacchus. (Herodotus iii. 8.; iv. 175.) This tuft is called sisoe by the Septuagint who seem to have alluded o the Hebrew term tsitsith. See Ezechiel viii. 3. The ancient scholiast says, this was left in honour of Saturn. It resembled a crown. The same custom was observed by the Syrians, (Lucian) Idumeans, &c. (Jeremias ix. 25.) --- Beard. Hebrew, "the angle, or extremity of your beard." These regulations would seem beneath the attention of a lawgiver. But they were made in opposition to some profane customs of the surrounding nations. The Jews still observe this direction, and leave the beard from the ear to the chin, (where they let it grow pretty long) and also two mustaches, or whiskers, on the top lip. The Egyptian mummies have only the beard on the chin. The eyebrows and other hair of the gods and inhabitants of Egypt, were entirely cut off. In mourning the chin was also shaved. God forbids his people to imitate them. (Calmet) --- But heretics need not hence infer, that the tonsure of priests and monks is reprehensible. (Radulph.) --- Superstition and affected delicacy in curling, &c., are to be avoided. (Tirinus)

Dead. Adonis or Osiris; as if you were mourning for them, in which sense the former verse may be explained. At funerals it was customary to cut off the hair. Achilles and his soldiers did so at the death of Patroclus. (Homer) --- The Persians also cut the manes of their horses, to shew their grief for the loss of Masistius, (Herodotus ix. 24,) as Alexander did when Hephæstion died. (Plutarch) --- The Egyptians, Assyrians, &c., cut their hair on the like occasions, and the Hebrews did so too; whether they neglected this law, or it was rather designed only to hinder them from joining in a superstitious lamentation for some idol. They also cut their bodies, Genesis l, and Jeremias xli. 5. The pagans did so, intending thereby to appease the anger of the infernal deities: ut sanguine....inferis satisfaciant, (Varro, Servius): or to please the deceased. (Plutarch, de consol.) Thus Virgil represents Anna, Æneid iv.: Unguibus ora soror fædans & pectora pugnis. The Roman and Athenian laws restrained this cruelty of women towards themselves. But in Persia, the children and servants of great men still make an incision upon their arms, when their father or master dies. The women in Greece also observe a solemn mourning, with loud lamentations, tearing their cheeks and hair, and reciting the memorable actions of the deceased. The Christians and Jews of Syria inflict still more dangerous wounds upon themselves. The latter have always esteemed it lawful to adopt the customs of the nations with whom they lived, provided they were not attended with superstition; which makes us conclude, that what Moses here forbids, was done in honour of some idol. --- Marks, made with a hot iron, representing false gods, as if to declare that they would serve them for ever. (Philo) --- The Assyrians had generally such characters upon their bodies. Philopator ordered the converts from the Jewish religion to be marked with ivy, in honour of Bacchus. (3 Macchabees) Theodoret (q. 18,) mentions, that the pagans were accustomed to cut their cheeks, and to prick themselves with needles, infusing some black matter, out of respect for the dead, and for demons. Allusion is made to these customs, Apocalypse xiii. 16, and Isaias xlix. 15. Christians have sometimes marked their arms with the cross, or name of Jesus. (Procopius in Isai. xliv. 5.) (Calmet) --- As St. Jane Frances de Chantal did her breast. (Breviary, August 21.) Nomen pectori insculpsit. St. Paul says, I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body, Galatians vi. 17. The Church historians relate, that St. Francis and St. Catharine received miraculously the prints of his wounds. (Haydock)

Strumpet, which was done formerly in the honour of idols. "They gave to Venus the prostitutions of their daughters." (St. Augustine, City of God xviii. 5.) "In Cyprus they lead the unmarried women to the sea-shore, in order to acquire a dowry by these means on certain stated days, as a libation to Venus." (Justin.) --- Such things were common in the East. See Lucian de dea Syr.; Strabo xvi. -- Joel (iii. 3,) reproaches the Jews with prostituting their sons and daughters for bread; for there were also effeminate men among them. (3 Kings xiv. 24 and 4 Kings xxiii. 7.) See Baruch vi. 42 and Osee iv. 14. (Calmet)

Wizards. Hebrew oboth, denotes familiar spirits, (1 Kings viii.[xxviii.?] 7,) which gave answers from the belly or breast, as from a bottle; whence such wizards are called by the Greeks, engastrimuthoi; and by Sophocles, sternomanteis. (Calmet) --- Soothsayers, are properly those who judge what will happen by inspecting victims. (Menochius) --- Hebrew yiddehonim, means connoisseurs, intelligent people, gnostics, or those who pretend that they can penetrate the secrets naturally impenetrable to the mind of man. Septuagint epaoidoi, "enchanters," who undertake to keep off all misfortunes. "Surely, (says Pliny, xxx. 1,) to learn this art, (of magic) Pythagoras....and Plato undertook long voyages by sea, or rather went into banishment. This they extolled at their return; this they kept as a secret. Hanc in arcanis habuere."

Aged man. Such are supposed to be possessed of wisdom and experience. The Egyptians and Lacedemonians rose up out of respect to an old man. (Herodotus ii. 80.) The Rabbins pretend that a person ought to rise up when the old man is four cubits distant, provided he be, as he ought, a man of wisdom; for otherwise he is entitled to no honour. But this would be making inferiors judges of their merit. The Chaldean, Philo, &c., comprise those "learned in the law," under the name of old men.
Rule; Hebrew, "taking dimensions" with a yard, tape, &c.
Weights. Hebrew, "stones of justice," for stone weights were formerly used, Proverbs xvi. 11. --- Bushel, &c. Hebrew, "a just epha, and a just hin." (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 11

Recently there was recited in the ears of the Church the word of God saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God". What this name "holy" intends for itself, and what it signifies in the divine Scriptures, must be inquired into more diligently, so that, when we have learned the force of the word, we may also be able to fulfill its work. Let us therefore gather from the divine Scriptures those things over which we find the word "holy" said, and we discover that not only human beings, but even dumb animals are called "holy"; we find also that "vessels" of the ministry are called "holy", and that vestments are said to be "holy", and no less the places which are set within cities or suburbs and assigned to the priests. Among the dumb animals indeed, the "firstborn" of oxen or of flocks are commanded by the law to be sanctified to the Lord, and it is said: do not, it says, perform any work with them, since they are sanctified to the Lord. Concerning vessels, however, when in the tabernacle of testimony the vessels of the ministry, the "censers" or "bowls" or the rest of this kind, are called "holy" "vessels". Concerning vestments too, when the "robe" of the high priest Aaron and the "linen tunic" and the rest of the vestments of this kind are said to be "holy". If therefore we consider in what sense all these have been named "holy", we shall perceive how we too ought to give effort, that we may be able to be holy. A firstborn ox has been born to me: it is not permitted to me to employ it for common work; for it is consecrated to the Lord, and therefore it is called holy. We understand therefore from this dumb animal how the law, that which it wills to be holy, commands to serve no other but the Lord alone. Again, the "cups" or "bowls" which it calls holy are those which are never commanded to go out from the temple, but always to be in the holy places, nor to serve any human uses whatsoever. Similarly also the "vestments" which are named "holy" are not commanded to serve for use within the house of the high priest, but to be in the temple and never at all to be carried out from there, but to be consecrated to this alone, that the high priest ministering to God with them may be clothed, and that they may always be in the temple; while for the other common uses he uses common garments. Similarly also with these "cups and bowls" which are called "holy", it is not permitted to use them for human and common uses, but only for the divine ministries. But if you have understood how an animal or a vessel or a vestment is called holy, understand consequently that by these observances and laws a human being too is called holy. For if anyone has devoted himself to God, if anyone has entangled himself in no worldly affairs, "that he may please him to whom he has proved himself"; if anyone is separated and set apart from the rest of human beings who live carnally and are bound to mundane affairs, not "seeking the things that are upon the earth, but those which are in the heavens", that one is rightly called holy. For as long as he is mingled with the "crowds" and is tossed about in the multitude of those who are fluctuating, and is not free for God alone, set apart from the common throng, he cannot be holy. For concerning those what shall we say, who hasten with the crowds of the gentiles to the spectacles and defile their own sight and hearing with shameless words and deeds? It is not ours to pronounce concerning such. For they themselves can perceive and see what portion they have chosen for themselves. You therefore, who hear these things, to whom the divine law is recited, whom the very word of God itself addresses, saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God", understand wisely the things that are said, so that you may be blessed when you have done them. For this is what is said to you: "Separate yourself" from every one, not only every man, but even "from a brother walking disorderly and not according to" the apostolic "traditions". "Be separated", indeed, "you who carry the vessels of the Lord, and go out from the midst of them, says the Lord". "Separate yourself" from earthly deeds, "separate yourself" from the concupiscence of the world: "for everything that is in the world", according to the Apostle, "is the concupiscence of the flesh and the concupiscence of the eyes, which is not from God". When therefore you have separated yourself from all these things, devote yourself to God as a firstborn calf; let sin not work through you, nor let malice impose a yoke upon you, but be set aside and set apart, given over only to priestly uses like a firstborn animal. Be set apart and severed, like holy "bowls" and holy "censers" free only for the uses of the temple and for the ministry of God. Separate yourself and set yourself aside from all pollution of sin, and be set aside and set apart within the temple of God like the holy garments of the high priest. For that man is set apart and separated within the temple of God, "who meditates in the law of God day and night" and who "greatly desires his commandments". "Be holy" therefore, "says the Lord, for I too am holy". What is: "for I too am holy"? Just as I, he says, am set apart and far separated from all things that are adored or worshiped whether on earth or in heaven; just as I exceed every creature and am set apart from all things that have been made by me: so also be you set apart from all who are not holy nor dedicated to God. But we say that one is set apart not by places, but by deeds, and not by regions, but by manners of life. Finally, the very word which in the Greek language is spoken, ἅγιος, signifies as it were to be outside the earth. For whoever shall have consecrated himself to God will rightly be seen to be outside the earth and outside the world; for he too is able to say, walking upon the earth: "we have our manner of life in the heavens". Solomon also in the Proverbs says: "it is a snare for a strong man hastily to sanctify something of his own; for after he has vowed it, it comes about that he repents". And this indeed is what he says, lest perhaps anyone, "when he gathers fruit from the threshing floor or wine from the presses", and has said: I wish to offer only so much to the Church, or to supply only so much for the use of the poor or of pilgrims; if afterward he presumes to take something for his own uses out of that measure which he vowed, he has now not presumed upon his own fruits, but has violated the holy things of God. And therefore "it is a snare for the strong man to sanctify something", that is, to vow it to God and afterward, led by repentance, to recall to his own uses those things which he had consecrated. But even if we consecrate and offer ourselves to God, or also if we vow others, let us observe this "snare", lest perhaps, after we have vowed ourselves to God, we again be subjected to human uses or deeds. Now each one vows himself, for example, as the Nazirites used to do, consecrating themselves to the temple of God for three or four or however many years it pleased, so that they might always be free there, observing those things which are written concerning the Nazirites; that they should nourish the hair of the head, and "no iron should go up upon their head" throughout the whole time of their vow, that they should not touch wine nor anything "from the vine", and whatever else the profession of the vow had embraced. But someone also vows another to God, as Hannah did with Samuel; for before he was born, she offered him to God, saying: "and I will give him to the Lord, given all the days of his life". From all which it is clear how each one of us, who wishes to be holy, ought to consecrate himself to God and to be occupied besides with no affairs or deeds which pertain in no way to God.
The Stromata Book 2

During the harvest, [the law] forbids owners to gather up the bits which fall from the sheaves and similarly advises that in harvesting something should be left behind unreaped. By this it gives excellent teaching to owners in the practice of generous sharing by leaving some of their property for those in need and providing the poor with a chance for food.
The Stromata Book 2

Do you see how the law proclaims simultaneously the justice and goodness of God, who provides food unstintingly for all? Again, in the grape harvest the harvesters are forbidden to go back and cut anything that has been left over or to collect fallen grapes. The same rules are applied to olive gatherers. In fact the principle of tithing crops and flocks was an education in honoring the divine. We are not to be totally absorbed by profit but to share humanely with the neighbor as well.
LETTER 62 (19).3

Let no one deny the hireling the wage he is owed, since we too are hirelings of our God, and from him we look forward to the reward of our labor. And if you indeed, whatever type of businessman you are, deny your hireling a monetary payment that is a perishable trifle, you shall be denied the reward of heaven that has been promised. You shall not defraud, as the law says, the hireling of his pay.
THE BOOK OF PASTORAL RULE, Part 3

For to curse the deaf is to disparage one who is absent and does not hear; but to put a stumbling-block before the blind is to act indeed with discernment, but yet to give cause of offence to him who has not the light of discernment.
LETTER 79.1

"You shall not be partial to the poor," a precept given lest under pretext of showing pity we should judge an unjust judgment. For each individual is to be judged not by his personal importance but by the merits of his case. His wealth need not stand in the way of the rich man, if he makes a good use of it; and poverty of itself can be no recommendation to the poor if in the midst of squalor and want he fails to stay away from wrongdoing.
COMMENTARY ON MATTHEW 3

The second commandment is like it, since it is the love of a human being who was made according to the image of God, and perhaps also according to his likeness. But in the exposition of the commandment which is set down concerning the love of one's neighbor, these things also must be said. For, according to what is said in the tenth Psalm, "he who loves iniquity hates his own soul", and according to what is said in Proverbs, "he who rejects discipline hates himself", it is manifest that no one who loves iniquity loves his neighbor as himself, since he does not even love himself; and no one who rejects discipline loves his neighbor as himself, seeing that he does not love his very self either. And thus it comes about that he who "loves iniquity", and "hates his own soul", cannot keep the second commandment. Likewise also "he who rejects discipline" loves some sin; and therefore he too who rejects any word of God's discipline "hates his own soul".
LETTER 177

Long before Christ it had been said, "You shall not covet"; long before it had been said, "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," a phrase which, as the apostle says, expresses the fulfillment of the whole law. And as no one loves himself unless he loves God, the Lord says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend on these two commandments.
40 Homilies on the Gospels - Homily 20

For since it is written in the law: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself," he is proven to love his neighbor less who does not share with him even those things necessary to himself in his neighbor's time of need. Therefore the precept is given about dividing two tunics with one's neighbor, because this could not be said of one tunic, since if one is divided, no one is clothed. For with half a tunic, both he who receives remains naked and he who gave remains naked.

n: Moloch. See chap. xviii. 21.

I will thus execute vengeance upon him by the hands of the people; and, in case they neglect it, or the crime be secret, I will surely punish the guilty person, and all who may have consented to his wickedness, ver. 5. (Haydock) --- Face: Chaldean, "wrath," which manifests itself on the countenance. (Du Hamel)
My commandment: Hebrew, "If the people hide their face not to see:" (Calmet) or Septuagint, "look over on purpose, and neglect the man who has given of his seed to the ruler."
Them. To have recourse to them, is to deal with the devil and to commit idolatry. See chap. xix. 31.
Sanctify you, and order you to keep at a distance from the impure worship of other nations. (Haydock)

Die. The Rabbins say, by being strangled, when nothing farther is added: but if the following addition be made, stoning is understood. But their authority is not of much weight, and is contradicted, ver. 2. Stoning was the most usual method of putting to death in the days of Moses, and is commonly meant; or perhaps the judges might determine the mode of execution. --- Upon him. He deserves to die. He can blame no other. See Matthew xxvii. 25. (Calmet) --- For greater infamy, the person to be stoned or hung, was stripped of his clothes. (Tirinus) --- The punishment of lapidation (ver. 2,) seems to be designed for the following crimes, as it was for adultery, Deuteronomy xxii. 24. (Menochius) (John viii. 5.)

Adulteress. Philo (de Josephus) says, whoever discovered a man in the very act, might kill him; and the Roman law allowed the same liberty, impunè necato. But God requires a juridical process, and witnesses, as we see in the case of Susanna, (Daniel xiii.) and in that of the woman who was brought to our Saviour. [John viii.] One witness might authorize a person to put his wife away, and if he then retained her, he was esteemed a fool, Proverbs xviii. 23. But more witnesses were requisite before she could be put to death. They put their hands on the heads of the guilty, thus taking their blood upon themselves, if they accused them wrongfully. Solon allowed the husband to kill the adulterer. The woman was not permitted to wear any ornaments, or to enter any temple afterwards. If she did, any one might tear her clothes, and beat, but not kill her.

Father. See chap. xviii. 8. It is supposed that the father was dead, otherwise the punishment would probably be greater than for adultery. The Samaritan, "with the wife of his father's brother." (Calmet)
Crime. Hebrew tebel, "confusion," the same term which is used in speaking of bestiality, (chap. xviii. 23,) though the latter crime be more enormous. (Haydock)

Alive, is not in the original; but must be understood. The Rabbins say melted lead was to be poured down the throats of the guilty. The words of Moses seem rather to refer to external fire. (Calmet) --- With them, if they both gave their consent to the crime. (Menochius)

The beast also ye shall kill. The killing of the beast was for the greater horror of the crime, and to prevent the remembrance of such abomination. (Challoner) --- The beast was to be killed with clubs; the man was stoned to death. (Jonathan)
Them. This monstrous abomination, teras, as Herodotus, an eye-witness calls it, was not unknown to the Egyptians. Gunaiki tragos emisgeto; (B. ii. 46,) nor to other nations. (Apuleius, Met. 10.)

A crime. Hebrew chesed, commonly signifies an act of piety or goodness, as if Moses intended to insinuate that such marriages were at first lawful. (Thalmud; Selden, Jur. v. 8.) But a softer term is used to denote a great impiety, as the Hebrews say to bless, when they mean to curse, or to blaspheme; (Calmet) and the Greeks call the furies Eumenides, or "the good-natured." --- One another's. Hebrew, "He hath uncovered his sister's," &c. Whether they saw what was indecent or not, if they admitted of any unlawful commerce, they were to be stoned to death. (Haydock)

People, if the action become public; otherwise the man may be purified, chap xv. 24. This intemperance was by a positive law declared a mortal offence in the Jews, though in itself it might be venial. (Sanchez ix. 21.) The text shews that the woman here gives her consent. --- And she open. Hence she deserves to die, for exposing herself and her children to great danger. (Haydock)
Flesh, or relation. (Menochius)

Children. The Sadducees read, "they shall die naked." The present Hebrew has simply, "they shall be without children;" their offspring shall be illegitimate. (St. Augustine, q. 76.) God will not bless their marriage. "Such we know can have no children." (St. Gregory, q. 6.; St. Augustine, Apost. Anglorum.) The guilty shall be slain without delay. (Grotius) (Calmet)
Honey. Most fertile and delicious. (Menochius)
Mine. This is the reason of these different prescriptions, that they may know the dignity to which they have been raised, and may avoid the manners of the profane. (Calmet)

Spirit. Hebrew ob, means also a bottle. See chap. xix. 31. If those who consult such people be guilty, the authors of the delusion deserve death still more. (Haydock) --- The spirit of python is no other than the spirit of the devil, or of Apollo, who was called Pythius, on account of his having slain the serpent python. His oracles were in great request, as he was supposed to know the secrets of futurity. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 11

After these things it is written: "keep", it says, "my precepts and do them, I am the Lord", and to these it added: "a man, a man, if he shall have cursed his father or his mother, let him die"; and after many things which it commanded, to which it also appended the penalties of transgression, it adds in the conclusion: "and keep all my precepts and my justifications and my judgments". Whence it seems to me consequent to inquire what is indicated in these single terms. For my part, according to what I have been able to observe, a "precept" or "commandment" is that which, for example, in the decalogue is said: "you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery"; for this only is enjoined, and the penalty of the deed is not appended. But now indeed the same things are repeated, but with penalties added; for it is said: "a man, a man, whoever shall have committed adultery with the wife of a man and the wife of his neighbor, by death let him die, he who commits adultery and she who is committed adultery with. And if anyone shall have slept with the wife of his father, he has uncovered the shame of his father, by death let them die, both are guilty". Concerning these, however, precepts had already been given in the former passages, but what penalty awaited the one not observing them had not been appended. Now therefore the same things are repeated and the penalty of each single sin is decreed; and therefore these are rightly called justifications and "judgments", by which he who sins is judged to receive what is just. But observe the order of divine wisdom; it did not straightway establish the penalties together with the first precepts. For it wills that you should keep the precepts of the Father not from fear of punishment, but from love of piety; but if you have despised them, the punishment is now enjoined not so much upon a man as upon a despiser. First, therefore, you are summoned by kindness as a son: "for I have said: you are gods, and sons of the Most High, all of you". But if you are unwilling to be an obedient son, you are struck as a despiser, like a slave. After these things it says: "and if anyone shall have slept with his daughter-in-law, by death let them both die, they have done impiety, they are guilty". And these laws or these precepts he had given above without penalties; for he had said: "the shame of your daughter-in-law you shall not lay bare, since she is the wife of your son, you shall not reveal her shame", and all that follows. And this passage he appended in a like manner there without punishments, but here with various kinds of punishments. In which place I recall that word which the blessed Apostle Paul, writing to the Hebrews, says: "anyone making void the law of Moses dies without any mercy under two or three witnesses; of how much greater punishments will he be thought worthy, who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God and reckoned the blood of the testament polluted, in which he was sanctified, and done contumely to the Spirit of grace?". But for what cause I have made mention of this scripture, listen. According to the law the adulterer or "adulteress by death used to die", nor could they say: we seek repentance and we implore pardon. There was no place for tears, nor was any faculty of amendment conceded, but it was necessary in every way that he be punished who had incurred the law. And this was observed also in each and every crime to which the penalty of death was appended. Among Christians, however, if adultery has been committed, it is not commanded that the "adulterer or adulteress" be punished with bodily destruction, nor is power given to the bishop of the Church to condemn the adulterer to present death, as then according to the law was done by the elders of the people. What then? Shall we say that the law of Moses is cruel which commands the "adulterer or adulteress" to be punished, and that the gospel of Christ, through indulgence, dissolves its hearers into what is worse? It is not so. For this reason we set forth above the word of Paul saying: "by how much more is he worthy of worse punishments who shall have trodden underfoot the Son of God" and so forth. Hear therefore how neither then was the law cruel, nor now does the gospel seem dissolute on account of the largess of pardon, but in both the kindness of God is maintained by a different dispensation. This, that according to the law, for example, the "adulterer or adulteress" was punished with present death: on account of this very thing, that he bore the penalty of his sin and paid the worthy punishments of the crime committed, what will there be after this that threatens vengeance to their souls, if they have transgressed in nothing else, if there is no other sin which condemns them, but they committed this alone and only then, when they were punished and bore the punishment of the law for this? "The Lord will not take vengeance twice for the same thing"; for they received back their sin and the penalty of the crime is consumed. And therefore this kind of precept is found to be not cruel, as the heretics assert, accusing the law of God and denying that anything of humanity is contained in it, but full of mercy, for the reason that through it the people would be purged from their sins rather than condemned. But now the penalty is not inflicted upon the body, nor does the purgation of sin come about through bodily punishment, but through repentance; whether one bears this worthily, so as to be able to merit pardon for it, see to it. For there are many who neither are inclined to this nor seek the refuge of repentance, but, when they have fallen, are unwilling to rise up any further; for they delight to wallow in that mire in which they have stuck. We, nevertheless, do not forget that precept in which it is said: "with what measure you shall have measured, with the same it will be measured back to you". For we say also to God: "you have given us the bread of tears, and have given us to drink in tears in measure". There are therefore those "sins" which are said to be "unto death"; whence it is also consequent that, as often as anyone commits such a sin, so often does he die. For that there are many deaths of sin the Apostle Paul also signifies, when he says: "who has snatched us from so many deaths and will snatch us; in whom we hope that he will still snatch us". What deaths then does he here commemorate as many, except those of sins? For if he were not saying this concerning the deaths of sins, Paul would seem, according to his own opinion, to be going to remain immortal from this common death, who says: "he has snatched us from so many deaths and will snatch us; in whom we hope that he will still snatch us". For if he both "has snatched" and "will snatch", there will never be a time when he dies, whom the Lord will always "snatch". And therefore, according to those things which we have discussed, it must be seen whether perhaps it is even somewhat graver for us, who are by no means punished with this death for a common sin, than for those whom the sentence of the law condemned bodily; because for us vengeance is stored up for the future, while for them the paid punishments of their deed used to absolve them. But even if there is anyone who perhaps has been overtaken in sins of this kind, being now admonished by the word of God let him flee for aid to repentance, so that, if he has committed it once, he may not do it a second time, or, if he has already been overtaken a second time or even a third, he may add no further. For with a just judge there is a moderation of the penalty, not only according to the quality, but also according to the quantity.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

But when we wish to examine the very letter of the words as given by Matthew, "He that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death," consider whether it was taken from the place where it was written, "Whoso strikes his father or mother, let him die the death; and he that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death." For such are the exact words taken from the law with regard to the two commandments; but Matthew has quoted them in part and in an abridged form, and not in the very words.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 11

Among the other sins therefore which are punished with death, the divine law reports that also "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". The name of father is a great mystery, and the name of mother is a hidden reverence. Your father according to the spirit is God; your mother is the "heavenly Jerusalem". Learn these things from prophetic and apostolic testimonies. This same Moses writes in the canticle: "is not this same one your father who acquired you and possessed you?". But the Apostle says concerning the "heavenly Jerusalem" that: "she is free", he says, "who is the mother of us all". First, therefore, your father is God, who begot your spirit, who also says: "I have begotten sons and exalted them". But James the Apostle also says: "let us obey the father of spirits and we shall live". Secondly, your father is the father of the flesh, by whose ministry you were born in the flesh and came into this world, who carried you "in his loins"; as it is said of Levi that: "he was still in the loins of Abraham, when Melchizedek met him", "returning from the slaughter of the kings, and he blessed him, and received tithes from him". Because therefore the name of father is so sacred and so venerable, for that reason "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". Similar things are to be reckoned also concerning the mother, by whose labor, by whose care, by whose ministry you were both born and nourished. And you ought, according to the Apostle, to render an equal thanks to your parents. For if you dishonor your carnal father, the contumely of this returns to the "father of spirits"; and if you do injury to your carnal mother, the injury overflows to that "mother, the heavenly Jerusalem". So too a slave, if he is irreverent to his master, hurls contumely through this bodily master upon the "Lord of majesty"; for that Lord imposed his own name upon this carnal master. And therefore in no manner is a contention to be had against father or mother, not even in word, nor contradiction to be stirred up. He is a father, she is a mother; as seems good to them, let them act, let them do, let them say; they themselves shall know. However much of obedience we render, we do not yet repay the return of the grace by which we were begotten, by which we were carried, by which we drew in the light, by which we were nourished, perhaps also educated and instructed in honorable arts. And by them perhaps as authors we came to know God and came to the Church of God and heard the word of the divine law. On account of all these things, therefore, "whoever shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". But if these things are decreed concerning bodily parents, what will they do who provoke God the Father with cursing voices? who deny that he is the founder of the world, or who, understanding with unworthy senses the "heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all", drag the prophetic sayings to the condition of some earthly city? It is good therefore to take care that we never venerate either the carnal father or the heavenly one with less than worthy honor, and likewise the mother; to observe also every commandment which commends to us modesty and chastity, so that neither in the present life may we be liable to death according to the law, nor according to the spiritual law may the future penalty of eternal fire await us; from which may our Lord Jesus Christ grant to us all to flee and escape, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".
Letter XXVI

A woman accused of adultery was brought by the Scribes and Pharisees to the Lord Jesus with the malicious intent, that, if He was to acquit her, He might seem to annul the Law, if He condemned her, that He might seem to have changed the purpose of His coming, since He came to remit the sins of all men. To the same purport He said above, "I judge no man." So when they brought her they said, "This woman was taken in adultery, in the very act; now Moses in the Law commanded us that such should be stoned, but what sayest Thou?"

While they were saying this, Jesus stooped down and wrote with His finger on the ground. And as they waited for His answer, He lifted up His head and said, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her." What can be more Divine than this sentence, that he should punish sins who is himself free from sin? For how can we endure one who takes vengeance on guilt in another and excuses it in himself? When a man condemns in another what he commits himself, does he not rather pronounce his own condemnation?

Thus He spake, and wrote upon the ground. What then did He write? This, "Thou beholdest the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye." For lust is like a mote, it is quickly kindled, quickly consumed; the sacrilegious perfidy which led the Jews to deny the Author of their salvation declared the magnitude of their crime.

He wrote upon the ground with the finger with which He had written the Law. Sinners' names are written in the earth, those of the just in heaven, as He said to His disciples, "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven." And He wrote a second time, that you may know that the Jews were condemned by both Testaments.

When they heard these words they went out one after another, beginning at the eldest, and sat down thinking upon themselves. "And Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst." It is well said that they went out who chose not to be with Christ. Without is the letter, within are the mysteries. For in the Divine lessons they sought, as it were, after the leaves of trees, and not after the fruit; they lived in the shadow of the Law, and could not discern the Sun of Righteousness.

Finally, when they departed Jesus was left alone, and the woman standing in the midst. Jesus about to remit sin remains alone, as He says Himself, "Behold the hour cometh, yea is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave Me alone;" for it was no messenger, no herald, but the Lord Himself Who saved His people. He remains alone, because in the remission of sins no man can participate with Christ. This is the gift of Christ alone, Who "took away the sins of the world." The woman too was counted worthy to be absolved, seeing that, on the departure of the Jews, she remained alone with Jesus.

Then Jesus lifted up His head, and said to the woman, "Where are those thine accusers, hath no man condemned thee? She said, No man, Lord. And Jesus said unto her, Neither do I condemn thee, go, and sin no more." See, O reader, these Divine mysteries, and the mercy of Christ. When the woman is accused, Christ stoops His head, but when the accusers retire He lifts it up again; thus we see that He would have no man condemned, but all absolved.

By the words, "Hath no man condemned thee?" He briefly overthrows all the quibbles of heretics, who say that Christ knows not the day of judgment. He Who says, "But to sit on My right hand and on My left is not Mine to give," says also in this place, "Hath no man condemned thee?" How is it that He asks concerning that which He saw? It is for our sakes that He asks, that we might know the woman was not condemned. And such is the wont of the human mind, often to enquire concerning that which we know. The woman too answered, "No man, Lord," that is to say, Who can condemn when Thou dost not condemn? Who can punish another under such a condition as Thou hast attached to his sentence?

The Lord answered her, "Neither do I condemn thee." Observe how He has modified His own sentence; that the Jews might have no ground of allegation against Him for the absolution of the woman, but by complaining only draw down a charge upon themselves; for the woman is dismissed not absolved; and this because there was no accuser, not because her innocence was established. How then could they complain, who were the first to abandon the prosecution of the crime, and the execution of the punishment?

Then He said to her who had gone astray, "Go, and sin no more." He reformed the criminal, He did not absolve the sin. Faults are condemned by a severer sentence, whenever a man hates his own sin, and begins the condemnation of it in himself. When the criminal is put to death, it is the person rather than the transgression which is punished, but when the transgression is forsaken, the absolution of the person becomes the punishment of the sin. What is the meaning then of, "Go, and sin no more?" It is this; Since Christ hath redeemed thee, suffer thyself to be corrected by Grace; punishment would not reform but only afflict thee.

n: An uncleanness; viz., such as was contracted in laying out the dead body, or touching it; or in going into the house, or assisting at the funeral, &c. (Challoner) --- At the death. Hebrew, "for a soul;" by which name the carcass is here denoted, because it had once been ruled by the soul. (St. Augustine, q. 81.) This law related only to the family of Aaron, when no absolute necessity or near relationship required their attendance. When such offices of charity should be deemed defiling, it is not easy to say. But the ancients generally looked upon them in this light, chap. x. 6. Porphyrius enquired of Anebo, why the holy inspector touched not the dead, since in all sacred transactions, the death of animals generally intervenes. We know not the answer of this pretended prophet Egypt; and Jamblicus confesses, that he cannot resolve the difficulty. The Romans placed a branch of cypress before the door where a corpse was lying, lest any priest might see it unthinkingly, and be defiled. (Servius) "At their return from a funeral they sprinkled themselves with water, and passed over fire." (Festus) The Rabbins say, that no one could be buried in Jerusalem, nor in the towns of the Levites, on account of the sanctity of those places, and for fear lest the priests might thus contract some uncleanness. (Calmet) --- To account for all these regulations, we only need to observe that such was the will of God; and here it may surely be said, stat pro ratione voluntas. He might thus intend to exercise their obedience; to keep their minds from being too much depressed by the sight of the dead, and to remind us all that we ought carefully to avoid sin, which kills the soul, and renders us really unclean before God. (Haydock)
Sister, of the same parents. (Vatable) --- Husband; for if she have, he ought to bury his wife, and to mourn for her. To be deprived of these advantages, was then esteemed a great misfortune.

Prince. Hebrew, "Let not the prince (of the priests, Acts xxiii. 5,) render himself unclean," by attending the funerals of any of the people; or "let not the husband," &c. He may be allowed to attend his wife to the grave: or, as others more probably assert, even this is not permitted. She is not one of the persons privileged, ver. 2, and Ezechiel xliv. 25. Ezechiel (xxiv. 16,) receives a command not to bewail the death of his wife. The Romans thought their priests would be defiled, by attending the funerals even of their own wives; and Sylla, going to dedicate a temple to Hercules, sent Metella a bill of divorce, and ordered her to be removed from his house, when she was just expiring. (Plutarch)

Flesh. This would indicate an impotent grief, and want of patience. (Haydock) --- They were not allowed to put on the usual signs of mourning, as the common people were, provided they did it not in honour of an idol, chap. xix. 27.

Vile, (ver. 14,) defiled, (sordidam). Hebrew chalala, "a profane woman," (Pagnin) or one of ill-fame; as captives, inn-keepers, are generally esteemed. Zone, means a common prostitute. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] iii. 3.) None of these fit matches for the priests.
And offer. Hebrew addresses this to Moses. "Thou shalt sanctify him, therefore, because he offereth the bread of thy God."

Fire. Provided she be betrothed, and still in her father's house; so that the infamy fall upon him. (Jonathan) --- For if she be with her husband, she must undergo the usual punishment of stoning. Other young women received no corporal punishment for simple fornication: the man was bound to marry them, if the father consented; and, at any rate, he was forced to give them a dowry, Exodus xxii. 16. (Calmet) --- But if the woman pretended falsely that they were virgins, they were stoned, Deuteronomy xxii. 20.
Head. Septuagint, "by taking off his cidaris, or tiara." He shall not shave his head, chap. x. 6. --- Garments, at funerals, nor the sacred vestments at all. (Calmet)

Places. This is to be understood in the same sense. He must not leave his sacred functions to attend any corpse whatever. Having the honour of representing God, and being his first minister on earth, the utmost purity is required of him. Inferior priests may mourn on some occasions; and the Levites are not distinguished, in this respect, from the people; to shew that God requires sanctity in his officers, proportionate to their exaltation. --- Oil. Hebrew, "He is the Nozor; or the crown of the anointing oil of," &c. Joseph has the title of Nazir, (Genesis xlix. 26,) which is borne by the prime ministers of the Eastern kings. Such is the high priest in the temple. Let Christian priests hence learn what sanctity will be required of them. But why is the pontiff forbidden to bury his father, since he obtains that dignity after his decease. St. Augustine (q. 83,) answers, that he was to be consecrated immediately after, that he might offer incense. Another might, however, perform that office. On some occasions, the high priest was deposed, or the dignity transferred to another family. Infirmities might also hinder him from performing the duty. (Calmet) --- Priests must be detached, as much as possible, from all things which might divert them from their sacred offices. The greatest holiness is required of those who receive the body of Jesus Christ. (Du Hamel)

Wife. Josephus says he could not divorce her. The Rabbins allow him only one wife at a time. It is said that Joiada had two. But that might be successively; and it is not certain that he was the high priest; (2 Paralipomenon xxiv. 3.; Calmet) though he has that title in the Vulgate, 2 Paralipomenon xxii. 11. (Haydock) --- His wife must be an Isrealite. The Septuagint intimates, "of his own race." But this is denied by others. He could not marry his brother's widow, (Selden) nor a girl under twelve and a half. "The Egyptian priests marry only one, while others have as many wives as they please." (Diodorus i.) (Calmet)
Widow. Other priests might marry the widows of their fellow priests, Ezechiel xliv. 22.

Nation. The wife of the high priest must be of noble birth, that he may speak to kings and princes with more authority. (Menochius) --- Hebrew, "he shall not defile his race," &c., by marrying one of another nation, or contrary to law. If he do, the children shall have no share in the priesthood.

A blemish. These corporal defects or deformities, which disqualified the priests from officiating in the old law, were figures of the vices which priests are to beware of in the new law. (St. Gregory, Cura pastorum.) (Challoner) --- The Rabbins reckon 140 blemishes on which the Sanhedrim had to pass sentence. They also require in the high priest superior beauty, strength, riches, and wisdom.

Nose. Hebrew, "a flat nose, or any thing superfluous." Septuagint, "the nose, (hand) or ears slit." This verse rejects those whose members are too large, as the next does those who have them too small.

Eyed. Hebrew dak, may denote "a dwarf." Syriac, or something very thin, Exodus xvi. 14. --- Pearl, (albuginem) whiteness. --- Rupture, (herniosus). One perhaps troubled with the stone, (Menochius) whose testicles have been bruised, (Onkelos) or who has only one (Septuagint and Syriac).

Veil, which separates the sanctuary from the court. The Athenians chose the most handsome man ot be the king of ceremonies; and the people of Eli appointed such only to carry the sacred vessels, &c. (Atheneus xiii. 2.) (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

Everyone who is a priest among men is small and slight in comparison with that priest of whom God said: "you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek". But he is the "great priest" who is able "to penetrate the heavens" and to pass beyond the whole of creation and to ascend to him who "dwells in light inaccessible", the God and Father of the universe. For this reason the one too who among the Jews was called the "great priest" did indeed enter into the holy places, but ones made by hand, built of stones; he did not ascend into heaven nor was he able to stand before the "Father of lights". But because he was fulfilling the shadow and image of these things, therefore also he bore the name of "great priest" by way of shadow and image. Whence the Jews too, precisely through that by which they ought to have been nearest to the faith — because among them a certain foreshadowing and image of the truth had shone beforehand — while they thought the types were the truth, rejected the truth itself as though it were a lie. But we, who receive the "great priest", ought to understand how he himself is truly the "great priest". Truly he is the "great priest", who forgives sins not "by the blood of bulls and goats" but "by his own blood". Since therefore we have come to know who the "great priest" is, and we confess that the things which are written in the law about the "great priest" are written about the Savior — whom the treatise above showed to be truly the "great priest" — let us now see what those things are which the law writes about him in the prophetic spirit.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

"And the great priest" it says "from among his brethren, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured and who has his hands perfected to put on the holy vestments, shall not take the mitre from his head, shall not rend his garments, and shall not go in to any dead soul; in his father or in his mother he shall not be defiled, and he shall not go out from the holy places and shall not pollute the name which is hallowed, the name of God upon him, because the holy oil of the anointing of his God is upon him; I am the Lord. He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred. But a widow and one cast out and one defiled and a harlot, these he shall not take; but he shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Among the Jews too there was indeed an image of this observance, and the things which the law appointed were kept by the high priests of the Jews; but even if everything was diligently observed and even if all the things which the law commanded were fulfilled, not even so could all this observance make a great priest. For how can he be called a "great priest" who is able to sin? And that all the great priests too were under sin, we readily perceive from this very thing, that the law commands "that the priest should offer a victim first for his own sins, and afterwards also for the sins of the people". How then is he "great" who is set under sin? But my great priest Jesus is "great" for this reason, because "he did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth", and because "the prince of this world came to him and found nothing in him". Therefore also Gabriel the archangel, announcing his birth, says: "he shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High". Sin makes a man small and slight, virtue renders him eminent and great. For just as sickness of the body makes a man's body meager and slight, but health makes it flourishing and strong, so understand that sickness of sin makes the soul too lowly and small, but the health of the inner man and the works of virtue make it great and eminent, and the more it grows in virtues, the more it renders the greatness of itself extensive. Thus do I understand that which is written of Jesus: that "he advanced in wisdom and in stature and in grace with God and men". For who among men is there who does not "advance in stature" in boyhood, that this should be written of Jesus as though it were something remarkable? To you I say this, who hear in a bodily way that Jesus "advanced in stature". Understand therefore that "he advanced in the stature" of the soul, and his soul became great because of the great and enormous works which he did. Indeed the Apostle too, knowing that this stature is to be understood of the inner man, writes thus: "until we all meet in the perfect man, in the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ". For to grow according to the body and to become great is not in our power. For the body takes the material of its quantity from its generative origin, so as to become either great or slight; but the soul has in us the causes and the freedom of choice, so as to be either great or small. If therefore the soul be "little" and small, it can even "be scandalized"; for so it is written in the gospel: that "it is better to be cast headlong into the deep of the sea than to scandalize one of these little ones". He who is great is not "scandalized", but he who is "little". He who is great, whatever he sees, whatever he suffers, does not turn aside from the faith. But he who is "little" in mind and small, seeks occasions how he may "be scandalized", how he may seem to be tripped up in the faith. Therefore, in fine, we must take counsel most of all for those who are small in faith, nor ought we to expend as much care about the great and strong as about the "little ones" and beginners. For the strong man "bears all things, endures all things, and never falls". But with the "little ones" and the "weak in faith" it must be watched that they be not tripped up by occasion of us and fall back from the faith and fall away from salvation. Or show me from the Scriptures where anyone a sinner or of little merit has been called "great". Nowhere, I think, will you find it. But hear who they are who are called "great". Of Isaac it is said that "he advanced greatly, until he became great, great exceedingly". Moses was called "great" and John the Baptist was called "great", but now Jesus is called "great", and after him no one henceforth has been called "great". For before he was present who is truly "great", the saints, of whom we made mention above, were called "great" in comparison with the rest of men. But when he himself came, who was truly "great" not from comparison with the rest but by his own greatness — of whom also it is written that "he exulted as a giant to run his course" — thereafter no one henceforth has been called "great". This, then, is he of whom it is written: "the great priest from among his brethren". Which "brethren"? Those of whom he said, when he had risen from the dead: "go to my brethren and say to them: I ascend to my Father and to your Father and to my God and to your God". But if you wish to learn the brethren of Jesus also from the ancient writings, read the twenty-first psalm, where in the person of Christ it is said: "I will declare your name to my brethren, in the midst of the church I will praise you". "From among his brethren" therefore is Jesus "great", from those who had earlier been called "great"; and just as he is "shepherd of shepherds" and "high priest of high priests" and "Lord of those who rule" and "King of kings", so also he is great among the great; and therefore it added: "great from among his brethren".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

But after these things: "upon whom" it says "the oil of anointing has been poured, upon his head". Do not seek on earth that "oil" which is poured "upon the head" of the "great priest" that he may become Christ; but if it seems good, learn from the prophet David what this "oil" is: "you have loved" he says "righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "oil of gladness" which, "poured upon his head", made him Christ. But it adds still further to his praises: "who has his hands perfected" it says. To what man, I ask, is it fitting that this be said? In what mortal can we find "perfect hands"? Even if this be Aaron, of whom mention seems to be made, how will he be thought to have had "perfected hands", with which "he fashioned the calf", with which he carved an idol? Even if you bring forward Moses himself, how will he seem to have had "perfected hands", who did not glorify the Lord "at the water of contradiction"? For which fault he is even commanded to depart from life. But if you wish to name some other of the saints, there meets you the word of Scripture which says that "there is no man upon earth who does good and does not sin". Rightly then does Jesus alone have "perfected hands", who alone "did no sin", that is, who has the perfect and whole works of his hands. And therefore of him it is rightly said: "who has his hands perfected, to be clothed with the holy things". For this is he who is truly "clothed with the holy things", not those which were "in type", but those very things which are truly "holy". But if you wish to hear of his more exalted garments, receive the prophetic words: "clothed" it says "with light as with a garment, the deep as a garment is his clothing". This is the habit of my great high priest, by which it is signified that he is clothed with the profound light of knowledge and wisdom, which are truly "holy" garments. "He shall not" it says "take the mitre from his head". We have already said before that the "mitre" is a kind of covering which, set upon the head, affords adornment to the high priest. This "great high priest" of mine therefore never lays aside the adornment of his sacred head. But what the "head of Christ" is, learn from the Apostle, who says: "but the head of Christ is God". Rightly therefore he never lays aside this adornment of his head, which is "God", because "the Father is" always "in the Son, as the Son" is always "in the Father". "And he shall not rend his garments". Truly this is he who "shall not rend his garments", but will always keep them clean, always whole, always chaste.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

"And he shall not go in to any dead soul". What is a "dead soul"? One that is dead; the prophet says: "the soul that sins, it shall die". Upon this dead soul, then, Christ does not come, because he is "wisdom", and wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul. For that soul is dead, because in whom malice is present, sin also is present. "And sin, when it is consummated" it says "begets death". And on account of this Jesus "does not enter in to a dead soul". But if the soul lives, that is, if it has not in itself a mortal sin, then Christ, who is "life", comes to the living soul; because just as "light cannot be with darkness nor righteousness with iniquity", so neither can life be with death. And therefore if anyone is conscious to himself that he has within him a mortal sin and has not cast it from himself through the repentance of fullest satisfaction, let him not hope that Christ "enters in to" his "soul", who "does not enter in to any dead soul", because he is the "great priest".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

"In his father and in his mother he shall not be defiled". This passage of Scripture is most difficult to explain, but if by your prayers you entreat God the Father of the Word to deign to enlighten us, by his own gift it will be able to be explained. Everyone who enters this world is said to be brought into being in a certain defilement. On account of which Scripture also says: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day". This very thing, then — that he is placed "in the womb" of his mother and that he takes the material of his body from the origin of the paternal seed — can be said to be "defiled in father and mother". Or do you not know that, when a male child has been made forty days old, he is offered at the altar, that he may there be purified, as one who was polluted in the very conception, whether of the paternal seed or of the maternal womb? Every man, therefore, "is polluted in father and in mother", but Jesus my Lord alone entered clean into this generation, "he was not polluted in his mother". For he entered "an undefiled body". For it was he who had also long ago said through Solomon: "but rather, since I was good, I came to an undefiled body". "He was not" therefore "defiled in his mother", nor even "in his father". For Joseph furnished nothing in his generation except ministry and affection; whence Scripture granted him the appellation of father for his faithful ministry. For thus Mary herself says in the gospel: "behold, I and your father have been seeking you sorrowing". So then this alone is the "great priest" who "was defiled neither in father nor in mother". But let us see whether we can still find something more sublime and worthy of the dignity of so great a high priest. The true Father of all is said to be God. But the Apostle says our "mother" is "the heavenly Jerusalem". All therefore who sin "are defiled in the father" by whom they were created. For whether we have done anything impious or spoken it or thought it against God, when we have not believed God, "we have been defiled in the father". But would that it had then been done only through unbelief, and had ceased after we believed! So then we are also "defiled in the mother", if, believing God, we either injure the church or defile the liberty of our "heavenly mother" by the unworthy servitude of sin.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

But our Lord Jesus Christ alone, "who knows no sin", "was defiled neither in father nor in mother" and "did not go out from the holy places". There were indeed some things to be set before the Jews in the passages above, to which they could not respond, but omitting those, what do they for the present tell us on this discourse, either they themselves or those who wish the law to be understood according to their sense: if these things are not referred to our high priest and Savior, how will it be proved according to the letter that "the great priest did not go out from the holy places", who nevertheless even took a wife, as is said below, "a virgin of his own kindred"? If "he does not go out from the holy places", if he goes forth nowhere, how or for what uses is he commanded to "take a wife"? For it must not be supposed that he could remain within the holy places with a wife. But let those suppose these things to whom "Jewish fables" are pleasing. But we have a "great priest" "after the order of Melchizedek", Christ Jesus, "never going out from the holy places"; for he is always in the holy places and remains always holy in his words, holy in his acts, holy in all his wishes, and he alone is the one who is never found outside the holy places. For he who sins "goes out from the holy places", and as many times as anyone sins, so many times is he made to be outside the holy places. But Christ, "who never sinned", "never went out from the holy places". But you too, who follow Christ and are his imitator, if you remain in the word of God, if "you meditate on his law day and night", if you are exercised in his commandments, you are always in the holy places and never depart from there. For the holy things are not to be sought in a place, but in acts and life and morals. If these are according to God and are held according to the precept of God, even if you are in your house, even if in the marketplace — and why do I say in the marketplace? — even if you be found in the theater serving the word of God, do not doubt that you are in the holy places. Or does it not seem to you that Paul, when he entered the theater or when he entered the "Areopagus" and preached Christ to the Athenians, was in the holy places? But also when he walked among the altars and idols of the Athenians, where he found written: "to the unknown God" and from this word took the beginning of his preaching of Christ, even there, "surveying" the "altars" of the gentiles, he was set in the holy places, because he was pondering holy things. But also whoever guards himself, after receiving the grace of God, lest he fall "into homicide, into adultery, into theft, into false testimony" and other things like these, but remains clean from every contagion of sin, this man "did not go out from the holy places", and did not defile the sanctification of his God in himself, because the holy "oil of anointing" of his God is upon him. That "oil" of which it is written in Exodus — how can it according to the letter properly be called the oil of God, which was compounded by the perfumer's art by an unguent-maker? But if you wish to see the oil of God, hear whom the prophet says to have been anointed with the oil of God, him without doubt of whom he says: "therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows". This, then, is the "great priest" who alone was anointed with the oil of God and in whom the "oil of the anointing" of God remained always holy.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

But what is added after these things? "He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred, but a widow and one cast out and a harlot he shall not take, but he shall take a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Since therefore the order of the whole exposition has been recalled to the true "great priest", Christ, let us now see also what ought to be understood about his nuptials. Paul the Apostle says: "but I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, your senses be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ". Paul therefore wishes to "present all the Corinthians as a chaste virgin to Christ"; which assuredly he would never wish, unless he saw it to be possible. Whence perhaps it may seem wonderful how these, who came to the faith of Christ corrupted by diverse sins, are all together called a "chaste virgin"; a virgin so holy, so chaste, that she deserves even to be joined to the nuptials of Christ. But since we cannot refer these things to the integrity of the flesh, it is certain that they pertain to the integrity of the soul, whose — according to the very judgment of Paul — "the simplicity of the faith which is in Christ" has been called her virginity; and through this, because, when the sophistries of the philosophers or the Jewish superstitions ceased, Christ took the church to himself in simple faith, "he took to wife a virgin of his own kindred". For her faith is not corrupted by the philosophic sense nor by the ambition of circumcision, but she remained in the simplicity of confession as in virginal integrity. For so also he had long ago promised through the prophet, saying: "I will betroth you to myself in faith". "Everyone" therefore, according to the Apostle, "who is in Christ is a new creature". And as the same Apostle says: "that he might present to himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and immaculate". How then does he make her, who is wrinkled, to be without "wrinkle", except that he "renews" her according to that which is written: "for even if our man who is without is corrupted, yet he who is within is renewed from day to day"? A "widow" indeed "and a harlot and one cast out Christ does not take", nor does such a soul enter the bridal chamber of the bridegroom. For he who "has entered there not having the wedding garment" will endure that which you know is written in the gospel. "A virgin" therefore he will take, "a widow he will not take nor a harlot nor one cast out or defiled". Why Christ should not take "a harlot" and a "rejected" soul "and a polluted" one into marriage, it is no labor to expound; but why a "widow" should not be received must be more diligently considered. Paul the Apostle, writing to the Romans, calls "the law the husband of the soul", and declares "that she, when the husband is dead, is loosed from the law of the husband, so that she is no longer an adulteress, if she has married Christ". But if it should happen that the law of the soul itself dies to it — that is, that the soul departs from the law and yet does not bind itself with the disciplines of a chaster wedlock, and, departing from the law, does not take up the yoke of the evangelical teaching: this soul will not be able to "marry Christ", having sought the wantonness of liberty, not the cultivation of a virginal and simple faith. This "great priest", therefore, "will take a virgin wife of his own kindred". It can also for this reason seem to be said "of his own kindred", because the soul of Christ was from the kindred and from the substance of all human souls. It can also, according to this — that he calls those who believe in him brethren — be said to be "of his own kindred", the soul which is joined to him in faith as in nuptials. Yet I do not want this to escape us, that the Hebrews deny they have it written, what we find among the Seventy translators: "of his own kindred". And rightly do they not have it written. For the nearness of God has been taken away from them, the adoption of sons has been taken away and transferred to the church of Christ. They therefore do not have it written that they are "of the kindred" of Christ, just as they did not deserve to be. But we who have this written and read it, let us indeed rejoice at the condescension of God, but let us carefully and anxiously take care lest our life and acts and morals at any time make us degenerate, lest this very thing be brought unto our condemnation, that, "when we are the kindred of Christ", we serve unworthy and foul and diabolical acts. "He who has" therefore "a bride is a bridegroom". You hear how Christ is called "bridegroom", but his "bride" is said to be the soul which is proved uncorrupted and virgin by the simplicity of faith and the purity of acts. For the Lord says also through Jeremiah the prophet: "have you not called me as Lord and Father and prince of your virginity?".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 12

"But a widow and one cast out and one defiled he shall not take". If any of us has sinned, he is "cast out"; even if he is not cast out by the bishop, whether because it lies hidden or because he is sometimes judged unto grace, he is nevertheless "cast out" by the very consciousness of sin. Nor does the grace of man avail, when Christ does not receive such a soul into marriage as "cast out". Therefore "neither a widow", as we said above, "will he take, nor one cast out nor one polluted". She is called "polluted" who, even if she has not completely committed the sin, yet by this very thing that she thought it, that she wished it, that she desired it, even if she did not carry it out, is "polluted" and is not chosen by the "great high priest". For he requires an exceedingly pure, exceedingly clean and sincere soul, which he may join to himself, because "he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit". Whence also this is shown, that there are differences of sins, and that he who has sinned "a sin unto death" is "cast out", but he who does not "sin unto death" but something lesser, is "polluted".
