When John preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, the sentence of the Law ceased, which held sinners guilty; the burdens of the Law also ceased, which had been given on account of the hardness of the Jewish heart in foods, new moons, sabbaths, and the rest. For when mercy came, vengeance ceased. But the burdens of the Law have ceased forever. The sentence, however, ceases and is abolished for those who remain in the benefit obtained. But for those who return to the old man, the authority of the Law is revived, because, forgetful of benefits, they return under the sentence of the Law. Circumcision and the sabbath indeed were in force until that time when the commandment of the new law was preached. For they were given in such a way that, when the law of faith arrived, they should cease. Therefore the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4). And Daniel signifies this also, when he prophesies both concerning the coming of the Lord and the weeks of time, that the anointing and judgment and sacrifice and the city itself were to cease (Dan. 9:24–27). For when the spiritual law arrived, it was necessary that the carnal things should cease. Then God was served in part by the body, now in part by the soul; formerly visibly, now invisibly; then in the flesh, now in the mind. For to God, who is spirit, one must serve in spirit (Jn. 4:24). Therefore the Law is not undone because it has ceased, but something has succeeded it when the time was fulfilled. Nor is its administration or judgment accused if indulgence is given to sinners; for from this it is rather clearly shown to have been rightly and justly given, since it is not denied that those over whom it ruled were sinners, because, “The Law,” he says, “is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1:9). Therefore, because mercy is to be preferred, righteousness must not on that account be thought shameful; for if there were no reverence for it, mercy itself would have no fruit. For unless they keep righteousness after receiving mercy, indulgence will profit them nothing. For the Law said, “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor adore the things that are in heaven above or on the earth beneath”; and, “You shall not swear falsely”; and, “Honor your father and mother”; and, “You shall not kill, nor commit fornication, nor steal, nor bear false witness, nor covet anything that is your neighbor’s” (Exod. 20:4–17). Are these to be said to have ceased? Far from it. For without these, who could even in this life be judged acceptable? And therefore the other things which we mentioned above have ceased, new moons, sabbaths, the law of foods, sacrifices, circumcision, and so on. From this it is that the Apostle says among other things: “Rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13:3). Observing these makes men good, though not yet perfect. Therefore the Savior: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). By adding better things to these, the Savior did not in any way dissolve the Law, but fulfilled it. For the intention of the Law pertains to man’s salvation, for example, “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Lev. 24:20): so that, fearing lest he suffer what he is forbidden to do to another, he might restrain himself from wickedness. But the Savior, adding a higher righteousness to this sense, says, “But I say to you, do not resist the evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matt. 5:39); so that by not returning evil in kind, he may be perfect. For to repay in kind is righteousness, but not full; but if he overlooks the injury, it is full and overflowing righteousness. To retaliate brings joy for a time; to forgive brings joy for the future. Therefore the Savior fulfilled the Law, in that those whom it taught to be righteous, He made more righteous, which it could not do. Wherefore it is the joy of the Law that its disciples have become more skillful. He would indeed have destroyed the Law if He had taught men to sin with freedom. But rather He suspended the sentence, so that he who acts wickedly may have time to repent; if not, the sentence returns upon him with increase, because he did not understand that he was forgiven for this purpose, that he might improve himself.

n: The rest (sabbathises sabbatum). The land was to enjoy the benefit of rest every seventh year, to remind God's people that he had created the world, and that he still retained dominion over it, (St. Augustine, q. 91, 92,) requiring the spontaneous fruits of that year as a tribute, part of which he gave to the poor. In the mean time, all creatures rested from their labours, and the people were taught to have an entire confidence in Providence. (Calmet) --- This law was given in the desert of Sinai, in the month of Nisan, the second year after the exit: but it did not begin to be in force, till the Hebrews entered into the land of Chanaan. (Haydock)

Reap entirely, but only take a part, ver. 6. --- First-fruits. None shall be this year presented to the Lord. Hebrew has the word Nezireka, "Nazareat," alluding to the custom of those who, out of devotion, let their hair grow; as here only the spontaneous fruits of the unpruned vine were to be eaten; they were separated, as the word also means, or "sanctified," (Septuagint) being abandoned indifferently for the use of any one that pleased to eat of them, and no longer fenced in by the proprietor, (Calmet) though he might take the first, or choicest fruit, for his own use, (Menochius,) or at least he might take his share like the rest. (Tirinus)

Cattle. This last term in Hebrew, Septuagint, &c., means "wild beasts," which must also live. At this period of the seventh year, debts were to be remitted, the law read, &c., Exodus xxi. 2 and Deuteronomy xv. 2, and xxxi. 10. But in the jubilee year, even those Hebrew slaves, whose ears had been pierced, and those who had sold their land, regained their liberty and possessions. (Calmet) --- Their children and wives, according to Josephus, went out with them, ver. 41. Houses and suburbs for gardens, &c., might be sold for ever, if they were not redeemed the first year, excepting those of the Levites, ver. 34. (Tirinus)

Years. It is dubious whether the 49th or the 50th year was appointed for the jubilee. The former year is fixed upon by many able chronologers, who remark, that if two years of rest had occurred together, it would have been a serious inconvenience; and Moses might have said the 50th year for a round number, or comprise therein the year of the former jubilee, as we give five years to the olympiad, and eight days to the week, though the former consists only of four years, and the latter of seven days. (Rader; Scaliger; &c.) But others decide for the fiftieth year, ver. 10. (Philo; Josephus, [Antiquities] iii. 10.; St. Augustine, q. 92.; Salien; &c.) (Calmet) --- On the feast of expiation of the 49th year, they promulgated the following to be the year of jubilee. (Menochius) --- Usher places the first in the year of the world 2609, 49 years after the partition of the land by Josue in 2560: Salien dates 50 years from the entrance (ver. 2,) of the Hebrews into Chanaan, in the year of the world 2583, six years sooner; and places the first jubilee [in] 2633, immediately after the sabbatic year, which fell in the 32nd year of Othoniel. He supposes that both were proclaimed at the same time, on the 1st of Tisri, Ros Hassana, "the head of the year;" though the heralds went about the country only on the 10th. The writers both of the Synagogue and of the Church generally adopt the 50th for the year of jubilee; and the pretended inconvenience of two years' rest is nugatory, since God promised a three years' crop, ver. 21. (Haydock)

Remission; that is, a general release and discharge from debts and bondage, and a reinstating of every man in his former possessions. (Challoner) --- Jubilee: Hebrew jubol means "liberty" (Josephus); "re-establishment" (Philo); (Calmet) --- "deliverance" (Abenezra). The Rabbins falsely assert, that a ram's horn was used on this occasion: but Bochart shews that it is solid and unfit for the purpose. (B. ii. 42.) They also maintain, that from the 1st of this sacred month, as it is called by Philo, till the 10th, the slaves spent their time in continual rejoicings in their master's house, and on the latter day they were set free. Cunæus (Rep., i. 6,) observes, that the jubilee was discontinued after the captivity, though the sabbatic year was still kept. (Calmet) --- Indeed the Jews were often very negligent in these respects, and God complained and punished them for it, chap. xxvii. 32.; &c. The avarice of the great ones chiefly caused these wise regulations to be despised, though, from time to time, God enforced their observance, that it might be clearly known from what family the Messias sprung. After his birth they were abrogated, as no longer necessary. (Haydock) --- Something similar was instituted by Solon, and styled "the shaking off burdens," for the redemption both of men and goods. (Laertius) (Menochius) --- The Locrians could not alienate their patrimony. (Aristotle, polit. ii. 7, and vi. 4.) The Rabbins deviate from the spirit of their lawgiver, when they assert, that persons might sell their inheritance for a greater number of years than 50, if they specified how many, &c. (Selden, Succes. iii. 24.) In the Christian dispensation, the jubilee denotes a time of indulgence, in consequence of the power left by Jesus Christ, Matthew xvi. 19 and 2 Corinthians ii. 10.) The first was given by Pope Boniface VIII in 300; and others were granted every century, till Pope Clement VI reduced the space to 50 years, 1542. Pope Gregory XI would have them dispensed to the faithful every 33 years, and Pope Paul XI every 25th, that more might partake of so great a benefit. This has been done since his time, and the Popes often grant them when the Church is in great danger, and also in the year when they are consecrated. (Calmet) --- They are designed to promote the fervour of piety, and the remission of punishment due to sin. (Haydock) --- Family. Slaves shall obtain their liberty. This law set a restraint upon the rich, that they might not get possession of too much land, or oppress the poor. Lycurgus, with the same view, established an equality of lands among the Spartans, and Solon acknowledged the propriety of the regulation, which he probably saw practised in Egypt. (Diodorus i.) (Calmet) --- The Agrarian laws at Rome, were often proposed; but they caused nothing but confusion and riot. (Haydock)
Eat them. No wine was to be made of the grapes, nor the corn heaped up, to the detriment of the poor. All is claimed by God, as his own property.

Grieve. Hebrew, "deceive not." St. Chrysostom observes, that to engage another to sell us any thing for what we know is beneath its value, is theft. (Grotius, Jur. ii. 12.) The Rabbins also decide that, if an Israelite be defrauded a sixth part, restitution must be made, ver. 17. (Selden, Jur. vi. 6.)

Three years. After the harvest of the sixth year was gotten in, the land rested from September to September, the beginning of the 8th year, when it was tilled again. Nothing would be ripe till about March; yet the harvest of the 6th year would suffice to furnish food till that time, or even for a year longer, as it would be requisite, when the year of jubilee succeeded that of rest, ver. 8. (Haydock)

For ever. Samaritan version, "absolutely." The only exception to this law is, when a person makes a vow to give some land to the Lord, and will not redeem it, chap xxvii. 20. In that case, God re-enters upon his property, and it belongs to his priests. (Calmet)

Fruits. An estimation shall be made of what the buyer would probably have gotten for the fruits of the land, till the year of jubilee, and that sum shall be given to him; (Calmet) or what benefit he has already derived from the land shall be computed; so that, if he purchased it for 100 sicles, and had received the value of 80, he should be content with the addition of 20 more, ver. 53. (Haydock)

City. These houses are of greater consequence, and therefore God dissuades his people from selling them; though if they think proper to do so, he holds out an encouragement to those who buy, that they may afford a better price, on the prospect of keeping possession for ever. (Menochius)
Owners. The Levites had no other possessions, but these cities and 2000 cubits of land around them. The priests might buy of one another, Jeremias xxxi. 7.
And thou. Hebrew, "thou shalt receive him: and of the stranger....(36) take no usury." There are two precepts; to relieve those in distress, and not to injury any one. (Calmet)

Hireling, who has engaged to work for a term of years, either of six, or at most 49. After the year of the jubilee, he might enter into fresh engagements with his late master. (Haydock) --- The Hebrews have always hated slavery. We have never been slaves to any, John viii. 33. They were not allowed to part with their liberty, except from absolute distress; (Maimonides) and then they do not submit to what they call intrinsical slavery. --- [Ver. 41.] Children. His wife and children were not made slaves with him. But if his master gave him a second wife, her children belonged to their common master. (Selden, Jur. vi. 1.)

Servants, or slaves, whom you may treat with greater severity than the Hebrews, and keep for ever, even though they may have embraced the true faith. But still you must remember that they are your brethren.
Stranger, or Gentile, who engages at least to keep the precepts given to Noe[Noah]. (Haydock)
Himself. He might have saved up something by greater industry. The Athenians allowed their slaves the same privilege. (Calmet)

Wages. Hebrew, "as a yearly hired servant shall he be with him." What was customarily given to a hired servant for a certain number of years, might be a rule to judge how much was to be paid for redemption. (Haydock) --- Thus if a man had engaged to serve 20 years for 100 sicles, and at the expiration of 10 years wished to redeem himself, he might do it for half that sum. Some think, that those Hebrews who had sold themselves to a Gentile, sojourning among them, could not take the benefit of the sabbatic year, (Exodus xxi. 6,) because Moses is silent on this head. But this argument is not satisfactory. (Calmet)

f: The Stromata Book 2

So do we now understand how the law educates us in piety, sharing, justice and humanity? Well? Does it not enjoin that the land lie fallow through the seventh year and invites the poor not to be afraid to use any crops that grow by God's grace, nature acting as farmer for any who will?
ON PRAYER 27.14

Who is there who has grasped the mind of Christ so well that he knows the meaning of the seventh year of freedom of Hebrew slaves and the remission of debts and the intermission of the cultivation of the holy land? Over and above the feast of every seventh year is the feast called the jubilee. No one can ever come near divining its precise meaning or the true import of the prescriptions enjoined by it, except him who knows the Father's will and his disposition for every age according to "his incomprehensible judgments and unsearchable ways."
Homilies on the Gospels 2.17

In the law the fiftieth year was ordered to be called [the year] of jubilee, that is, "forgiving" or "changed." During it the people were to remain at rest from all work, the debts of all were to be canceled, slaves were to go free [and] the year itself was to be more notable than other years because of its greater solemnities and divine praises. Therefore by this number is rightly indicated that tranquility of greatest peace when, as the apostle says, at the sound of the last trumpet "the dead will rise and we shall be changed" into glory. Then, when the labors and hardships of this age come to an end and our debts, [that is] all our faults, have been forgiven, the entire people of the elect will rejoice eternally in the sole contemplation of the divine vision. And that most longed-for command of our Lord and Savior will be fulfilled: "Be still, and see that I am God."
On the Tabernacle 2.2

We read in the law that the fiftieth year was ordered to be designated as a jubilee (that is, a [year for] releasing or exchanging), in which the whole people should rest from all cultivation of the land and everyone's debts should be canceled. And we know that in the New Testament the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost (that is, the fiftieth day of the Lord's resurrection) and hallowed the beginnings of the church that was being brought into existence by its coming. It is agreed then that by this number can rightly be figured either the grace of the Holy Spirit or the joy of future blessedness, to which one is brought through the gift of the same Spirit and in the perception of which alone is true rest and joy.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 15

But let us rather quickly refer these things to ourselves, to whom the law of Christ, if we follow it, permits us to have neither possessions on earth nor houses in cities. And why do I speak of houses? It does not grant us to possess even several tunics, nor much money: for "having", he says, "food and clothing, let us be content with these". How then shall we observe the laws given concerning houses, whether set "within a walled city" or "in villages that have no walls"? We find in other places of Scripture that the divine word names a house with a certain greater mystery, as when it speaks of Jacob and sets it down as if for his praise: "for Jacob", it says, "was a simple man, dwelling in a house". And again I find it written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "and because", it says, "the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses". We see, then, that for the midwives the cause of making houses was the fear of God, while for Jacob simplicity and innocence gave the cause that he "dwelt in a house". Finally Esau, because he was evil, it is not written of him that he dwelt in a house, nor is it written of any other who did not have the fear of God that he built himself a house. What, then, this "house" is, and what kind of building it is, the Apostle Paul expounds more openly, when he says: "we have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens". This, then, is the "house" which no one can build unless he fear God. This is the "house" which no one can construct or inhabit save in simplicity of mind and purity of heart. But since it is wont to happen that even one who has built well and has constructed for himself a heavenly house by acting well and living well and believing rightly, may incur the debt of some sin and be compelled by a most cruel usurer to sell it and to pour out his labors into another, the piety and clemency of the lawgiver comes to meet him, so that within a fixed time it may be redeemed. "If however your hand shall find", he says, "the price which you may restore". What kind of "price"? Gathered, without doubt, by the tears of repentance and found by the hands, that is, by the labor of good work. But that "year" can be understood which the Lord came to call "the acceptable year", in which he might release the broken into remission and grant salvation to those confessing their sins. But as to what he says, "a house in a walled city", rightly, as I judge, the "house" which is said to be "in heaven" is understood "in a walled city". For the wall of houses of this kind is the very firmament of heaven. But such a house only a rare few can have, those perhaps "who, walking upon the earth, have their conversation in the heavens" and of whom the Apostle says: "you are God's building". But the rest have houses "in villages that have no wall", yet there lies adjacent to them a fruitful field—those perhaps who prepare for themselves a dwelling "in the land of the living" and in that land which the Lord promises to "the meek", saying: "blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth by inheritance". These houses, then, if perchance some lapse should occur, as we expounded above, there is "always" the possibility of recovering—so that, to speak by way of example, if some mortal fault should find us, one that consists not in a mortal crime, not in blasphemy of the faith, which is girded by the wall of ecclesiastical and apostolic teaching, but rather in a fault of speech or of conduct; this is to have "sold the house" which is in the field or "in a village that has no wall". This sale, then, and a fault of this kind can always be repaired, nor is it ever forbidden you to bear repentance for things committed of this kind. For in graver crimes place for repentance is granted only once; but these common faults, which we frequently incur, always admit of repentance and are redeemed without intermission.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 15

We see three distinct laws concerning the sale and redemption of houses given through Moses in Leviticus. Let us first treat their content according to the historical sense, so that afterward we may be able to ascend also to the spiritual sense. Some houses are "in walled cities", others "in villages or fields that have no walls". He says, then, that "if anyone sell a house in a walled city, let him have the opportunity of redeeming it for a full year, but after the year no power of recovering it is granted". "For it shall be", he says, "the settled possession of the buyer, if he who sold it has not been able to free it within the year". The second law is that "if the house which has been sold be in a village that has no wall, but a village to which a field lies adjacent, it shall be lawful for the seller both after the year and whenever he is able, to restore the price and recover the house which he had sold". The third law is that "if perchance the house be a Levite's or a priest's, wherever such a house shall be, whether in a walled city or in a village that has no wall, it shall always and at every time be lawful, that whenever the Levite or the priest is able, he may redeem his house"; nor do the divine ordinances ever permit a priestly or Levitical possession to be confirmed to another who is not of the same order. These, then, are the laws which that former people used, even according to this very thing which is set forth through the history, providing quite religiously and piously for the priestly or Levitical orders.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 15

"But if this house be a priest's", he says, "or a Levite's, wherever it be, whether in a city or in a field, it always has redemption". In this place I seek the priestly sense and the Levitical understanding. For the hearer of these things ought not, if it can be, to be inferior to that very one who wrote and sanctioned these things. What is it, then, that the priest and the Levite "always" and wherever it be "has redemption" of his house? According to the spiritual understanding a priest is called a mind consecrated to God, and he is named a Levite who unceasingly stands beside God and ministers to his will. Perfection, therefore, in understanding and work, in faith and deeds, is to be taken as the priest and the Levite. And so, if it should ever happen to this perfect mind to sell the "house which it has not made with hands, eternal in the heavens", and to give it into the hands of another—as befell once the great patriarch David, when "from his roof" he "looked upon" the wife of Uriah the Hittite—straightway he redeems it, straightway he repairs it; for straightway he says: "I have sinned". Nay rather, we ought to look at something still more sublime in this sense: how the house of priests and Levites, that is, of perfect minds, always has its sins redeemed and is always purged. If ever we read the divine scriptures and review in them certain faults of the holy fathers, if according to the sentence of the Apostle Paul we say that "all these things happened to them in figure, but they were written for our admonition", in this way "their house is always redeemed", because for their faults purgation and satisfaction is always applied by the teachers who show from the divine scriptures that these were forms and images of things to come, not by which the sins of the saints were reproved, but by which it was shown that sinners and the impious are enrolled into the portion and fellowship of the saints. Never, then, is the priestly possession separated from the priest; even if it be taken away for a time, even if it be sold, it is "always redeemed", "always" repaired, as if he should say, "charity", which is "perfect", "endures all things, hopes all things, bears all things, charity never falls". So, then, also the possession and house of the saints "never falls", is never taken away, is never separated from their right. For how can a house be separated from priests which has been built "upon the foundation of the Apostles and prophets, in which Christ Jesus himself is the cornerstone"? But that this house can sometimes be sold, that is, that a building of this kind may fall into sin, hear how the Apostle Paul speaks concerning such: "as a wise architect I laid the foundation", he says, "another builds upon it, but let each one see how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides that which is laid, which is Christ Jesus. But if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, stubble". You see, then, that there can be "built upon the foundation of Christ wood, hay, stubble", that is, works of sin; and whoever "builds" these has without doubt "sold his house" to the worst buyer, the devil, from whom each of those who sin obtains the price of sin, the satisfaction of his desire. If perchance anyone should incur this—which God forbid—let him quickly redeem it, quickly repair it, while there is time for repairing, while there is place for repentance, praying in common that we be not defrauded of the habitation of the eternal house, but be held worthy "to be received into the eternal tabernacles", through Christ our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!".

n: To adore it. This explains the prohibition of making graven things, &c. The Protestants translate as usual, "Ye shall make you no idols, nor graven image, neither rear ye up a standing image, neither shall ye set up any image of stone in your land to bow down unto it." They seem terribly afraid of images, as if they were all idols. See Exodus xx. 4. (Haydock) --- Pillars. Hebrew mattseba, "statue, or monument." Such were erected by Jacob, Josue, and even by Moses himself, without any offence or danger of idolatry, Genesis xxviii. 8 and Josue iv. 4 and Exodus xxiv. 4. Apuleius (Flor.) makes mention, among other species of superstition, "of a stone anointed, and of an altar crowned with flowers." --- The stone, which is here condemned, is one set up "for adoration." (Onkelos) --- Hebrew, "a stone of sight," placed on some eminence, or on the high roads. Strabo, (xvii.) speaking of those which he had seen in Egypt along the roads, says, "they are lofty, polished, and almost like a sphere, some 12 feet in diameter. There are sometimes three, of different dimensions, one upon another. Some were to be seen upon Mount Libanus. They were objects of adoration." The Greeks raised heaps of stones on the high roads, in honour of Mercury, Proverbs xxvi. 7[8?]. (Calmet) --- We are not forbidden to place land-marks, &c.: but we must not adore them. (Du Hamel)

Reverence. The Rabbins inform us, with what respect their ancestors appeared in the temple. They left their sticks and shoes behind them, and washed their feet; entering solely to perform some act of religion, and not to go a shorter road to another street. When they had ended their devotions, they retired slowly without turning their back to the sanctuary. (Outram, Sacrif. lib. 3. n. 7.)
Due seasons. Before harvest, in spring; and after that in autumn; when they sow their wheat and barley in Palestine. (Calmet)

Time. So great shall be the abundance, that you will scarcely have time to get all the work done before you will be called off to something else. (Haydock) --- These promises would be so much the more agreeable to them, as in Egypt, they had been forced to keep in their houses two or three months together, on account of the overflowing of the Nile. In that country, as well as in Greece and Palestine, people sow both wheat and barley about October; while in other countries the latter is sown in spring. The harvest is ready in about six months, and that of wheat in seven. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xviii. 18.; Hesiod, ep. ii.) (Calmet)
Five. Thus Gedeon's 300 men put to flight the great army of the Madianites; (Judges vii. 22,) and the Machabees destroyed vast numbers with a small force.

Old; Being unable to consume all. (Menochius) --- Hebrew, "ye shall eat old store, and bring forth the old because of the new." Septuagint, "you shall eat the old of old, and you shall bring out the old from the face of the new." Like a householder, who bringeth forth out of his treasury new things and old, Matthew xiii. 52. (Haydock)

Upright; and be no longer bowed down with a heavy yoke, like oxen. "I have broken the locks of your prison, and have set you at liberty," Arabic. (Calmet) --- A Greek proverb says, "Never was a slave's head right, but always crooked, like his neck." (Menochius)

Heat. Hebrew kaddachath, is rendered "scab and jaundice," by the Septuagint: and by others "a dangerous wind," like that which causes so many diseases in Egypt. The precise meaning of some terms in this verse is not well known.
More, (septuplum.) "Very often, or very much;" in which sense it is used in this chapter. (Calmet)
As brass (æneam.) "Brazen," without moisture, and barren. (Onkelos)
Desolate, none being left to frequent them: or the few who remain, shall keep within doors, lest the wild beasts should meet and devour them, Isaias xxxiii. 8.

Bread; or that which supports you. You shall be deprived of the necessaries of life. --- One oven shall be used by 10 families, so little bread shall be baked, and even that little shall be delivered out by weight. I will also deprive it of its nutritive qualities, so that it shall not satisfy your craving appetite. (Calmet) See Psalm civ. 16 and Isaias iii. 1.
Fury. You will gain nothing by opposing me, but your own destruction. I will treat you, as you would deal with me. (Haydock)
Daughters. To such extremities were the Jews reduced, at the sieges of Samaria and Jerusalem. (4 Kings vi. 28 and Lamentations iv. 10.) (Josephus, Jewish Wars vii. 8.)

Places. The temple of Solomon was built on Mount Moria or Sion. The Persians sacrificed upon the mountains, and the Romans and Athenians built their most magnificent temples on the highest parts of their respective cities. --- Idols. Hebrew chammanim, denotes the chariots dedicated to the sun; (4 Kings xxiii. 11,) or the pyreia, or enclosures for the sacred fire, in honour of the god Homanus, (Strabo xv.) whose name is probably derived from this Hebrew word, (Calmet) as well as Hammon, a title of Jupiter. (Menochius) --- Ruins. Hebrew, "and cast your carcasses upon the carcasses of your gods of dirt, and my soul shall vomit you out." The Egyptians embalmed the carcasses of their sacred animals. God threatens that, if his people be so stupid as to adore them, they shall die, and be deprived of sepulture.
Odours. Even the sanctuary of the Lord shall be destroyed, as you will be unworthy to have it among you, or to offer sacrifices to me. (Haydock)

Desolation. It shall be uncultivated; and though you would not comply with my injunctions to let it rest one year out of seven, it shall now remain desolate for many years together. (Haydock) --- Theodoret (q. 37) says for 70 years; the number of sabbatic years, from the reign of Saul till the captivity of Babylon, during the space of 490 years. This verse seems evidently to allude to those days of distress. (Calmet) (2 Paralipomenon xxxvi. 21.) --- But we can hardly suppose that none of the sabbatic years should have been duly observed during the reigns of David, Solomon, &c. (Haydock) --- Instead of enjoy, Hebrew may be "shall expiate her sabbaths," or the neglect of them. The same term, tirtse, is used, (ver. 41 and 43,) and the Vulgate generally renders it agreeable, speaking of sacrifices, chap. i. 4 and xxii. 20. (Calmet)
Your sabbaths, holidays and years of rest, and of jubilee. The earth is represented as entering into the views of God, and rejoicing at his judgments. (Haydock)

Fear. Septuagint, "timidity, or slavishness." Hebrew morec, "softness and inactivity." (Calmet) --- Their haughty temper shall be broken; and though they have dared to rebel against their God, the fall of a leaf shall now terrify them. (Haydock)
Brethren, in their flight; while each one is endeavouring to save himself. The Rabbins say they shall be punished for the sins of their brethren, if they have not endeavoured to prevent them.

Consume you. The Hebrew spies said that the land of Chanaan devoured its inhabitants. Such shall be in reality the enemies' country in your regard. You shall not be able to establish yourselves or be happy there.
Own. The sins of their fathers, which they have imitated, shall fall upon them; so that they shall pine away with remorse and misery.

Mind. Hebrew, "heart," wicked, rebellious, and unclean. (Menochius) --- Pray for. Hebrew and Syriac, "please themselves in," &c. They shall see what advantage they have derived from their sins. (Calmet) --- Then they shall enter into themselves, like the prodigal son. (Haydock)
Jacob is placed first, because he was the father of no other nation; as Abraham and Isaac were. (Worthington)

I did not. He speaks of a future event, which he sees will certainly come to pass, as if it had already happened. As God had preserved his people, in Egypt, conformably to his covenant with the patriarchs, so he will be reconciled to them, after they shall have done penance, and acknowledged all their excesses, in the captivity of Babylon. (Haydock) --- The church never ceases all together. (Worthington)

Moses. What has been hitherto recorded, was mostly prescribed by God at Mount Sinai, as some of the following laws were also. (Calmet) --- It would seem as if this were the conclusion of Leviticus. We must remember, however, that these divisions were not introduced by Moses, as he wrote his five books without any interruption, like one verse. So St. John seems to conclude his Gospel, (chap. xx. 31,) though he afterwards adds another chapter. (Haydock)

f: ON IDOLATRY 4.1-2

For this reason, in order to root out the materials of idolatry, God's law proclaims, "You shall not make an idol"; and by adding, "Nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven or in the earth or in the sea," it utterly forbade such crafts to the servants of God. Enoch had anticipated this law when he prophesied that the demons and the spirits of the rebellious angels would turn to idolatry every element and property of the universe, everything which heaven and sea and earth contain, to be consecrated as a god against God. So it is that human error worships everything but the very Creator of everything. Their images are idols; the consecration of images is idolatry. Whatever sin idolatry commits must be put down to all the makers of all the idols.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

In bodily contests certain grades and distinctions of the several ranks are customarily observed, so that each one may be rewarded with the prize of victory according to the quality of the struggle. For instance, if someone should have a contest among boys, or among youths, or among men, what observance ought to be kept for each rank, what may be done and what may not be done, and what rule of the contest is to be guarded, and what palm of reward the victor deserves after these things—all this is nonetheless provided for by the very laws of the games. So now too Almighty God, appointing for mortals in this world a contest of observing His law, after He had handed down very many things to be observed and had prescribed what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fittingly, at the very end, in the book of Leviticus, in which it is laid down concerning each of the several observances, announces what reward he carries off who has fulfilled them and what penalty he undergoes who has not observed them. But if the law, according to what the Jews will have it and those who think the Scriptures are to be understood in their sense, is not "spiritual" but carnal, there is no doubt that, observed carnally, it also bestows carnal blessings on those who observe it. But if, as it seems to Paul the Apostle, "the law is spiritual", then without doubt it is to be observed spiritually, and from it a spiritual reward of blessings is to be hoped for. For it is of the whole consequence that "the spiritual law" gives spiritual blessings, and it is nonetheless of the same consequence that also the curses and condemnations of "the spiritual law" are not bodily.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

But let us now see what is the opening of the blessings in Leviticus. "If", He says, "you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments and do them". There are three things which He says: "one must walk in the precepts, one must keep the commandments and do the things which are commanded". Whence it seems to me that a precept is, for instance, when it is enjoined that he who has not kept the sabbath "be stoned by the whole synagogue", or "he who has cursed God, that he be destroyed with stones", and any such things that are enjoined. But that commandments are those by which it is enjoined, for instance, that tithes be offered to the Levites, or "to appear before the Lord three times in the year", or "not to appear empty in the sight of the Lord". "To keep" therefore is "the commandment" to understand or to attend to the things which are enjoined; but "to do" is "the commandment" to fulfill the things which are enjoined. Thus therefore I think it is to be understood, what He said: "if you walk in my precepts, and keep my commandments and do them".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

But let us see what is the first blessing for those who have fulfilled the things which are commanded. "I will give", He says, "you rain in its season". Therefore let us first say to the Jews and to those who suppose these things are to be understood simply or bodily: if this "rain" is given as a reward for labors to those who "keep the commandments", how is it that also to those who do not keep the commandments one and the same "rain" is given in its seasons, and the whole world makes use of the common rains given by God? For "He rains upon the just and the unjust". But if "rain" is given "to the just and the unjust", it will not be an exceptional reward for those who have kept the commandments. See therefore that, even if the Jews do not acquiesce in the words of Jesus our Lord, yet you, who are reckoned by His name and are called a Christian, ought to believe Him when He says that His heavenly Father "rains" this common rain "upon the just and the unjust", and you ought not to think that He has set apart for "the just" an exceptional portion, this which He has appointed common even with "the unjust". Let us therefore seek in the Scriptures what is the "rain" which is given to the saints alone and concerning which "it is commanded to the clouds that they rain not this rain" upon the unjust. What then this "rain" is, Moses himself, the lawgiver of these things, teaches us. For he himself says in Deuteronomy: "Attend, O heaven, and I will speak, and let the earth hear the words from my mouth; let my utterance be awaited as rain". Are these my words? Do we by rhetorical arguments violently bend the sense of the divine law? Is it not Moses who says that what he speaks is "rain"? "Let my utterance", he says, "be awaited as rain, and let my words come down as dew, as a shower upon the grass, and as snow upon the hay". Attend diligently, O hearer, lest you think we do violence to the divine Scripture, when, teaching the church, we say that either waters or showers or other things which seem to be said bodily are to be understood spiritually. Hear Moses, how he now names the word of the law "rain", now calls it "dew", now "shower", now even says "snow". And just as Moses speaks various and diverse things, as though speaking out of the grace of the manifold wisdom of God, so also Isaiah, when he says: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken". But also each one of the prophets, when he has opened his mouth, brings down showers "upon the face of the earth", that is, upon the ears and hearts of the hearers. Knowing this, the Apostle Paul also said: "For the earth, drinking in the rain that comes often upon it and bearing herb fit for those by whom it is tilled, receives blessings from God; but that which brings forth thorns and thistles is reprobate and near to a curse, whose end is unto burning". Did the Apostle say these things about this earth? But neither does the earth receive blessings from God "when it has drunk in the showers" and produced fruit; nor, if after the rain "it has brought forth thorns and thistles", does it obtain curses from God. But our earth, that is, our heart, if it should receive "the rain that comes frequently upon it" of the doctrine of the law and should bring forth the fruit of works, receives blessings. But if it should have, not spiritual work, but "thorns and thistles", that is, the cares of the world, or the desires of pleasures and riches, it is "reprobate and near to a curse, whose end will be unto burning". Therefore each one of the hearers, when he comes together to hear, receives "the shower" of the word of God; and if indeed he has brought forth the fruit of a good work, he will obtain "blessing"; but if he has despised the word of God he has received, and has neglected what he has often heard, and has subjected himself to the care of worldly affairs and to lust, as one who has choked the word with "thorns", he will procure "a curse" instead of a blessing, and instead of the end of beatitude he will find "the end of burning". "I will give", therefore, He says, "you rain in season". Necessarily He added also "in season". For just as this earthly shower, if it come unseasonably, that is, when the harvest is being gathered, when the grain is threshed on the threshing-floors, will seem to hurt rather than to help, so also those to whom "the rain" of the word of God is committed to be ministered ought to observe this which the Scripture says, that they furnish it "in season", that is, that they not press the word of God upon one who is glutted and drunken, nor upon a mind occupied with other things, when it cannot be attentive, or when it is constricted by the languor of some vice, and the inner hearing is offered not to the teacher but to one's own disease. Prudently therefore let him conjecture where the mind can be at leisure, where the hearer is sober, where watchful, where attentive, and there let him minister "the rain in season"; so also "the faithful and prudent servant" in the Gospel is bidden "to give to his fellow-servants their measure of wheat in season". But in another way too we can understand this which is commanded, "the shower is to be given in season". Someone is a child and "a little one in the faith": he needs rain, but the "rain" of "milk"; for so says he who knew how to dispense "rains in season": "I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able". He has advanced after these things in the faith, "he has grown in age and wisdom": without doubt he has become fit to receive "more solid food". Someone is weak and, not according to the season but according to weakness, cannot receive the things that are robust; for instance, he cannot fully receive a discourse about chastity: one must have compassion and measure the doctrine according to the quality of his strength, and to such ones marriage is to be conceded. This is to feed "the weak one" with "vegetables" and to fit to measures of the soul of this kind, as it were, the thin "rain" of the word, like unto "dew". But there is another earth which can receive strong "showers", and even bear "rivers" of the word of God and carry rushing "torrents". For concerning such ones the prophet says in the Psalms: "and you will give them to drink of the torrent of your delight".

"I will give", therefore, He says, "you rain in its season, and the earth shall give its births". After the first blessing of rain, this is the second, in which it is said that "the earth", having received the rain, "gives its births". We find that Isaac also, blessing Jacob, says: "May the Lord give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth, an abundance of grain and wine". Do you suppose that Isaac was giving in blessing to his son Jacob such grain as sinful men also have, and with which even the impious Pharaoh abounded? Was this the blessing of so great a patriarch? Do you wish that I still show you how others also, the unjust, have a multitude of grain? Behold that man in the Gospel, whose "field brought forth many fruits, who says": "I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many goods laid up for many years; eat, drink, and be merry". Do we therefore believe such to be the goods which by divine blessings were handed over to the saints and to the faithful? Other fruits of the earth do I behold, and otherwise do I regard the multitude of "birth". For if my "earth" bring forth fruit, if it produce "its births" out of the Lord's blessing, my understanding will perceive and be able to explain what and of what kind is this "earth" which, having received the heavenly rain, brings forth the "births" of rational crops. Take a testimony from the Gospels, how "he who sows went out to sow, and some indeed fell along the way, but some upon the rock, some among thorns, but some upon the good earth". If therefore those things which "fell upon the good earth" have brought forth fruit, "the earth has given its fruit" and "its births", it has produced "a hundredfold and sixtyfold and thirtyfold".

"But also the trees", He says, "of the fields shall give their fruit". We have within our very selves also "the trees of the fields which produce their fruit". What are these "trees of the fields which produce their fruit"? Perhaps the hearer says: what is this word-hunter doing again? Why does he seek out words from everywhere, so as to escape the explanation of the reading? How will he teach that there are "trees" and shrubs within us? If you do not rashly disparage, you will now hear that: "a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit". We have therefore trees within us, whether good or bad; and those which are good "cannot bear bad fruits", just as those which are "bad bear not good fruits". Do you wish that I set forth for you also the terms and appellations of the very trees which are within us? It is not a fig or an apple or a vine, but one tree is called justice, another prudence, another fortitude, another is named temperance. And if you will, learn yet a greater multitude of trees, with which perhaps the paradise of God will be thought more worthily planted. For there is there a tree of piety, and there is another tree of wisdom, and there is another of discipline, and there is another "of the knowledge of good and evil". But above all is "the tree of life". Does it not seem to you rather that the heavenly "Father", "the husbandman", cultivates trees of this kind in your soul and establishes plantings of this kind in your mind? Thus therefore says the Savior: "a bad tree cannot bear good fruits, nor a good one bad fruits". This is what He teaches: the tree of chastity is "good", it cannot bear the fruits of unchastity; the tree of justice is "good" and cannot bear the fruits of injustice. So also, on the contrary, if you should have the root of "a bad tree" planted in your mind, it cannot render "good fruits". For if there be in you a root of malice, it will not give "good fruits"; if there be within your heart a plant of folly, it will never bring forth the flower of wisdom; if it be a tree of injustice, if of iniquity, never can such trees rejoice in "good fruits". If therefore we keep the commandments of God, having received "the rain" of the word of God, of which we spoke above, the trees also which are planted in the fields of our soul and in the breadth of our heart will bring forth glad fruit of good sweetness. But do you wish that I show you from the Scriptures that these several virtues, which we mentioned above, are called trees or shrubs? I bring forward as witness the most wise Solomon, saying concerning wisdom: "it is a tree of life", he says, "to all who embrace it". If therefore "wisdom is a tree of life", without doubt there is also another tree of prudence, and another of knowledge, and another of justice. For it is not consequently said that of all the virtues wisdom alone deserved to be called "a tree of life", but that the other virtues by no means received the appellations of a like lot. "The trees", therefore, "of the field shall give their fruit". This, I believe, blessed David also felt concerning himself, when he said: "but I am like a fruitful olive in the house of God". From which he manifestly shows that a just and holy man is called a tree of olive.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"And the threshing shall reach for you unto the vintage". If good seed has been sown in my soul and, having received "rain" from God, it has grown and come to the ear, of necessity the harvest also will follow; and if the harvest, then also "threshing" will follow, in which the grains are cleansed. For indeed the soul which germinates from the word of God and, watered by the heavenly "rain", produces its sprout unto harvest, it is necessary that the very harvest which it brings forth be cleansed on the floor, that is, that the meanings which the soul has begotten it bring forth into the midst, and confer them—the things which it perceives—either with the other teachers or even with the divine volumes themselves; so that, if there be anything in them empty and superfluous, if there be anything like chaff or awns, it may shake it out with the spirit of discernment blowing within it, and retain the pure grain, by which alone it can nourish its fellow-servants and "dispense the measure of wheat in season". "And there shall reach", He says, "for you the threshing unto the vintage". Since "bread", as the Scripture says, "strengthens the heart of man, and wine gladdens it", whatever things are said concerning continence, concerning observances and the keeping of the commandments, these can be seen as grain, out of which "bread" is made and "strengthens the hearts" of the hearers. But those things which pertain to knowledge and by the explanation of hidden things "gladden" the minds of the hearers will seem to be fitted to "wine" and the vintage. For gladness is bestowed on the heart when the things that are hidden and obscure are explained. — "And the vintage", He says, "shall reach unto the sowing". As if we should say: first I sowed the things which are of the law and, after the sowing was done, I prayed that "the Lord would give rain in season": the harvest was made. After this I do not remain idle, but again I sow; I take the prophetic Scripture and from it I sow the lands and the fallow-grounds of the hearers. After these things I sow also other things from the evangelical discourses. Diverse are the things that are sown; through the whole year we can sow; for we can also cast many seeds from the apostolic writings. There is always something to be sown; in the whole of our life there is no time of idleness. As long as we breathe, let us sow; only let it be that "we sow in the spirit, that of the spirit we may reap eternal life". — "And you shall eat your bread in fullness". Neither do I take this to be of bodily blessing, as though he who keeps the law of God obtains this common bread in abundance. For what? Do not the impious and the wicked eat bread not only in abundance, but even in delicacies? Rather therefore, if we look to Him who said: "I am the living bread, who came down from heaven; and he who eats this bread shall live forever", and if we advert that He who said these things was "the word" by which souls are fed, we understand of what bread it was said in the blessings from God: "and you shall eat your bread in fullness". Things similar to these Solomon also pronounces in the Proverbs, saying concerning the just man: "the just man eating shall fill his soul; but the souls of the impious shall be in want". If you take this according to the letter, that "the just man eating shall fill his soul, but the souls of the impious shall be in want", it will seem false. For rather the souls of the impious take food with avidity and are eager for "fullness"; but the just at times even hunger. In fine, Paul was just and said: "even unto this hour we both hunger and thirst and are naked and are buffeted". And again he says: "in hunger and thirst, in many fastings". And how does Solomon say that "the just man eating shall satisfy his soul"? But if you consider how "the just man" always and "without intermission" eats of "the living bread" and fills his soul and satisfies it with the heavenly food, which is the word of God and His wisdom, you will find how out of the blessing of God the just man "eats his bread in fullness". — "And you shall dwell secure upon your land". The unjust is never inwardly, but is always moved and "tossed and carried about with every wind of doctrine, in the deceit of men, unto the deception of error". But the just man, who keeps the law of God, "dwells secure upon his land". For firm is the understanding of him who says to God: "confirm me, O Lord, in your words". "Confirmed" therefore and "secure" and "rooted" he "dwells upon the land", "founded in the faith", because "his building is not set upon the sand" nor is his root "upon the rock", but "his house" indeed "is founded" upon the land, but his plant is rooted "in the depth of the land", that is, in the inmost parts of his soul.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

Rightly therefore to a soul of this kind it is said in the blessings: "and you shall dwell secure upon your land; and I will give peace upon your land". What "peace does" God "give"? That which the world has? Christ denies that He gives this. For He says: "my peace I give to you, my peace I leave to you; not as this world gives peace, do I also give to you". He denies therefore that He gives "the peace of the world" to His disciples, because elsewhere too He says: "do you think that I came to send peace on the earth? I came not to send peace, but a sword". Do you wish then to see what "peace God gives upon our land"? If the land be that "good" one which "bears fruit a hundredfold or sixtyfold or thirtyfold", it will receive from God that "peace" which the Apostle speaks of: "but the peace of God, which surpasses every mind, shall guard your hearts and your understandings". This then is the "peace" which "God gives upon our land".

"And you shall sleep and there shall be none to terrify you". Solomon too in the Proverbs said: "for if you sit, you shall be without fear; and if you sleep, you shall gladly take sleep; and you shall not fear the terror coming upon you, nor the assaults of the impious coming upon you". These things he said concerning the just and wise man, and these things are said in the blessing: "you shall sleep, and there shall be none to terrify you". For if I become just, no one can terrify me; I fear nothing else, if I fear God; for "the just man", he says, "is confident as a lion", and therefore he does not fear the lion, the devil, nor "the dragon", Satan, nor "his angels", but says according to David: "I will not fear the nocturnal terror, the arrow flying by day, and the business walking in the darkness, the ruin and the noonday demon". He adds also this: "The Lord is my illumination and my Savior, whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life, of whom shall I tremble?". And again: "if camps stand against me, my heart shall not fear". You see the constancy and virtue of the soul that keeps the commandments of God and has the confidence of an inborn liberty. After these things, "and I will exterminate", He says, "the evil beasts from your land". Those bodily beasts are neither evil nor good, but something in between; for they are dumb animals. But those evil beasts are spiritual, which the Apostle calls "spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places". And that is the evil beast of which the Scripture says: "but the serpent was wiser than all the beasts that are upon the earth". This itself, then, is that "evil beast" which God promises "He will exterminate from our land", if we keep His commandments. Do you wish to see also another evil beast? "Your adversary", he says, "the devil, as a roaring lion goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in the faith". But if you wish to learn yet more beasts, the prophet Isaiah will teach you, who, under "the vision" which he entitled "of the quadrupeds in the desert", speaks by the prophetic spirit certain such things concerning beasts: "in tribulation", he says, "and anguish, the lion and the lion's whelp; thence also the offspring of flying asps, who carried upon asses and camels their riches to a nation which shall not profit them". Can these things in any way be seen as said of bodily beasts, even by those who are exceedingly friends of the letter? For how can "the lion and the lion's whelp" or "the flying asps" "carry upon camels and asses their riches"? But evidently the prophet, filled with the Holy Spirit, enumerates the contrary powers of the most wicked demons, and designated that they place "the riches" of their deceptions upon souls stolid and perverse, which by a figure he compares to camels and asses. And that his soul might not be handed over to these beasts, fearing God he prayed, saying: "deliver not to the beasts the soul that confesses to you". — "And I will exterminate", He says, "the malignant beasts from your land, and war shall not pass through your land". Many are the "wars" which "pass through our land", if we do not keep the law of God nor observe His precepts. Let each one return to his own soul and shake himself out by inner recollection, and see how our land, that is, our flesh, is now pressed by the spirit of fornication, now by that of anger and fury, now is agitated by the darts of avarice, now is struck by the weapons of envy, now is bored through by the arrows of lust, and in whatever ways "the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh", it is always agitated by inner battles. But what shall I say of the wars of thoughts, which the enemy suggests to our heart, that he may strip us of the faith of Christ and of the hope of our calling? For when he has stirred up for us the afflictions of temptations and the troubles of the world, consequently he then suggests to the thought that it is superfluous and foolish to endure these things for Christ, that it is much better to lead a secure life and without persecutions. Knowing this, the Apostle Paul too said: "destroying thoughts and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of Christ". He therefore who "keeps the divine precepts and keeps His commandments and does them", does not suffer this war and these battles, but God takes them away "from" his "land" and does not permit them "to pass" through the soul of the just.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"And you shall pursue your enemies". What "enemies", except "the devil" himself "and his angels" and the malignant spirits and "the unclean demons"? We shall pursue them not only that we may drive them away from ourselves, but also from others whom they assail, if we keep the divine precepts. "You shall pursue", He says, "your enemies, and they shall fall before you by death". If "God should crush Satan under our feet swiftly", "the enemies shall fall before us by death". By whose "death"? I think, by ours; for if we "mortify our members, which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness", if we inflict this death upon our members, "they shall fall before us". How "shall they fall before us"? If you be just, injustice has fallen "before" you; if you be chaste, lust has fallen; if you be pious, impiety has collapsed before you.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"And five of you shall pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you shall pursue many thousands". Who are those "five" who can "pursue a hundred"? The number "five" is set both among the praiseworthy and among the culpable. There are "five wise virgins" and "five foolish". So therefore also the number of a hundred can be taken to either part. If then we be of the five praiseworthy, that is, of the five wise, we shall pursue a hundred foolish. For if we fight wisely and provably in the word of God, if we discourse prudently concerning the law of the Lord, we shall convince and put to flight a multitude of the unfaithful. For just as the number five indicates both the wise and the foolish, so also the number of a hundred indicates both the faithful and the unfaithful. For under the number of a hundred years Abraham is described as having believed God and been justified, and "the sinner who dies at a hundred years shall be accursed". And here a "hundred" unfaithful are put to flight by "five" wise, and again a "hundred" faithful, marked not so much by the number of a hundred as by perfection, "shall pursue many thousands" of the unfaithful. For the faithful teachers put to flight innumerable demons, lest by the ancient fraud they deceive the souls of believers. — "And your enemies shall fall before you by the sword". Who the "enemies" are, we said above; but by what "sword" they are said "to fall", let us inquire. The Apostle Paul teaches us what this sword is, when he says: "for the word of God is living and effective and more penetrating than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the joint of soul and spirit, of the members also and the marrows, and is a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart". This is the "sword" by whose edge "our enemies shall fall". For it is the word of God which lays low "all enemies" and puts them "under His feet", "that the whole world may be made subject to God". Do you wish to learn still from another epistle of Paul that the sword is the word of God? Hear him, when he prepares arms for the soldiers of Christ, how he says: "and take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, through all prayer and supplication", most evidently pronouncing also through these things that by "the word of God", which is "the two-edged sword", "our enemies shall fall before us".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"And I will look upon you and increase you". Full of beatitude is this very thing, if "God look upon" anyone. Do you wish to see, if "the Lord look upon" a man, how great is salvation? Peter had once almost perished and, by the devil breathing through the mouth of "the maidservant of the high priest", had been snatched from the consecration of the apostolic number; but when "Jesus only looked upon him", when He turned toward him the countenance of a placid face, at once, returning into himself and recalling his foot slipped from the precipice, "he wept", it says, "most bitterly", and thus, looked upon by God, by weeping he recovered his place, which by denying he had lost. — "I will look", therefore, He says, "upon you, and increase you". As if the sun should look upon a crop and bring forth its fruits—which surely, if it had not looked upon it, would have remained fruitless—so God, "looking upon" the crop of our heart and illuminating us with the rays of His word, "increases us" and multiplies us, that we may no longer be "little ones", but be made "great", just as "Isaac was made great", and Moses was made "great", and John "great". — "And I will establish my covenant with you". See how great blessings are promised, if we keep the commandments.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 10.15

For we eat with blessing the old things, the prophetic words and the old things of the old things, the words of the law. And, when the new and evangelical words came, living according to the gospel, we bring forth the old things of the letter from before the new. He sets his tabernacle in us, fulfilling the promise which he spoke, "I will dwell among them and walk in them."
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"I will establish", He says, "my covenant with you. And you shall eat the old things and the old of the old, and you shall cast out the old from before the face of the new". How do we "cast out the old from before the face of the new"? "The old" things: "we had the law and the prophets"; but "the old of the old" are those things which were before the law, from the beginning, when the world was made. There came the new Gospels, there came also the Apostles. From before the face of these we cast out "the old things". How do we cast them out? We cast out the law according to the letter, that we may establish the law according to the spirit. We can also say in this manner: before the man came "from heaven" and the "heavenly man" was born, we were all "earthly" and "bore the image of the earthly"; but when there came "the new man, who was created according to God", we cast out "from before the face" of him "the old things", "putting off the old man and putting on the new", "who according to the interior man is renewed from day to day".
On Cain and Abel 2.6.19

For just as the teachings of the new and old Testaments should come together, as it is written: "Consume the old things of the ancients, and remove the old things from the face of the new ones." Let the knowledge of the patriarchs be food for us, let the soul feast on the oracles of the prophets: let the inner being be nourished by such sustenance. But now let it not be the appearance of a lamb, but rather the reality of the body of Christ. Let it not be the shadow of the law that blinds the eyes, but rather let the grace of the Lord's passion openly reveal, and let the splendor of the resurrection illuminate the mind's sight.
On the Tabernacle 1.9

And we eat the oldest of the old [grain] when we retain in our hearts the sweet memory of the old commandment which was given to the human race from the beginning, by loving the Lord our God with all our heart, all our soul and all our strength, and by loving our neighbor as ourselves. And we cast away the old [to make room] for the new that is coming on when we cease to keep the typic statutes of the Mosaic law according to the letter but keep these same statutes quite gladly as they are understood through the Spirit. Our hearts [are] being renewed in the hope of the heavenly kingdom in accordance with that [saying] of the apostle: "If then anyone is in Christ a new creature, the old things have passed away; behold, things have been made new," and [with that saying] in the Apocalypse: "And he that sat upon the throne said, 'Behold, I make all things new.'"
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"And I will set my tabernacle among you". If we have these things in us which were said above, if, the "old man" having been cast off, our heart has been renewed, God comes to us and dwells in us, He who said: "and I will set my tabernacle among you, and my soul shall not abominate you". "The soul of God" will not "abominate" us, if we observe the things which are written. Yet I should wish to inquire what is "the soul of God". Shall we perhaps suppose that God has a soul as a man has? It is absurd to think this of God. But I dare and say that the soul of God is Christ. For just as Christ is "the Word" of God and "the wisdom of God and the power of God", so also He is the soul of God. And in this manner it is said: "my soul shall not abominate you", that is, my Son, but "I will walk among you".
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

It does not seem to me that God promises this, that He will walk in the land of the Jews, but that, if anyone should deserve to be of so pure a heart as to be capable of God, in him God says that He "walks". — "And you shall be to me a people".
City of God 22.30

God will be the source of every satisfaction, more than any heart can rightly crave, more than life and health, food and wealth, glory and honor, peace and every good—so that God, as St. Paul said, "may be all in all." He will be the consummation of all our desiring—the object of our unending vision, of our unlessening love, of our unwearying praise. And in this gift of vision, this response of love, this paean of praise, all alike will share, as all will share in everlasting life.
HOMILIES ON LEVITICUS 16

"I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, when you were servants, and broke the yoke of your bond". Truly "He brought us out of the house of servitude", for "we were servants" of sin, because: "everyone who sins is a servant of sin". And "He broke the bond of our yoke, the yoke" which he had imposed upon our necks who had "led us into captivity" and bound us with the bonds of sins. "He broke", therefore, the "bond" of sin and shook off the "yoke" of our captivity, our Lord Jesus Christ, and imposed upon us His own sweet yoke of faith and charity and hope and of all sanctity. To Him be glory unto the eternal ages of ages! Amen.

n: Estimation. Hebrew is obscure, "Whoever has separated, or made a singular vow; the souls to the Lord according to thy estimation." (Calmet) --- Septuagint, "shall vow as it were the price of a soul to the Lord." (Haydock) --- The person or the beast shall belong to the Lord; but if it be redeemed, the priests shall fix a price, according to the following regulations. Whatever was vowed must be subject to these rules, or it shall remain for the service of the altar. The priests may sell it, if it be an impure animal. Those which were fit for sacrifice, were to be immolated, ver. 9, &c. No change of them was allowed, lest a worse should ever be substituted for a better; (Calmet) and because God is better pleased with things that are offered to him by vow. (Worthington)
Fifth. The parents might make a vow of their children. (Menochius)
The estimation. Hebrew is pointed improperly, "thy estimation;" for the price was fixed already. The priest had leave to reduce it only in favour of the poor. (Houbigant) See ver. 2, and following.

That offereth it. This addition of the Vulgate shews, that if any other purchased the animal, he would not have to give a fifth part more than the value. That only concerned the person who had made the vow, to punish him for his inconstancy, and that he might not have a desire to get possession again of what he had once consecrated to the Lord. If the beast was valued at 40 sicles, he would therefore have to pay 50. (Calmet)

House. The Rabbins say this fifth part went towards repairing the temple. We may suppose it was laid on to indemnify the priests, for the loss which they sustained by selling a house, or a field, (ver. 16,) to the former owner; since if any other had purchased them, the priests would have been able to sell them again at the return of every jubilee. At that period, even the former proprietor would not obtain a title to possess them for ever; (ver. 21,) and therefore he would not need to pay any more than the stated value. (Tostat) (Calmet)

Possession, or inheritance. If he had only purchased the field, he could not, by his vow, transfer the property of it to the priests beyond the year of jubilee, ver. 22. --- Seed, not of the produce, which is uncertain. The goodness of the soil must also be considered. --- Silver: which rent must be paid every year, except on those of rest, when the earth was not cultivated. (Calmet)

Consecrated. Hebrew, "a field of anathema," devoted and separated from common uses for ever to the Lord. (Haydock) --- Priests. They were bound to sell it from one jubilee to another to some of the same tribe, to which the person, who vowed it, had belonged. (Menochius) --- In the new law, religious people often consecrate themselves and their effects to the service of God; and it would be a sacrilege to alienate them from such pious uses to any thing profane. They are anathéma, a deposit of offering to the Lord; while those who violate them, are anathema, accursed. (Haydock) (Tirinus)
Obols. Hebrew, "gerah." which were worth 1d.-2687; so that a sicle amounts to 2s. 3d.-375. (Arbuthnot.)

First-born. Septuagint add "of beasts." Men, though belonging to the Lord on that title already, (Exodus xiii. 2,) might still be more particularly consecrated to him by vow, as Samuel was. (Calmet) --- A vow must be concerning some greater good to which we are not otherwise bound. Such vows are agreeable to God, and can never be broken without sin. See Genesis xxxi. 13 and 1 Timothy v. 12. (Worthington)

Unclean, either on account of some blemish, or because it is of those species which cannot be sacrificed; such as the horse, camel, &c., which might nevertheless be vowed to the Lord, and sold for the benefit of his priests. --- By thee. Moses and the succeeding priests. Many manuscripts read, with the Septuagint and Chaldean, "by him," leaving the matter to the person's conscience; but the printed Hebrew and Vulgate agree. (Calmet)

Devoted. Hebrew, "anathema," different from the other vows. In this case all that had life was slain, (or consecrated to God; Haydock) houses were demolished, the land belonged to the priests for ever, so that they could only let it out to laymen for a certain rent. Moses thus devoted the Amalecites to destruction; (Exodus xvii. 14) and Saul had orders to put in execution what he had denounced, 1 Kings xv. It is doubtful whether people could thus devote their children and slaves. Most authors suppose, that it was necessary that God or the nation at large should pronounce such a sentence, as was done with respect to Achan, Josue viii. See Numbers xxi. 2 and Judges xi. 31. (Calmet)
Die. Grotius says, only public enemies and deserters could be thus devoted. Other men and women were only consecrated for ever to the divine service. (Du Hamel)

Tithes. Abraham and Jacob paid tithes, out of devotion, Genesis xiv. and xxviii. 22. Moses first made a law on this subject, which began to be in force when the Hebrews had obtained quiet possession of Chanaan. The people paid them more exactly when they were determined to keep God's law, and had pious princes at their head, 2 Paralipomenon xxxi. 5. At other times they were very negligent, Malachias iii. 10. This forced Esdras to appoint inspectors, Namnim, to collect them. The Pharisees affected a degree of exactitude in this respect, (Luke xi. 42 and Matthew xxiii. 23,) paying what some Jews do not suppose to be necessary, though our Saviour says it was. Since the destruction of the temple the Jews pay none. The first-fruits and tithes of wheat, barley, figs, raisins, olives, pomegranates, and dates, were required, though it be not certain what quantity of the first-fruits was given; some say between the 40th and the 60th part of the produce. Wine and wool were also to be offered. The tithes were taken after the first-fruits and the heaved oblations (thorume) were paid. They belonged to the Levites, and these gave a tithe to the priests, Numbers xviii. 28. See chap. xix. 24. The Eastern kings required a tithe of their subjects, for the support of their families, 1 Kings viii. 15. God does the like, Malachias iii. 10. The Persians, Carthaginians, Greeks, Romans, and even the Arabs and Scythians, religiously paid their tithes in honour of their false gods. See Cyrop. iv. and Q. Curtius iv. 2.; Herodotus ii. 135.; Pliny, [Natural History?] xii. 14.; Mela. ii. 5, &c. The Romans often consecrate the tithes of their spoils to Hercules, as the Carthaginians did also. The Scythians sent them to Apollo. (Solin 27, &c.) (Calmet) --- Scaliger and Amama dispose the tithes, and the oblations of the Hebrews, in the following order. Supposing a person's annual produce amount to 6000 bushels, an oblation (thorume) of at least 100 was to be made to the priests: out of the remaining 5900, a first tithe of 590 belonged to the Levites, out of which they paid 59 to the priests. The residue, of 5310 bushels, paid a second tithe of 531, to be consumed in feasts in the temple, (a custom which the ancient Christians imitated in their love-feasts, called agape; Calmet) The original produce was thus reduced to 4779 bushels; and both the tithes amounted to 1121 and the oblation to 100. The thorume consisted of flour dressed, and of oil, wine (Amama) and wool, (Calmet) to be given to the priests on the feast of Pentecost, chap. xxiii. 15. It could not be less than the 60th part of the produce, (Ezechiel xlv. 13.) and it was necessary to pay it before any could be used in the family. Hence these oblations are often called first-fruits, and have been confounded with those sheaves which were to be offered at the beginning of harvest. (Amama)

Of them. When the distance from Jerusalem was great, so that a person judged it more convenient to sell his tithes, and with the money purchase more for a feast in Jerusalem, (which the Rabbins call Zudui, Charisterion, grace or thanksgiving) he had to pay something additional, 12, for example, instead of 10. (Scaliger)

Rod; on which was some red colouring, to mark the tenth animal as it passed through a narrow gate. If it was proper for sacrifice, its blood was poured out around the altar, and its flesh was returned to the giver. If it could not be offered in sacrifice, it was slain. The priest received none of the victim, no more than the paschal lamb. (Outram, sac. i. 11.) But a feast was made of flesh for the person's friends, and he gave a portion to the poor and to the Levites. --- The Lord, as a sacrifice of thanksgiving, in which the greatest part of the victim is consumed by the person who offers it. The priests have but a small share, chap. iii. (Calmet)
Sinai. The laws specified in the ten first chapters of the following book, were given here also. (Haydock)

f: Homily 40 (Forty Gospel Homilies)

For whatever is said through the law is less than what is commanded through the Lord. For the law commands that tithes be given, but our Redeemer commands that everything be given up by those who follow perfection.

intro: < Previous Chapter ----- Next Chapter > THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS. INTRODUCTION. This Book is called Leviticus: because it treats of the offices, ministries, rites and ceremonies of the Priests and Levites. The Hebrews call it Vayyicra, from the word with which it begins; (Challoner) "and (the Lord) called." The a at the end of this word is printed in a smaller size, to insinuate that little children should begin to read this Book first, if we may give any credit to those who attempt to account for all the irregularities sanctioned by the great Massora! But such irregular letters are the faults of some transcribers, and are of no authority. (Kennicott, Dis. 1.) --- This Book is styled also, "The Priests' Law." (Haydock) --- The seven first chapters explain the sacrifices; the sixteen next, the offices and ordination of the Priests and Levites. From the 23d chapter to the end, the feasts are designated, and some regulations respecting vows are interspersed. All these rites and sacrifices foreshewed the eucharistic sacrifice of Jesus Christ, (St. Leo, ser. 8. de pas. Trid. sef. 22. c. 1.) and tended to keep the Hebrews employed, and at a greater distance from idolatry. (St. Jerome on Isai. i. &c.) --- These prescriptions were given during the month of Nisan, in the second year after the exit, while the Hebrews remained at the foot of Mount Sinai. God spoke from the New Tabernacle. (Tirinus) --- In the Book of Deuteronomy we find but few regulations respecting sacrifices, as Moses had sufficiently explained them in this book. (Du Hamel) --- If we confine ourselves to the letter, we may say these precepts are not good, and carnal; (Ezechiel xx. 25.; Hebrews vii. 16.) but if we consider the spirit, we shall confess that they are excellent, and spiritual. (Romans vii. 14.; 2 Corinthians iii. 6.; Origen, contra Cels. vii.) (Calmet)
